His research extends to multi-modal systems like Pixtral 12B and the Open Catalyst 2020 dataset for renewable energy storage. Lavril’s previous work includes developing keyword spotting systems and voice platforms for embedded devices.

researcher.name: Thomas Chabal
researcher.headline: AI Scientist, Robotics @ Mistral AI, Previously PhD Student @ Inria
researcher.bio: Thomas Chabal's Ministral 3 provides a family of small language models optimized for edge computing and low-latency applications. Currently a researcher at Mistral AI, they focus on the intersection of CV and robotics. Chabal developed Recursive Implicit Maps to build spatial representations for autonomous robotic pathfinding. Their research also includes Voxtral realtime and Voxtral tts for efficient audio and speech processing. Recently, Chabal introduced Robostral Navigate to integrate vision-language capabilities into robotic navigation tasks. They earned a PhD from Ecole normale superieure, where they studied object-centric representations for robotic sensing and planning.

researcher.name: Thomas ROBERT
researcher.headline: Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously R&D Team Lead & Deep Learning Research Engineer @ Heuritech
researcher.bio: Thomas ROBERT’s Magistral optimizes inference efficiency for LLMs. They work in Science at Mistral AI, specializing in efficient ML. Robert also co-developed Ministral 3, a series of LLMs focused on compute-efficient performance. To improve training, they authored Microadam for memory-efficient adaptive optimization with provable convergence and LDAdam for optimization using low-dimensional gradient statistics. Robert has also worked on Devstral for coding agent fine-tuning and the Voxtral series for speech and voice applications.

researcher.name: Thomas Wang
researcher.headline: Research Engineer @ Mistral.ai, Previously Researcher @ Hugging Face
researcher.bio: Thomas Wang co-authored Mixtral of experts, a sparse mixture-of-experts model that routes tokens to specific parameter subsets to improve inference efficiency. They are a Research Engineer at Mistral.ai, where they focus on deep learning and the development of LLMs. Wang previously contributed to Mistral 7B, a model that utilizes grouped-query attention and sliding window attention for efficient computation. Before joining Mistral.ai, they were a Researcher at Hugging Face and collaborated on the creation of Bloom, a large-scale open-access multilingual model. Their work also includes Starcoder, a model designed for code generation, and Obelics, a dataset of interleaved image-text documents for multimodal training. They have additional experience as a researcher at INRIA and a machine learning engineer at Nabla. Wang earned an MSc in ML from École Normale Supérieure Paris-Saclay and an MSc from École Polytechnique.

topAffiliation.description: Works on large language models.

researcher.name: Tim Lawson
researcher.affiliation: AI Scientist, Mistral AI; PhD student, University of Bristol
researcher.headline: AI Scientist @ Mistral AI, PhD Student @ University of Bristol
researcher.bio: Tim Lawson co-developed Ministral 3, a family of language models released by Mistral AI. Lawson is an AI Scientist at Mistral AI and a PhD student at the University of Bristol. Their research focuses on LLM interpretability and transformer efficiency. In Automated Interpretability Metrics, Lawson demonstrates that sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents appear interpretable even in randomized models because of inherent token embedding sparsity. They also introduced Jacobian Sparse Autoencoders to sparsify computations between model components and analyzed the residual stream using multi-layer SAEs to track latent activations across layers. Lawson holds a Physics MSci from the University of Cambridge and has experience in data analytics software.

topAffiliation.description: Working on language models.

researcher.name: Timothée Lacroix
researcher.headline: Co-Founder & CTO @ Mistral AI, Previously Research Engineer @ Facebook
researcher.bio: Timothée Lacroix co-created Llama, a family of foundation LLMs released for open-source use. Lacroix is currently the Co-Founder and CTO of Mistral AI. At Mistral, they developed Mistral 7B and Mixtral of experts, a model that employs a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture. They also worked on Pixtral 12B, a multimodal model for image and text processing. Prior to Mistral, Lacroix was a Research Engineer at Meta AI, where they focused on foundation model development. They earned a PhD from École des Ponts ParisTech, where they researched ML methods for tensor completion and knowledge bases. This work included creating PyTorch-BigGraph for large-scale graph embeddings and Canonical Tensor Decomposition for relational data.

researcher.name: Tom Bewley
researcher.headline: AI Safety Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously Research Scientist @ J.P. Morgan Explainable AI Center of Excellence
researcher.bio: Tom Bewley co-authored Ministral 3, a family of compact language models optimized for edge-device performance. They are an AI Safety Scientist at Mistral AI, where they focus on post-training, evaluations, and guardrails. Their broader research spans RL, AI alignment, and interpretability, including the development of Voxtral and the TripleTree representation for explaining black-box agents. Bewley also investigates mechanistic error reduction in To Steer or Not to Steer? to improve LLM reliability through abstention. Previously, they researched explainable AI at J.P. Morgan and completed a PhD at the University of Bristol and the Alan Turing Institute. Their work frequently applies tree-structured reward functions and imitation learning to create interpretable agent policies.

topAffiliation.description: Works on post-training, evals and guardrails.

researcher.name: Vedant Nanda
researcher.headline: AI Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously AI Researcher @ Aleph Alpha Research
researcher.bio: Vedant Nanda co-authored Fairness through robustness, which identifies the link between adversarial robustness and demographic disparity in deep learning. Now an AI Scientist at Mistral AI, Nanda focuses on building efficient foundation models and developing inference-friendly pretraining strategies. Their recent work includes Voxtral, a framework for real-time speech and text-to-speech synthesis, and Lawma, which adapts LLMs for specialized legal tasks. They previously worked as a researcher at Aleph Alpha, where they focused on inference optimizations and tokenizer-free model architectures. Nanda’s broader research explores trustworthy ML, including studies on diffused redundancy in representations and the long-term impact of algorithmic decision policies. They earned a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Maryland as part of the Maryland-Max Planck joint program.

topAffiliation.description: Research on efficient language models and inference-friendly pretraining.

researcher.name: Victor Jouault
researcher.headline: Research Scientist @ Mistral AI
researcher.bio: Victor Jouault’s Ministral 3 provides a family of efficient LLMs designed for edge device deployment and on-device performance. They are a researcher at Mistral AI, focusing on the development of compact language and multimodal models. Jouault also co-authored Voxtral realtime, which facilitates low-latency speech processing. Their research includes Voxtral tts, a system for generating high-fidelity audio from text. These works emphasize the creation of performant models that operate within resource-constrained environments. Jouault’s contributions at Mistral AI span LLM optimization and real-time audio synthesis.

researcher.name: Virgile Richard
researcher.headline: Researcher @ Mistral AI
researcher.bio: Virgile Richard’s Magistral enables high-performance reasoning within large-scale language model architectures. Richard is a researcher at Mistral AI where they develop LLMs and multimodal systems. They also co-developed Ministral 3, an efficient language model optimized for on-device and edge deployment. In the domain of audio AI, Richard’s research includes the Voxtral series, which encompasses speech-to-speech models and low-latency variants such as Voxtral realtime and Voxtral tts. They also authored Devstral, a framework for fine-tuning language models to support coding agent applications.

topAffiliation.description: Contributed to Magistral, Mistral's reasoning model and scalable reinforcement-learning pipeline.

researcher.name: Wassim (Wes) Bouaziz
researcher.headline: AI Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously AI PhD Student @ École polytechnique
researcher.bio: Wassim Bouaziz co-authored Llama 3, developing safety protocols to mitigate risks associated with model tool misuse. They are an AI Scientist on the Safety team at Mistral AI, focusing on AI security and alignment. Their research examines how training data can verify dataset ownership through methods like Data taggants or expose integrity risks through indirect data poisoning. Bouaziz also produced Ministral 3 and Iteration head, a mechanistic study of chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs. They completed a PhD at École polytechnique and Meta (FAIR) following studies in ML and CV at ENS Paris-Saclay.

topAffiliation.description: Member of the Safety team; worked on Llama 3 tool use safety and data poisoning as a security measure.

researcher.name: Wen-Ding Li
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ Cornell University, Previously EE MSc Student @ National Taiwan University
researcher.bio: Wen-Ding Li’s LiveCodeBench provides a contamination-free framework for evaluating LLM coding performance through time-gated competitive programming problems. He is at Cornell University researching ML and program synthesis. Li co-developed StarCoder 2 and The Stack v2 to improve open-source code generation models and their training datasets. His research on BigCodeBench assesses how models handle complex instructions and diverse function calls in programming tasks. He contributed to Humanity's Last Exam, which benchmarks LLMs on expert-level reasoning across scientific and technical domains. Li also created M1 to explore scalable test-time compute using Mamba-based reasoning architectures. His further work includes the Mmteb benchmark for multilingual text embeddings and studies on LLM synthetic data quality.

topAffiliation.description: Works with Kevin Ellis on machine learning for code generation and reasoning tasks.

researcher.name: Xinghui Li
researcher.headline: AI Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously CV PhD Student @ University of Oxford
researcher.bio: Xinghui Li’s When llms step into the 3d world provides a meta-analysis of how multimodal LLMs process, understand, and generate 3D data. He is an AI Scientist at Mistral AI in London. His research focuses on 3D CV, generative models, and multimodal LLMs, including the development of GaussCtrl for text-driven editing of 3D Gaussian splats. Li also created Dual-resolution correspondence networks, which applies neighborhood consensus filtering to high-resolution images for visual matching. At Mistral AI, he contributed to the development of the Ministral 3 model family. He previously researched camera pose regression with DFNet and benchmarking egocentric vision with the Oxford Day-and-Night Dataset. Li earned his PhD and undergraduate degrees from the University of Oxford.

topAffiliation.description: Developing multimodal LLM.

researcher.name: Xuanyu Zhang
researcher.headline: Researcher @ Mistral AI
researcher.bio: Xuanyu Zhang’s Magistral is an LLM architecture designed for improved model performance. Currently a researcher at Mistral AI, Zhang focuses on ML and AI development. They also created Voxtral and Devstral, which fine-tunes LLMs for coding agent applications. Zhang authored Recurrent Drafter, a method for fast speculative decoding in LLMs using a recurrent architecture. Their research focuses on the design and optimization of LLM systems.

researcher.name: Yassine EL OUAHIDI
researcher.headline: AI Applied Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously AI PhD Student @ IMT Atlantique
researcher.bio: Yassine EL OUAHIDI developed Ministral 3, a model series designed for efficient local inference and high-performance language tasks. Currently an AI researcher at Mistral AI, they focus on scaling foundation models across language and biological data. EL OUAHIDI created REVE, an EEG foundation model pretrained on 25,000 subjects that adapts to various sensor configurations for neural decoding. They also authored the Voxtral series for realtime speech processing and text-to-speech. Their prior work at IMT Atlantique established deep learning baselines for brain-computer interface motor imagery tasks and graph-based fMRI analysis. Additionally, they have applied ML to clinical medicine to predict pacemaker implantations and cardiac patient outcomes.

researcher.name: Yassir Bendou
researcher.headline: Researcher @ Sigma Nova, Previously Applied Scientist @ Mistral AI
researcher.bio: Yassir Bendou's Voxtral tts synthesizes speech from text inputs. They are a researcher at Mistral AI focusing on ML, deep learning, and statistics. Bendou also developed Voxtral realtime for low-latency audio and ProKeR, which applies a kernel perspective to adapt large vision-language models. Their earlier work includes EASY, a few-shot classification method utilizing ensemble components and data augmentation. They have further researched Wasserstein barycenters through gradient flows and statistical models for predicting generalization. Bendou was previously affiliated with Ecole nationale supérieure Mines-Télécom Atlantique.

topAffiliation.description: Research on scalable and regularized barycenter computation and Bayesian prompt learning.

researcher.name: Yimu Pan
researcher.headline: Applied Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously Informatics PhD Student @ Penn State University
researcher.bio: Yimu Pan’s EmotionCLIP extracts emotion representations from video and text using cross-modal contrastive learning. Pan is an Applied Scientist at Mistral AI, focusing on CV, multimodal models, and LLM post-training. At Mistral AI, they have worked on Voxtral tts and Voxtral realtime for efficient speech synthesis and processing. Their research in medical imaging includes S2S2 for robust semantic segmentation and AI-SAM for automated morphology assessments. Pan also developed vision-language contrastive distillation methods for analyzing placental photographs in work appearing in Patterns and MICCAI. They earned a PhD in Informatics and a BS in Computer Science from Penn State.

researcher.name: Zaccharie Ramzi
researcher.headline: AI Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously AI Research Scientist, Neural Interfaces @ Meta
researcher.bio: Zaccharie Ramzi co-authored the 2020 fastMRI challenge paper, reporting results on ML methods for MR image reconstruction. They are an AI Scientist on the alignment team at Mistral AI. Their research spans ML and image reconstruction, including NC-PDNet for non-Cartesian MRI reconstruction and Benchopt, a framework for reproducible optimization benchmarks. They previously worked on neural interfaces at Meta, studying EMG, and on deep learning at CNRS and ENS Ulm. Ramzi earned a PhD in AI from CEA and Inria, developing deep-learning models for MRI reconstruction.

topAffiliation.description: Works in the alignment team.

researcher.name: Zhenlin Xu
researcher.headline: Applied Scientist @ Mistral AI, Previously Applied Scientist @ Amazon AWS AI Labs
researcher.bio: Zhenlin Xu authored Random Convolutions, which applies random convolutional layers during training to improve the robustness and generalization of visual representation learning. Xu is a researcher at Mistral AI and previously worked as an Applied Scientist at Amazon AWS AI Labs. They co-developed The common pile, an 8TB dataset of public domain text, and RPGBench for evaluating LLMs as role-playing game engines. papers.title: Long-WAM: Scaling the Context of World-Action Models
papers.abstract: Real-time robot control demands enough visual history to infer motion and task progress, but processing that history can delay action. We present Long-WAM, a model-system framework for scaling the context of causal world-action models under real-time control constraints. Our central finding is that access to history is not the same as using it: longer histories pay off far more when the video foundation is pretrained autoregressively (AR). We first learn causal prediction from robot and egocentric videos without action labels, then preserve this history-to-future structure during world-action adaptation. On RoboCasa GR-1, increasing context from 0.0 to 19.2 seconds raises success from 63.3% to 78.7%, whereas a bidirectionally pretrained initialization shows no net gain; robot-domain AR pretraining further raises peak success on GR-1 and LIBERO-Long. Long-WAM also achieves the best results among compared methods on LIBERO-Long, RoboTwin 2.0, and DOMINO. Streaming observation encoding, asynchronous execution, and hardware-specific acceleration enable deployment on RTX 5090, DGX Spark, and Jetson AGX Thor without dropping future prediction; on RTX 5090, each action chunk, including future-video latent prediction, takes 107.4 ms. Real-time deployment on Unitree G1 and YAM supports dynamic and long-horizon manipulation, including 95% success on dynamic cup stacking, where Pi0.5 and Fast-WAM succeed in none of 20 trials. As a memory-informed executor, Long-WAM also complements higher-level planning in composite tasks.
papers.feed_description: Robot controllers can use longer visual histories more effectively when pretrained to predict future motion, improving success on extended manipulation tasks.

paper_summary.summary: Long-WAM trains a robot controller to predict future video from visual history, then uses those predictions to generate actions. On RoboCasa GR-1, robot-domain autoregressive initialization raises success from 66.3% with 2.4 seconds of history to 78.7% with 19.2 seconds, while bidirectional initialization stays near 62%. This simulated comparison supports, but does not prove, the explanation that autoregressive pretraining helps use history.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Robot controllers can use longer visual histories more effectively when pretrained to predict future motion, improving success on extended manipulation tasks.
originalProblem: A single image may not reveal object motion or progress through a multi-step interaction, limiting a robot’s ability to respond to dynamic scenes.
Longer visual histories can improve decisions but increase inference time, creating a tension between informed control and responsive execution.
Having access to history does not guarantee a model can use it effectively; the role of video pretraining in learning useful temporal dependencies is unclear.
solution: Pretrain an autoregressive video model on about 2.25 million video samples, then adapt it with an action expert for causal world-action control.
Use inverse dynamics modeling: predict future video latents and condition action generation on those latents, observed history, and robot state.
Overlap inference with robot execution and optimize deployment with streaming video encoding, low-precision video computation, and other hardware-specific techniques.
keyInsights: Context length alone is not enough: robot-domain autoregressive pretraining yields larger gains from longer history than the tested bidirectional initialization.
Useful context varies by task: RoboCasa GR-1 improves with history up to 19.2 seconds, while LIBERO-Long reaches 99.5% success with 2.4 seconds.
Future video prediction can aid control without decoding predicted frames into pixels, though excessive context can hurt when it extends beyond the training data’s history coverage.
results: On RoboCasa GR-1, success rises from 63.3% with current-observation-only control to 78.7% with 19.2 seconds of history; at 38.4 seconds it drops to 75.2%.
The model reports 99.5% average success on LIBERO and 94.4% on RoboTwin 2.0. On a Unitree G1, it stacks moving cups in 19 of 20 trials, while the two compared methods succeed in none of 20 trials.
Optimized inference takes 107.4 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090; asynchronous RoboTwin 2.0 evaluation retains 94.2% success versus 94.4% synchronously.

papers.title: Neural Networks Are Already Clean
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability of neural networks is examined through neuron- and circuit-level studies of image models and language models, including experiments that track neurons during training and test explanations through activation examples, interventions, and attribution graphs. The analysis argues that many apparent mixtures attributed to superposition instead reflect tool or architectural limitations and “recursive generalization,” in which neurons extend into related concepts. It reports that 99–100% of neurons in the final layer of a parameter-matched ConvNeXt were readily interpretable, and estimates that roughly 90% of neuron poles in Qwen3-32B have one main job, concluding that direct study of network mechanisms can be more informative than first decomposing them into learned features.
papers.feed_description: By tracing neurons and circuits directly, researchers can explain many apparent mixtures as meaningful generalizations, making mechanistic study of large models more promising.

papers.title: Evolving Agent Teams
papers.abstract: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget, Evolving Agent Teams consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget, Evolving Agent Teams generates a CUDA kernel that reaches 1.2x mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel from scratch and wins on 36 of 47 production workloads from FlashInfer-Bench (0.86-0.99x on the remaining 11). It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD MI350X (3.01x over vLLM) and NVIDIA B200 (3.44x over FlashKDA), MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon (30.3 tokens/s decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in MLX 4-bit on a 48 GB M4 Pro), and RoboDojo robot manipulation (62.1 on held-out seeds vs. 55.3 for the best leaderboard entry). Code is available at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT.
papers.feed_description: Dynamically reorganizing coding agents around emerging bottlenecks helps them escape local optima and produce faster GPU kernels than fixed teams or solo agents.

paper_summary.summary: Evolving Agent Teams changes how coding agents are organized during GPU kernel optimization. A supervisor diagnoses stalled progress, redesigns roles and coordination, and preserves lessons and code in a shared filesystem. On DeepSeek-V3 MLA paged decode, additional-budget runs achieve 1.21× geometric-mean speedup over production FlashInfer across 47 H100 workloads, with 36 faster; 11 remain slower, without beating the run-stage-only reference.

papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) of a model on non-verifiable tasks, such as open-ended research, faces a supervision bottleneck when its outputs exceed what even human experts can reliably assess, leaving the model itself (optimizee) as the best available optimizer and evaluator. However, a single model instance struggles to critique and improve its own complex reasoning under this homogeneous loop. To address this, we propose Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS), an RSI method that alternates between evolutionary workflow optimization and supervised fine-tuning on self-generated trajectories. Guided by early findings that multi-agent topologies excel at complex reasoning, MASS prompts a single base model to iteratively propose, execute, and self-evaluate multi-agent workflows. Through an evolutionary search constrained by structural guardrails, the model optimizes these computational-graph-like orchestrations, discovering the most effective distinct roles and information routing for a given task. Over two MASS cycles with Qwen3.6-27B, the model achieves 1.2-1.6x higher performance per output tokens on four open-ended public benchmarks. Because the improved model subsequently acts as a better optimizer and evaluator, this alternating framework enables a continuous, recursive bootstrapping of the model's capabilities. Moreover, multi-agent traces are also more training-efficient: a student trained on them outperforms a single-agent student trained on 1.4x more training tokens. These findings suggest that jointly learning orchestration and bounded subagent execution from multi-agent trajectories can provide an effective signal for RSI.
papers.feed_description: Training a model on coordinated agent traces improved its open-ended research performance and taught it to delegate more often without explicit workflow instructions.

paper_summary.summary: MASS improves open-ended research agents by having model copies coordinate through task-specific workflows, then fine-tuning their shared model on selected orchestrator and subagent trajectories. After two cycles, it achieves 1.2–1.6 times the base model’s score per output token on four research benchmarks. This does not extend to coding benchmarks, where the reported ratios are 0.96 and 0.94.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Training a model on coordinated agent traces improved its open-ended research performance and taught it to delegate more often without explicit workflow instructions.
originalProblem: Open-ended research tasks often lack fast, dependable external checks, while a model judging its own work may share the solver’s blind spots.
Training strong task-solving behavior requires useful examples of decomposition, delegation, verification, and synthesis; designing effective workflows by hand is costly.
solution: MASS alternates between searching textual multi-agent workflows with fixed model weights and fine-tuning the model on selected executions from the retained workflows.
The model serves as orchestrator, subagents, evaluator, and workflow optimizer; training traces teach both task execution and coordination, without supplying the searched workflow at inference.
keyInsights: Coordination traces can act as supervision beyond final answers: delegation rose from 1 of 110 base-model trajectories to 87 of 110 after two cycles, and code handoffs rose from 1 to 83.

Training on multi-agent traces may use supervised tokens more efficiently: one comparison reported a 68.3% win rate with 28.82 million tokens versus 64.0% with 42 million for a single-agent control, though the comparison was not fully matched.
Improvements in solving tasks were accompanied by better evaluator agreement and workflow search, suggesting that task-solving traces can transfer to other model roles.
results: On three synthetic held-out tasks, the second-generation model won 69.9% of comparisons against the base model and 60.8% against the first generation; agreement with external evaluator judgments increased from 73% to 93%.

On four research-oriented benchmarks, second-generation scores improved over the base model, with reported score-per-output-token gains of 1.2–1.6×. MLR-Bench and AstaBench had more completed reports, but average scores among delivered reports declined.

Performance was not uniform: Terminal-Bench 2.0 fell from 37.5% to 35.2%, and SWE-bench Verified from 62.6% to 61.1%. The study used one base model and two cycles, and its evaluations rely substantially on model-based judgments.

papers.title: Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Most robot policies keep a model in the control loop: a VLA maps observations to actions, and an Agent Harness, such as Agent-as-Policy or Harness VLA queries a VLM for decision making at run time. We propose a different view: the embodied world is an Embodied Turing Machine, whose tape is the robot and environment state and rules are the policy. If this state can be represented accurately, the decision making can be written entirely in code. We therefore propose Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP): code measures and tracks the robot, environment, and task state from camera images and proprioception, and makes every decision from it. The same code applies across episodes, and different tasks share one library without a VLM or VLA in the loop. Compared with VLAs and Agent Harnesses, we analyze three advantages of COAP: (i) Explicit State: the state can be stored in code; (ii) Execution: code makes decision making controllable, recovers from failures flexibly, and runs fast and cheaply online; (iii) Extensibility: new tasks reuse, inherit, or extend the shared library, so capabilities can accumulate over tasks. These advantages make COAP a suitable medium for recursive self-improvement (RSI): coding agents develop the library in a closed loop, and each change is explicit and controllable. On RoboDojo's 42 bimanual tasks, the resulting library reaches a success rate of 70.24% without a model at test time. The upper bound of COAP lies in how accurately the state is represented for decision making and how robust the code logic is. We thus propose COAP as a new paradigm for embodied tasks; since it applies across episodes, it can also serve as an efficient data engine for VLAs and Agent Harnesses.
papers.feed_description: A robot policy built from reusable code and explicit state solved 70% of 42 simulated bimanual tasks without a model during execution.

paper_summary.summary: COAP represents scene state in code and uses a fixed task program to choose actions, check outcomes, and update its records. At test time, it uses camera images and robot measurements without a model service. On RoboDojo, it reaches 70.24% overall success, versus 31.38% for PhysicalRSI. Results are from simulation and depend on state measurement and code robustness.
paper_summary.feedDescription: A robot policy built from reusable code and explicit state solved 70% of 42 simulated bimanual tasks without a model during execution.
originalProblem: Many robot policies keep perception and decision-making implicit in model weights or rely on repeated model calls during execution, making decisions harder to inspect and adding compute cost and variability.
Code-based robot approaches often depend on run-time models or external oracles, and it is unclear whether explicit, reusable code can support broad task coverage and iterative improvement.
solution: COAP represents environment, robot, and task information as explicit state, updates it using robot sensors and conventional image-processing code, and maps it to actions through a fixed program at run time.

A shared library provides perception, manipulation, and motion functions for task programs. Coding agents improve this library offline using recorded runs, validation checks, and regression safeguards.
The system was evaluated on 42 bimanual RoboDojo tasks using RGB cameras, proprioception, and task instructions, without depth, segmentation services, or model services during testing.
keyInsights: Explicit state and persistent episode memory let a fixed program track objects and subgoals, including when objects become occluded, and make policy decisions easier to inspect.
Reusable code supports task composition: the paper reports that 83% of the code executed by a new task comes from the shared library.
The approach depends on reliable state measurement; the authors attribute 62% of failures to measurement problems and 37% to incomplete logic or code design.
results: COAP records 70.24% overall success and a progress score of 75.45, versus 31.38% success for the strongest listed baseline, PhysicalRSI; it leads the reported results across all five benchmark dimensions.

Success rates are 89.9% on Memory, 75.1% on Precision, 64.1% on Open tasks, 65.7% on Generalization, and 56.4% on Long-Horizon tasks. Generalization success falls from 77.3% on standard layouts to 54.1% on randomized layouts.

Control steps take a median of 0.3 ms on a CPU. On four tasks added after the library was frozen, the system reached 47% average success within 15 hours; results are limited to simulation and require further real-world validation.

papers.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at this https URL.
papers.feed_description: Agents can reason internally in continuous representations while preserving readable checkpoints and tool use, reducing token generation without sacrificing performance across diverse tasks.

paper_summary.summary: HybridAgent lets a tool-using language-model agent reason in continuous hidden states and use text for tool calls and answers. HybridLink aligns hidden states with the model’s input-embedding space, while retained attention-cache entries carry context across turns. At 14B parameters, it scores 49.5 average on WebWalker versus ARPO’s 40.5, within evaluations of Qwen3-Base models on 11 benchmarks.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Agents can reason internally in continuous representations while preserving readable checkpoints and tool use, reducing token generation without sacrificing performance across diverse tasks.
originalProblem: Text-based agents must generate long verbal reasoning traces, increasing token use and inference time.
Latent reasoners can reduce verbalized computation but do not naturally support standard text-based tools, multi-turn interaction, or straightforward inspection.
A practical agent needs to retain useful context across tool calls while choosing when to reason internally and when to communicate explicitly.
solution: HybridLink lets a Transformer switch between text tokens and continuous latent states, with special markers controlling entry to and exit from latent reasoning.
The system preserves a KV cache containing text, latent states, and tool observations across turns, avoiding the need to convert latent history back into text.
HybridSFT uses self-conditioned training to prepare the model for its own latent inputs; HybridRL trains text decisions in recorded trajectories that also contain latent states and tool results.
keyInsights: Latent reasoning can be integrated into multi-turn tool use without decoding every internal step into text; the paper argues that preserving the full KV cache maintains the hybrid prefix during continuation.
Self-conditioned training improves performance beyond format training and adapter activation alone, addressing the gap between teacher-forced training and free-running latent inference.
Replacing or reordering latent states reduces mathematical accuracy, suggesting that the content and sequence of those states matter, rather than the gains coming only from extra computation.
results: Across benchmarks and model sizes, the authors report a 10.4% average improvement over relevant baselines and a 17.4% average improvement over the strongest agentic baseline on challenging agentic tasks.
The 14B model reports 43.3% on AIME25, 45.8% on AIME26, 88.2% on MATH500, 52.4% on GAIA, and 49.5% on WebWalker.
Compared with text-based agents, HybridAgents use 35.5%–54.7% fewer text tokens and are reported to run 1.8×–2.6× faster; estimated costs are 2.7×–3.7× lower under the paper’s stated assumptions.

papers.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
papers.feed_description: Generating text from coarse to fine lets language models match or improve diffusion-model quality while running substantially faster on tested language and summarization benchmarks.

paper_summary.summary: NCM generates text by encoding it into hierarchical discrete representations and predicting them coarse to fine, with codes at each level generated in parallel. It reports LM1B generative perplexity of 93.05 at 12 function evaluations, compared with DUO’s 97.30 at 128, alongside similar measured diversity and a reported 21× wall-clock speedup. These results are benchmark-specific, and larger-scale behavior remains open.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Generating text from coarse to fine lets language models match or improve diffusion-model quality while running substantially faster on tested language and summarization benchmarks.
originalProblem: Autoregressive generation has a long sequential path, while diffusion language models often require many full-sequence denoising passes, making inference costly.
Reducing diffusion steps can hurt generation quality or diversity, and each full-sequence pass remains computationally expensive.
Text compression must preserve details accurately: reconstruction errors can alter meaning or break structured outputs such as Sudoku solutions.
solution: Train a multiscale residual VQ-VAE tokenizer that represents text with progressively longer code sequences, using nested dropout to encourage useful information at coarse levels and accurate reconstruction at the finest level.
Train a transformer to predict all codes in each level in parallel, proceeding from coarse to fine; decode the completed hierarchy back into text.
Use imperfect preceding codes during training to reduce error accumulation at generation time, and apply prefix attention for conditional tasks.
keyInsights: The method reduces both the number of sequential generation stages and the work per stage by processing short coarse representations before finer ones.
The tokenizer reconstructs text with high exact-token accuracy on the reported datasets: 99.86–99.99% for three language-modeling datasets, 99.79% on XSum, and 98.79% on WMT14.
Low-cost generation can be paired with candidate selection: minimum Bayes risk selection improved summarization and translation scores when more inference evaluations were allocated.
results: On LM1B, NCM reached generative perplexity 93.05 with 12 function evaluations, versus DUO’s 97.30 with 128; on TinyStories it scored 15.41 with 12 evaluations, close to FMLM+’s 15.43 with 128.

For XSum, NCM achieved ROUGE-1/2/L of 35.0/12.8/28.0 with eight evaluations; with candidate selection it reached 37.3/14.0/29.6. On WMT14, it scored 22.6 BLEU with 11 evaluations and 25.2 with selection at 132 evaluations.

On Sudoku, it solved 99.5%, 96.5%, and 86.1% of easy, medium, and hard boards using 12 evaluations. Reported H100 timing showed 21× faster generation on LM1B and 31× on XSum than the strongest diffusion baselines in those comparisons.

papers.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence
papers.abstract: Moonshot AI's most capable 3T-class open-weight model, a post-trained Kimi K3 with a 1M-token context that approaches frontier proprietary models on coding, 3D creation, and finance, with cyber capability deliberately reduced before release.
papers.feed_description: Kimi K3.1 Pro ranks fourth on Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index and leads Terminal-Bench 4.0, with open weights planned for release.

paper_summary.summary: Moonshot AI introduces Kimi K3.1 Pro, a post-trained version of Kimi K3 and its most capable 3T-class open-weight model, with a 1M-token context window and a 2-3× faster Highspeed variant. Trained with far more RL compute across hundreds of domains, it matches or approaches leading proprietary models on coding, 3D creation, finance, and agentic benchmarks. Moonshot also removed cyber-related training data on purpose, so the open weights stay behind the frontier on offensive cyber capability. Full weights are due by Nov 4, 2026.
originalProblem: Scaling joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains requires efficiency across the whole stack, from the RL framework and long-context inference to sandboxes and rollout scheduling.
Financial research and analysis demand high factual accuracy, and K3 had a 23.4% claim-level hallucination rate on Moonshot's hardest internal stress test.
Cyber capability rose steadily as post-training scaled, because cyber content is embedded in general mid-training data and RL environment mixes, which is a risk for an open-weight release.
solution: Optimizes every layer of the post-training stack so each increment of RL compute turns into capability gains across coding, 3D, finance, and agentic tasks.
Trains the model to drive tools like Unreal Engine, Godot, Blender, FreeCAD, and trimesh through scripts, without MCP connectors, for 3D and game creation.
Makes targeted factual-accuracy improvements for real-world financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research.
Identifies and removes cyber-related data at both mid-training and RL, while keeping the general-purpose coding tasks the model needs to stay useful.
keyInsights: Removing cyber data works as a concrete control lever: the same pipeline without it solves 90.5% of xdev-bench-hard at pass@3, against 81.0% for the released model.
Moonshot commits to not releasing open weights that extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability, and plans to raise the cyber capability it makes available step by step.

On long-horizon tasks the model debugs its own setup: building a walking simulator, it probed the dynamics, found and fixed 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and retrained the controller.

papers.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
papers.abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.
papers.feed_description: Models with built-in memory can retain useful information across long interactions in fixed-size state, improving recall while reducing storage growth.

paper_summary.summary: MemT-1.0 gives models a compact persistent state, updated token by token and read alongside ordinary attention. It extends Metis with token-level updates and Mixture-of-Storage. Across 11 benchmarks, Flash and Nano ranked first and second among parametric-memory methods, averaging 50.6 and 47.0. On harness-triggered SWE-bench Verified, Nano averaged 69.73% success, comparable to textual experience, not evidence of autonomous learning.

papers.title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.
papers.feed_description: A learned refinement step makes diffusion models generate more coherent images without guidance, and its gains can be distilled into the base model without extra inference passes.

paper_summary.summary: The authors introduce a corrector for diffusion image generation that refines the denoiser’s clean-image prediction before each sampling update. Trained on the denoiser’s own predictions, the corrector can be applied repeatedly. On class-conditional ImageNet-256 with DiT-XL/2 at 250 network evaluations, it lowers FID-50K from 9.58 unguided to 2.07, versus 2.51 for CFG, with lower precision but higher recall than CFG.
paper_summary.feedDescription: A learned refinement step makes diffusion models generate more coherent images without guidance, and its gains can be distilled into the base model without extra inference passes.
originalProblem: Diffusion models are trained on noisy versions of real images but sampled from states shaped by their own earlier predictions, creating a training–inference gap in which errors can persist or accumulate.
Guidance can improve image quality but may reduce diversity or cause oversaturation, while simply adding denoising steps does not directly teach the model to fix structural mistakes.
solution: Train a separate corrector to refine the denoiser’s predicted clean image toward the same real-image target, with gradients from the correction loss stopped at the denoiser’s output.
During sampling, apply the corrector repeatedly at each step and use the refined prediction to update the noisy state; compare against baselines at roughly matched network-evaluation budgets.
Test parameter sharing and distillation so that correction’s quality gains can be retained with less added model size or inference cost.
keyInsights: Repeated correction often improves generation even though it can increase reconstruction error on inputs resembling the training distribution, suggesting that training-distribution reconstruction error alone does not predict sampling quality.

Corrected intermediate states become harder to distinguish from training-distribution states in classifier two-sample tests; this is consistent with reducing the training–inference gap but does not prove that mechanism.
Higher fidelity can come with lower recall, and too many correction iterations may reduce quality or impose overly regular structure.
results: On class-conditional ImageNet-256, FID improves from 9.58 to 2.07 for DiT-XL/2, from 8.55 to 1.92 for SiT-XL/2, and from 5.53 to 1.31 for SiT-REPA-XL/2. These gains are not universal: JiT-L/16 correction reaches FID 2.96 versus 2.35 for its reported CFG reference.

In unguided text-to-image evaluation, GenEval rises from 28.30 to 50.09 and DPG-Bench from 70.71 to 76.82; with CFG, the gains are smaller. In an 80-prompt preference study, raters favored CFG followed by correction for image quality in 60.75% of responses.

Distillation produces FID 2.04 at 250 network evaluations, close to the corrected teacher’s 1.92, and FID 2.26 at 83 evaluations; on unconditional ImageNet, correction also raises precision while lowering recall.

papers.title: VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction
papers.abstract: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.
papers.feed_description: A single video model can locate events in time and answer multiple-choice questions, reusing visual computation across queries for faster decisions.

paper_summary.summary: VideoJev scores candidate time intervals to locate events and candidate answers for video questions, reusing one video prefix across queries through cached or joint inference. It reports 65.3 mean temporal intersection-over-union, versus 58.6 for its 4B backbone, and a four-benchmark QA mean of 74.3, near 74.9 for Qwen3.5-4B Thinking; evaluations cover grounding and multiple-choice QA, not agent workflows.
paper_summary.feedDescription: A single video model can locate events in time and answer multiple-choice questions, reusing visual computation across queries for faster decisions.
originalProblem: Video MLLMs often generate structured decisions such as timestamps or answer choices token by token, adding latency when only a compact judgment is needed.
Separate systems and prediction heads for temporal localization and video QA make it harder to reuse the same video representation across tasks and repeated queries.
The work asks whether direct scoring can preserve broad language-conditioned video understanding while improving both efficiency and prediction quality.
solution: VideoJev replaces the standard output head with a scoring head that compares candidate representations with a query-level representation; candidates can be timestamp intervals or answer texts.
It supports cached inference, which reuses an encoded video for later queries, and joint inference, which processes multiple queries against a shared video prefix.
Training combines answer-choice cross-entropy with interval-level binary cross-entropy and a soft IoU objective for grounding.
keyInsights: Temporal grounding and multiple-choice QA can be framed as scoring candidates through one shared interface, rather than generating a text response for each task.
Reusing video computation supports repeated decisions about the same visual input, and joint training across grounding and QA improves average performance on both tasks.
Direct scores provide useful ranking signals but are not fully calibrated: both model sizes tend to overestimate QA correctness.
results: VideoJev-4B reaches 65.3 mean mIoU across three grounding benchmarks, while VideoJev-35B-A3B reaches 67.7; these are 6.7 and 10.8 points above their respective backbones.
Across four QA benchmarks, mean scores are 74.3 for VideoJev-4B and 79.5 for VideoJev-35B-A3B, exceeding the corresponding Instruct baselines by 8.0 and 5.7 points.

Measured grounding inference takes 0.276–0.336 seconds, versus 0.763–1.054 seconds for the backbones. On LVBench, VideoJev is about 100–129× faster than the compared Thinking-mode models under the reported setup.

papers.title: Video Prediction Policy 2: Predict Better, Act Better
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as an important class of generalist robot policies, aiming to transfer video prediction priors to action learning. However, we find that existing WAMs frequently produce incorrect motion predictions in open-ended environment, leading to erroneous actions. We attribute this limitation to two factors: (1) base video models are not optimized for manipulation, and (2) naively incorporating action components into video models can substantially degrade their generalization capabilities. We introduce Video Prediction Policy 2 (VPP2), a WAM that enables strong zero-shot generalization in both video prediction and action generation. First, we curate a large-scale, diverse dataset of manipulation videos to continue pretraining the base video foundation model. We annotate video clips with detailed captions and perform \textit{event-level} video pretraining to promote generalization across open-ended manipulation tasks. Second, we post-train and distill the video model into a single-step visual planner with fixed prediction horizon. Finally, we introduce action module via a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture to learn implicit inverse dynamics model. Experiments demonstrate three key results: (1) VPP2-14B outperforms Cosmos3-64B by 11.0\% points in video prediction instruction-following success rate on open-ended tasks; (2) VPP2 surpasses the strongest baseline by 18.5\% points in success rate on real-world zero-shot ALOHA manipulation tasks; and (3) following benchmark-specific post-training, VPP2 achieves the highest success rates among evaluated methods on the challenging LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-OOD, and RoboDojo benchmarks.
papers.feed_description: A robot policy that predicts manipulation trajectories before acting generalizes to unfamiliar tasks, outperforming strong baselines in real-world zero-shot trials.

paper_summary.summary: VPP2 predicts a described manipulation event from video, then uses that forecast to generate short action sequences. It is trained first on complete events and then on fixed-duration video chunks aligned with action learning. In real-world ALOHA tests without task-specific fine-tuning, it averages 58.5% success across 10 categories, versus 40.0% for π0.5; ALOHA was seen during training.

papers.title: FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving
papers.abstract:
KV cache reuse accelerates LLM serving, but existing systems manage host DRAM and NVMe SSD as a tiered hierarchy where DRAM acts as an intermediate cache. Production LLM workloads break both premises of this hierarchy. First, bimodal reuse defeats DRAM temporal filtering, since workloads are dominated either by one-shot blocks with long reuse distances or by multi-gigabyte agentic sessions that exceed DRAM capacity, putting SSD on the critical read path. Second, DRAM staging and eviction-ordered layout bottleneck SSD restoration. Holding host staging buffers for in-flight prefixes causes contention under load that aborts prefetches, while incremental eviction scatters a session's blocks across the SSD and prevents large sequential reads.
We present FlatCake, a flat KV storage architecture that exposes host DRAM and NVMe SSD as peer media in a unified 64-bit address space. Exploiting the fact that KV blocks are write-once, immutable, and reused at session scope, FlatCake places each block directly onto its target medium in session-contiguous, layer-major order at creation time and never migrates it. FlatCake streams coalesced SSD reads directly into a bounded GPU window via GPUDirect Storage and decouples DRAM and SSD request queues to prevent head-of-line blocking. On a production Claude Code trace with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, FlatCake sustains a 94% cache hit rate as load increases (versus 64% for Mooncake), eliminates Mooncake's $6.5\times$--$6.7\times$ SSD read amplification, and reduces peak-load mean TTFT by $1.6\times$ while improving total token throughput by $1.6\times$. Across 8K--128K contexts on Llama-3.1-70B, FlatCake further reduces mean TTFT by up to $2.4\times$ over Mooncake and $1.8\times$ over Mooncake-GDS.
papers.feed_description: Directly placing reusable LLM cache data on SSD in session order preserves cache hits under load and cuts response latency in tested serving workloads.

paper_summary.summary: FlatCake places language-model KV caches across DRAM and SSD for reuse of long histories. It assigns immutable blocks at creation, groups session data in layer-major order, and restores SSD data through coalesced reads to GPU memory. On a Claude Code replay with DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 1.0 QPS, it records 7.57-second mean TTFT and 98.3K tokens/s, versus Mooncake’s 12.24 seconds and 61.6K tokens/s.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Directly placing reusable LLM cache data on SSD in session order preserves cache hits under load and cuts response latency in tested serving workloads.

papers.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.
papers.feed_description: Predictive models help agents choose which actions to test, then use feedback to improve and retain system updates across coding, interface, planning, and chemistry tasks.

paper_summary.summary: RSI-Anything uses predicted outcomes to select actions for testing, then pairs predictions with observed results to guide policy updates and conditional world-model adaptation. With the coder fixed on CodeContests, hidden-test all-pass success rose from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% with fixed-model selection and 31.2% with adaptation, at similar online test usage. This does not establish sustained joint improvement.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Predictive models help agents choose which actions to test, then use feedback to improve and retain system updates across coding, interface, planning, and chemistry tasks.
originalProblem: External feedback—such as running tests, interacting with interfaces, or conducting experiments—can be costly, making it important to choose which candidate actions to evaluate.
As a policy changes, it may propose actions outside the world model’s reliable range; updating the policy or predictor independently can therefore make the combined system worse.
Existing approaches often focus on improving a policy, workflow, or predictor in isolation rather than managing their updates and compatibility together.
solution: Use domain-specific world models to estimate candidate outcomes, filter invalid actions, and prioritize candidates by predicted utility or uncertainty before requesting external feedback.
Pair predictions with observed outcomes to support policy or predictor updates, adapting the predictor only when reliability, data coverage, and budget justify it.
Evaluate proposed component versions and the assembled policy–model pair; retain previous versions when checks fail.
keyInsights: Prediction-guided selection can improve the value of a limited evaluation budget: in CodeContests, success reached 29.2% with a fixed world model versus 26.3% with a capacity-matched static verifier, and 31.2% when the predictor was also adapted.
System-level quality is not captured by a single metric: on MiniWoB++, an adapted configuration used fewer actions but had more incorrect submissions than the final configuration.

The framework’s applications use different update pathways and domain-specific models; the results do not yet establish sustained, joint policy-and-model improvement across multiple rounds in one setting.
results: On MiniWoB++ click-checkboxes, success rose from 51% to 99% and mean actions per episode fell from 5.30 to 3.21; on OSWorld, reported success was 5.5% higher relative to RLAnything.
Across five LabHorizon policy versions, the Level-2 Final Score increased from 21.80% to 46.01%, slightly exceeding the 45.32% Actor–Simulator–Selector reference.

papers.title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
papers.abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.
papers.feed_description: The paper organizes fragmented work on agentic robotics into a shared framework, helping researchers compare how robots learn, gather data, build environments, and coordinate execution.

paper_summary.summary: The authors survey agentic robots as systems that use goals, observations, capabilities, and execution feedback to choose actions, gather information, revise plans, or recover. They organize prior work into four domains and seventeen overlapping categories. An external RoboDojo evaluation reports 22.48% average success across 42 simulation tasks, versus 19.34% for trained DM0.5; this comparison does not isolate feedback’s effect.
paper_summary.feedDescription: The paper organizes fragmented work on agentic robotics into a shared framework, helping researchers compare how robots learn, gather data, build environments, and coordinate execution.
originalProblem: Research relevant to agentic robots is spread across robot learning, embodied AI, data generation, simulation, and runtime systems, making it difficult to compare contributions or identify gaps.
Stronger action prediction alone does not ensure success on long-horizon tasks: robots must monitor progress, respond to changing conditions, verify outcomes, and recover from failures.
Reported performance can depend on interfaces, tools, policies, feedback, and human assistance—not just the reasoning model—complicating fair evaluation.
solution: The authors survey representative work and propose a taxonomy with four domains—Model, Data, Environment, and Harness—divided into 17 overlapping functional categories.
They compare systems by their inputs, outputs, tools, feedback, and intervention points, linking robot execution with data collection, refinement, and future capability development.
The survey uses this framework to identify recurring design requirements and research priorities, including independent outcome checks, safe recovery, realistic evaluation, and transparent reporting.
keyInsights: Agentic robotics is defined by how a system selects, coordinates, and revises capabilities during execution; it does not require complete independence from people.
Reliability depends on the full system: stale memory, infeasible plans, weak tool interfaces, or unvalidated skill changes can undermine a capable model.

Individual studies illustrate that harness design can affect results: one cited system’s zero-shot success rose from 60% to 82% with smaller action steps, while a different interface change reduced question-answering accuracy from 74.0% to 59.1%.
results: The main contribution is a system-level framework for locating and comparing work across robot models, data pipelines, environment construction, and runtime coordination; the categories are functional and may overlap.
The survey finds no single best architecture or directly comparable field-wide performance measure, because reviewed studies use different robots, tasks, tools, and evaluation protocols.

The authors call for evaluations that isolate an agent’s contribution and test long-horizon behavior, changing environments, execution failures, real-robot deployment, and the validation of self-modifications.

papers.title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.
papers.feed_description: A robot can learn both how actions change what it sees and which actions to take, enabling faster goal-directed planning in contact-rich tasks.

paper_summary.summary: LeWAM jointly learns how actions change a scene and which actions are plausible, then uses proposed actions to plan manipulation. Its model predicts latent states and action distributions, refining candidate sequences against a goal. Across ten simulated tasks, it averages 93.5% success versus 50.9% for LeWM with CEM. These results concern task-specific goal reaching from offline data, not broad transfer.
paper_summary.feedDescription: A robot can learn both how actions change what it sees and which actions to take, enabling faster goal-directed planning in contact-rich tasks.
originalProblem: JEPA-based controllers often train world models separately from policies or depend on costly broad action search, which can be inefficient for contact-rich tasks.
Representations optimized to predict future states may miss action-relevant information, while deterministic action predictors can fail to capture multiple valid behaviors.
It remains unclear whether a single model can support both reliable action prediction and useful latent-space planning from offline visual demonstrations.
solution: Train an image encoder, latent dynamics predictor, and stochastic action-chunk model together from reward-free pixel-and-action trajectories, using prediction, flow-matching, and SIGReg losses.

At test time, either sample actions directly or generate policy-guided action candidates, refine them through differentiable latent dynamics toward a goal image, and execute plans in a receding-horizon loop.
Evaluate the approach across ten simulated visual-planning tasks, goal-agnostic tasks, and three physical-robot manipulation tasks.
keyInsights: Joint action modeling appears to make visual representations more useful for control; probes show improved action and proprioceptive information compared with a dynamics-only JEPA baseline.
Stochastic flow-matched action proposals can represent different valid behaviors, while SIGReg helps preserve useful latent structure and planning performance.
Policy-guided refinement can reduce the need for broad population search, with particularly large gains reported on contact-rich simulated tasks.
results: Across ten simulated tasks, LeWAM averaged 93.5% goal-reaching success, compared with 50.9% for LeWM using CEM; on ToolHang the rates were 94.7% versus 35.4%, and on Transport 83.3% versus 2.8%.

For four visual-goal tasks, planning averaged 52.50 plans per second versus 1.62 for the CEM baseline under the study’s specified configurations. At a 100-step goal offset, LeWAM averaged 46.2% success, with substantial variation across tasks.

Physical-robot success averaged 33.3% for LeWAM across three tasks, compared with 38.9% for Diffusion Policy and 28.9% for π0.5; the limited task set and mixed results constrain claims about real-world generalization.

papers.title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
papers.abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel scenarios. We introduce Harness^2, a plug-and-play, recursive agent harnessing framework that addresses these challenges through two connected levels of recursion. Task-level recursion refines the current task's harness using a contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose step that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. Harnessing-level recursion then extracts experience from these edits to update a continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four model-harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion budget increases.
papers.feed_description: Agents can refine their task-specific instructions and tools without correctness labels, while retaining lessons from each refinement to better handle future tasks.

paper_summary.summary: Harness² improves an agent’s editable task harness while preserving supported lessons for later edits, without changing the base model. It compares matched runs to identify behavioral changes, then selectively composes harness edits and updates an improvement library after each task. For GLM-5 under OpenCode, its WorkBuddy-Bench macro-average was 75.7 versus 64.2 for the base harness; contrasts do not verify correctness.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Agents can refine their task-specific instructions and tools without correctness labels, while retaining lessons from each refinement to better handle future tasks.
originalProblem: Agent performance depends on its runtime scaffolding as well as its model, but adapting that scaffolding is difficult when new tasks lack labels, answer keys, or reliable verifiers.
Task-specific edits may help the current assignment yet encode assumptions that do not transfer to later tasks; simply carrying forward a previous task’s harness risks misapplication.
Existing optimization approaches often rely on fixed task sets or task scores, limiting their usefulness for ongoing streams of unfamiliar professional work.
solution: Harness² keeps model weights fixed and refines eight editable harness components, including prompts, memory, tool guidance, skills, scripts, and middleware.

Its Propose–Probe–Compose loop generates general and domain-specific candidate edits, tests them on the same task as the reference harness, and uses differences in behavior and deliverables as evidence—not as proof of correctness—to select or combine changes.
After each task, a reflector can add supported edits and contextual lessons to an improvement library. New tasks still begin from a shared base harness, with the library guiding selective reuse.
keyInsights: Comparing runs under matched conditions can provide useful signals about whether an edit addresses a diagnosed failure, even when no ground-truth answer is available.
The refinement process itself can yield reusable experience: retaining the reasons and evidence behind edits is different from blindly transferring a task-specific execution harness.
Broader exploration helps: parallel recursion with five refinement candidates produced further gains over a single refinement step, though it requires additional model calls and compute.
results: A single refinement step improved scores over the base harness across every reported model–harness configuration. Maximum gains were 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points in LAB criterion pass rate.

At recursion budget k=5, parallel refinement added 2.9–3.9 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 3.0–4.2 points on JobBench, and 2.6–6.7 percentage points on LAB compared with k=1. Harness² exceeded the compared baselines on WorkBuddy-Bench average and JobBench across all four configurations, but did not lead every LAB comparison.

Ablations found lower WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench scores when the experience library, scoped proposals, or composition stage was removed.
