papers.title: A Balanced Data Diet: Addressing the Exploration Bottleneck in Mega-Scale RL for Robot Control
papers.abstract: General-purpose robots must perform a wide range of tasks from agile locomotion to dexterous manipulation. While sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has proven to be a useful tool for this goal, current RL pipelines depend on engineering-heavy, per-task structural priors such as shaped rewards and demonstrations. Recent work has shown that diverse simulator resets, combined with massively parallel simulation, can alleviate much of this engineering burden on several manipulation problems. However, we find that naively scaling this paradigm to more precise or dynamic problems remains non-trivial. While simulator resets can help with exploration, uniformly sampling over this distribution wastes a growing fraction of learning experience on task configurations the policy has already mastered or cannot yet attempt. This makes it challenging to see the expected benefits of scaling parallel environments for RL, since much of the learning signal in a batch is wasted during learning. To mitigate this, we introduce Success Guided Sampling (SGS), a simple adaptive sampler that concentrates RL training on task configurations around the frontier of the policy's capabilities. Doing so allows large-scale simulated RL to make the most out of the experience in a batch, enabling much more effective scaling to large-scale parallel simulation. Across experiments using up to $2^{20}$ (over one million) parallel environments, SGS enables RL to solve challenging multi-terrain quadruped locomotion and contact-rich assembly tasks that prior methods fail to solve. Finally, we distill the learned manipulation policies into RGB-based policies and demonstrate zero-shot transfer to several challenging assembly tasks on real hardware. Project website: this https URL.
papers.feed_description: Robots can learn difficult terrain navigation and precise assembly more effectively when training focuses on task configurations they are still learning.

paper_summary.summary: Success Guided Sampling (SGS) allocates training episodes across a fixed set of task configurations according to recent success rates, emphasizing situations with intermediate success while retaining nonzero sampling probability for all configurations. In settings, it improves results: Anymal-D locomotion reaches 73% success at 1 million environments, versus 54% with PLR. Hardware nut-and-bolt transfer succeeds in 18 of 48 trials.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Robots can learn difficult terrain navigation and precise assembly more effectively when training focuses on task configurations they are still learning.
originalProblem: As parallel simulation grows, uniform sampling can spend many episodes on configurations that are already easy or currently too difficult, limiting the learning value of additional compute.
Robot RL often relies on demonstrations, task-specific reward shaping, or manually designed curricula that are costly to create and tune.
It is unclear how to allocate experience across diverse simulator reset states while retaining the ability to revisit both mastered and difficult configurations.
solution: SGS tracks recent success over a fixed set of reset configurations and uses a softmax-weighted, beta-shaped score to prioritize configurations near a target success rate; all configurations retain some sampling probability.

The method is evaluated with PPO on multi-terrain quadruped locomotion and several robot assembly tasks, comparing against uniform sampling, PLR, SFL, and a hand-designed curriculum at different simulation scales.
For hardware evaluation, point-cloud policies trained in simulation are distilled into wrist- and third-person-camera RGB policies using DAgger, then tested on a UR5e without real-world fine-tuning.
keyInsights: A policy’s observed success rate can serve as a simple signal for allocating practice: intermediate-difficulty configurations are emphasized without imposing a fixed task order.

Adaptive sampling depends on the available reset distribution; for rod-in-hole insertion, removing near-goal resets prevented learning, while removing reaching resets had little effect in the tested setup.
Sampling improvements are most apparent on challenging tasks; on simpler tasks at sufficiently large scales, uniform sampling and other methods can also reach high success.
results: At one million parallel environments, SGS achieved 73% success on multi-terrain locomotion versus 54% for PLR; on Franka nut-and-bolt assembly it achieved 70%, compared with 6% for uniform sampling and 5% for PLR.

For UR5e nut-and-bolt assembly, SGS reached 90.04% simulated success, versus 48.83% for uniform sampling and 59.77% for PLR. In rod-in-hole insertion, SGS learned at 32,000 environments when uniform sampling and PLR achieved zero success; all methods approached 98% at 256,000 environments.
On real hardware, the distilled RGB policies succeeded in 18/48 nut-and-bolt trials (37.5%), 30/49 rod-in-hole trials (61%), and 47/50 gear-mesh trials (94%), showing task-dependent transfer gaps.

papers.title: Meta$^2$: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.
papers.feed_description: Agents can reuse lessons from completed tasks to adjust their tools and instructions mid-run, without carrying task-specific changes into future runs.

paper_summary.summary: Meta² teaches an evolver reusable guidance for changing a frozen model’s task harness during a run, rather than selecting one harness for every task. Its Meta-Skill guides when to edit, hold, or avoid changes; edits remain run-local, without held-out verifier feedback. With GPT-5.6-Terra, it reports mean@5 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and mean@3 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1, on two tested benchmarks.

papers.title: Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting
papers.abstract: Reliable multi-view forecasting requires videos from different cameras to describe the same evolving 3D scene. To this end, we introduce Video-Point Model (VPM), a world model that conditions on multi-view video histories and a language instruction to jointly forecast future videos from arbitrary viewpoints and the 3D trajectories of persistent scene points. We extend a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing that integrates complementary observations across cameras, and add a trajectory head that predicts how physical points move through time. Each trajectory tracks a single point across all views, and supervising these trajectories alongside video generation therefore anchors appearance changes in every camera to a shared description of 3D motion. To support training and evaluation, we build VPM-Data, a simulation corpus pairing synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, and VP-WorldBench, a forecasting benchmark spanning simulated and real environments. We further extend VPM to robot control by adding robot actions as a token modality in the generator. Action tokens share the point-supervised backbone and are denoised jointly with future videos, thereby grounding the policy in the same 3D-aware representation. On VP-WorldBench and existing 4D generation benchmarks, point supervision improves both video fidelity and 3D motion accuracy over a video-only counterpart, and in simulated and real-robot experiments, it also raises the manipulation success of the action-enabled model.
papers.feed_description: Forecasting persistent 3D point motion alongside video helps world models generate more coherent multi-view futures and improves robot manipulation in simulated and real settings.

paper_summary.summary: VPM forecasts multi-view video and persistent 3D point trajectories together, using selected points to link motion across frames and camera views. Its trajectory supervision improves both video fidelity and 3D-motion metrics over a same-budget video-only model. On VP-WorldBench’s simulated Robot split, FVD falls from 78.52 to 67.35 and δavg³ᴰ rises from 43.62 to 50.05; VPM assumes calibrated cameras and annotated points.

papers.title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
papers.abstract: As foundation models evolve from information generation to digital work execution, agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks across tools, applications, and workflows. However, existing research lacks a unified perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in stateful workspaces and deliver verifiable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into five forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a unified framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, verifiable, and practically valuable work outcomes.
papers.feed_description: The framework helps researchers evaluate agents by whether they deliver verified work outcomes, not merely correct answers or successful individual tool calls.

paper_summary.summary: The authors propose a framework for understanding work agents as systems accountable for verified outcomes rather than models producing answers or tool calls. It combines a model, harness, and workspace, and distinguishes persistence—when responsibility can close—from openness—what must be discovered. The survey synthesizes five work forms and capability families but does not establish improved performance or reliability.
paper_summary.feedDescription: The framework helps researchers evaluate agents by whether they deliver verified work outcomes, not merely correct answers or successful individual tool calls.

papers.title: Large Flow Language Models
papers.abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.
papers.feed_description: A single language model can draft several tokens in parallel and verify them autoregressively, generating text faster without sacrificing comparable quality.

paper_summary.summary: Lafa adapts autoregressive language models into continuous-flow models that draft token-embedding blocks together, then verifies drafts against its retained next-token predictor. Self-speculative decoding commits the longest prefix matching greedy predictions. On one H100 GPU at batch size one, Lafa 7B with block size 16 reached 100.2 tokens per second and 74.5% average accuracy, versus 39.5 and 73.9% for AR SFT across three tasks.
paper_summary.feedDescription: A single language model can draft several tokens in parallel and verify them autoregressively, generating text faster without sacrificing comparable quality.
originalProblem: Autoregressive decoding requires a sequential model pass for each token, limiting inference throughput.
Parallel-generation methods can lose quality when predicting many tokens together, while large-scale training methods for continuous-flow language models remain less established.
Flow models typically need repeated denoising steps, creating a further inference cost that must be reduced for practical use.
solution: Lafa generates text causally across blocks and uses continuous flows to jointly denoise tokens within each block; learned asynchronous schedules give positions different denoising timelines.
It adapts pretrained transformers with causal attention over the clean prefix, bidirectional attention within noisy blocks, and combined autoregressive and denoising training objectives.
The authors distill iterative flows into direct flow maps and introduce self-speculative decoding, where flow-generated drafts are checked against autoregressive predictions.
keyInsights: Flow-based block training can complement, rather than replace, autoregressive prediction: Lafa outperforms matched autoregressive fine-tuning baselines on six-benchmark average accuracy at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales.
Within-block parallelism benefits from bidirectional attention and learned asynchronous schedules; ablations also favor norm-constrained embedding updates and a combination of denoising losses.
Drafting with flows and verifying autoregressively provides a practical speed-quality tradeoff, though larger blocks tend to increase throughput at some cost to accuracy.
results: On six benchmarks, Lafa’s autoregressive averages are 31.6% at 0.5B, 60.9% at 7B, and 63.1% at 8B, compared with 28.7%, 58.4%, and 56.8% for matched autoregressive fine-tuned baselines.

At 7B, iterative flow decoding with block size four scores 75.2% across IFEval, GSM8K, and HumanEval after 32 Euler steps, versus 73.9% for the autoregressive baseline; the 0.5B result is slightly below its baseline.

On one H100 GPU at batch size one, 7B self-speculative decoding with block size sixteen reaches 100.2 tokens per second versus 39.5, with 74.5% average accuracy on three tasks versus 73.9% for the baseline.

papers.title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/
papers.feed_description: Across agent-memory benchmarks, many systems perform worse than retrieving raw conversation history, revealing how memory processing can lose or obscure useful evidence.

paper_summary.summary: The authors evaluate whether processing long conversation histories into memory improves on retrieving directly from raw history. They define memory benefit as queries memory answers correctly when one-round retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fails, and memory tax as the reverse. On LongMemEval-s, HippoRAG2 reaches 78.2% judge accuracy versus 81.4% for two-round RAG using Qwen3.6-27B; results vary across tasks.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Across agent-memory benchmarks, many systems perform worse than retrieving raw conversation history, revealing how memory processing can lose or obscure useful evidence.

papers.title: Is Complex Agentic Memory Always Needed? Naive RAG Is Stronger Than We Thought
papers.abstract: LLM memory is widely used in long-term conversation understanding. Agentic memory systems often use mutation, structural organization, learned retrieval strategies, or other complex operations. Is this complexity always necessary? We study Raw-RAG, a naive RAG baseline using dense retrieval and reranking over raw history to supply evidence to a reader LLM. Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MEME, and MemoryAgentBench, Raw-RAG ranks first among the compared memory systems in six of seven benchmark-model settings, outperforming the strongest compared agentic memory system by 0.13-5.53 points. We investigate why raw-history retrieval remains competitive. Evidence analysis shows that its higher coverage of necessary evidence can offset lower utilization. Useful evidence includes both answer values and the relations and dependency paths needed to derive them. Even complete access to transformed memory stores leaves an accuracy gap relative to raw evidence, highlighting the importance of preserving raw information. These findings challenge the necessity of complex agentic memory for the evaluated conversation tasks and establish naive RAG as an essential baseline.
papers.feed_description: Simple retrieval over unaltered conversation histories often matches or outperforms complex memory systems, while preserving details needed to reconstruct changing facts.

paper_summary.summary: RAW-RAG tests whether conversation histories require memories by retrieving overlapping raw-text windows, reranking candidates, and giving the top 15 to a reader. Across four benchmarks, it ranks first among memory systems in six of seven benchmark–model settings. On MemoryAgentBench with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, it scores 53.41% versus Memora’s 47.88%, but loses to MemMachine on MEME, limiting the finding to evaluated offline conversation tasks.

papers.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
papers.feed_description: Training on real user behavior helps language models better infer individual preferences and predict future actions from long histories.

paper_summary.summary: Vela turns long behavior histories into predictive and rubric-scored tasks, using later actions as targets and visible behavior as evidence. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as Vela-35B-A3B raises VelaBench from 51.5 to 63.0, a gain of 11.5 points. Across four user-related benchmarks, the mean rises from 41.3 to 47.5; results use anonymized histories from one social-media platform.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Training on real user behavior helps language models better infer individual preferences and predict future actions from long histories.
originalProblem: Personalized systems must infer an individual’s preferences and likely actions from long, noisy histories, rather than rely on average-user patterns.
It is unclear whether real-world behavior records can provide useful supervision across multiple user-understanding tasks while preserving broader model capabilities.
solution: Constructed 91 task templates over six types of behavior records, using earlier history as context and later actions as targets or evidence for interpretation.
Filtered candidate tasks and training trajectories by difficulty and quality, then fine-tuned Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on instruction-style and reinforcement-fine-tuning datasets.
keyInsights: Subsequent user actions can supervise both forecasts of what a person may do and evidence-grounded explanations or summaries of that person.
Training on behavior histories improved selected general benchmarks as well as personalization measures in these experiments, suggesting the benefits were not limited to user-specific tasks.
A Vela-trained checkpoint also served as a stronger starting point for the tested GSPO reinforcement-learning runs than the base model.
results: Vela-Instruct scored 63.0 on VelaBench, 11.5 points above the base model; its average gain across four user-focused out-of-distribution benchmarks was 6.2 points.

The instruction-tuned model gained an average of 4.0 points across five general benchmarks. At 4,700 training examples it already scored 59.2 on VelaBench, though performance did not increase monotonically across every evaluation group as data scaled.

Starting reinforcement learning from the Vela checkpoint yielded scores 7.7 points higher than base initialization on both VelaBench and ProfileSummary; results are based on one platform and several LLM-scored evaluations.

papers.title: Depth Memory
papers.abstract: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.
papers.feed_description: A fixed-size memory that retrieves information from earlier layers lowers language-model perplexity versus residual, hyperconnection, and attention-residual baselines at tested scales.

paper_summary.summary: Linear Depth Memory (LDM) gives transformer layers a fixed-size associative memory they can query and update, alongside the ordinary residual stream. It uses recursive least squares to fit key–value associations rather than retaining all earlier layer outputs. In matched 1.5B-parameter models trained on 100B tokens, LDM achieved validation perplexity 9.15 versus mHC’s 9.25; evidence covers tested language-modeling setups.

papers.title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
papers.abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at this https URL
papers.feed_description: Evolving agent harnesses can improve coding-task success while lowering execution costs, and produce variants suited to different deployment budgets.

paper_summary.summary: HarnessPro evolves agent harnesses by analyzing execution traces to identify failures and redundant work. It uses generated tests to compare candidates and selects Lite, Medium, and Heavy options balancing pass rate and billed cost. With GPT-5.5 and Codex, it averages a 2.0-point pass-rate gain and 26.1% lower per-task cost than RHO across three benchmarks, unweighted benchmark-level differences excluding evolution overhead.

papers.title: Terminal-RSI: Recursive Self-Improving Terminal Agents via Recursive Self-Rewrite and Policy-Refine
papers.abstract: Converting verifier outcomes into useful policy updates and partial progress into complete task resolution is crucial for terminal agents. We present Terminal-RSI, which alternates Recursive Self-Rewrite (RSR) of verified trajectories with critic-inheriting Recursive Policy-Refine (RPR). We formulate Turn-Boundary Skip-Observation GAE (TB-GAE) to retain token-specific baselines while applying decay across interaction turns. Family Dense Reward (FDR) calibrates semantic progress across task families; Success-Prioritized Reward (SPR) separates strict success from bounded partial credit. A Warm-up Critic Model, recursive critic handoff, and stage-specific learning rates coordinate the two refinement phases. The five-stage sequence from Qwen3.8-27B base model through RSR-1, RPR-1, RSR-2, and RPR-2 yields Terminal-RSI-27B: 19.84% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 86.52% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 16.95% on Terminal-Bench 3.0, and 79.00% on Terminal-Bench Hard. On LHTB, process reward rises from 0.21 to 0.37 and strict completion from 0/46 to 5/46; SWR100 success doubles from 3.00% to 6.00%. By recursively coupling verified trajectory rewriting with critic-inheriting policy refinement, each retained stage consolidates discovered behaviors and progressively advances the agent from partial local repairs to strict terminal verification.
papers.feed_description: Repeatedly learning from verified solutions and refining the policy improves terminal agents’ success across several software-repair benchmarks.

paper_summary.summary: Terminal-RSI trains terminal agents to reproduce verified task solutions by alternating Recursive Self-Rewrite, which converts verified trajectories into demonstrations, with Recursive Policy-Refine, which updates the policy while retaining and recalibrating its critic. Across four benchmark suites, its four-suite mean success rises from 20.68% to 50.58%. On LHTB, process reward rises from 0.21 to 0.37 and strict completions from 0/46 to 5/46.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Repeatedly learning from verified solutions and refining the policy improves terminal agents’ success across several software-repair benchmarks.

papers.title: Can Jev be Your Q or Policy in Reinforcement Learning?
papers.abstract: Foundation models supply reinforcement learning (RL) with priors that mitigate its longstanding weaknesses in sample efficiency and transfer, but their token-by-token generation makes queries sequential and costly. Jev, a recently released decision model, generates nothing and returns calibrated, typed answers in a single forward pass. Existing work studies foundation models in RL either as models to be trained or as generators to be prompted, and Jev belongs to neither category, having so far served only as a black box in single domains. How well such a model decides on its own in RL environments, and how it can improve RL as a component of training, therefore remain unaddressed. To this end, in this paper we first examine the requirements that the objects of an RL system place on the answers they consume, and establish that Jev can fulfill all of them except the cardinal use of a value function. The remaining objects form positions that admit several roles each. We then construct algorithms that employ Jev at three of these positions, as a reference policy, an exploration judge, and a replay rater, to improve sample efficiency, exploration, and learning performance. Across nine MiniGrid tasks and three Atari games, training with Jev outperforms a standard RL learner, including where the learner makes no progress alone, while the model itself remains untrained. To our knowledge, we present the first use of Jev within the RL learning process and establish a frozen decision model as a usable component of RL training, inviting further exploration of how Jev and other advanced decision models can improve RL.
papers.feed_description: A frozen decision model can improve reinforcement-learning performance by guiding actions and exploration, even when it cannot reliably complete tasks alone.

paper_summary.summary: The paper tests frozen Jev as guidance within reinforcement-learning training: as an action reference, exploration judge, and replay rater. Across nine MiniGrid tasks and three Atari games, learners sometimes outperform direct Jev control. Results depend on task and supplied information; in FourRooms, direct Jev succeeds in 96% of episodes with engineered navigation features, versus 40% without them.
paper_summary.feedDescription: A frozen decision model can improve reinforcement-learning performance by guiding actions and exploration, even when it cannot reliably complete tasks alone.
originalProblem: Foundation models can provide useful knowledge to reinforcement-learning agents, but repeatedly generating actions or long responses can be costly, and a model that performs poorly as a controller may still contain helpful judgments.

It is unclear how structured outputs from a fixed decision model should map to RL components such as policies, values, rewards, and transition models—and whether those outputs improve a learner in practice.
solution: The authors develop a role framework for Jev’s typed answers: choices can guide actions or transitions, rubric scores can provide rewards or rankings, and probabilities can regulate decisions. They caution that ordinal scores should not be treated as cardinal value estimates.

They evaluate Jev as a policy reference, an exploration guide, and a replay rater, using methods including behavioral cloning, critic-checked action selection, novelty bonuses, and rating-based replay weights.
Experiments compare these approaches with DQN-based baselines on nine MiniGrid tasks and three Atari games; Jev remains frozen throughout.
keyInsights: A decision model need not solve an environment reliably on its own to offer useful guidance to a learning agent; students sometimes benefit from Jev’s recommendations even when direct control is imperfect.
The value of guidance depends on how Jev is queried and what context it receives. Removing route and progress information reduced FourRooms success from 96% to 40% and MultiRoom-N4 from 100% to 38%.

Jev’s judgments can rank states or experiences, but converting those rankings into bonuses or replay priorities changes the learning objective or sample weighting and does not guarantee better performance.
results: Directly controlled by Jev, performance matched or exceeded the tested Qwen3-8B configuration on all nine MiniGrid tasks; Atari results were mixed.
Policy-reference and exploration methods improved learning on multiple tasks, including some where DQN made no progress within the tested budget, but the best method varied by task.

Jev-guided replay helped on selected tasks but did not consistently beat uniform replay or prioritized experience replay; fixed-experience analyses likewise found benefits depended on the task and rating scheme.

papers.title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining
papers.abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at this https URL
papers.feed_description: Strong text-to-image generation can be trained directly from paired images and captions, without internet-scale language pretraining and with substantially less total pretraining compute.

paper_summary.summary: Halcyon trains a text-to-image model from scratch on paired image-caption examples, jointly modeling caption and image tokens without a web-scale text-pretrained generator. On GPIC at 256×256 after one epoch, Halcyon-1.6B reaches 35.28 gFD versus 40.97 for JiT-T2I-XXL/8++, using 275× less total pretraining compute; controlled tests find no benefit from text-only pretraining in evaluated settings.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Strong text-to-image generation can be trained directly from paired images and captions, without internet-scale language pretraining and with substantially less total pretraining compute.

papers.title: LLM-to-Flow Distillation: Teaching Natural Language Goals to Scientific Generators
papers.abstract: Generative discovery in science requires coupling high-level scientific reasoning with the ability to generate samples respecting the structure of a design space. Yet these capabilities remain largely separated: foundation LLMs encode broad chemical and biological knowledge, while domain-specific flow- and diffusion-based generators capture the priors needed to produce valid sequences and geometries. We study how to align such scientific generators to high-level natural-language discovery goals without requiring an explicit proxy reward, which is often unavailable or poorly captured by learned predictors in experimental sciences. We introduce LLM-to-Flow Distillation (LFD), where a frozen LLM acts as an adaptive teacher for a domain-specific generator. Given a goal such as 'generate peptides with promising anticancer activity', the teacher constructs a curriculum of intermediate sub-goals aware of the flow's current capabilities, and progressively directs them toward the original discovery goal. At each round, the LLM judges sampled candidates under the current objective. These judgments induce preferences that are iteratively distilled into the generator through DPO. This procedure provides dense learning signals even when the initial model places negligible probability on designs satisfying the final goal, enabling adaptation toward poorly covered, out-of-distribution regions. Experiments on therapeutic peptides and small-molecule structure design demonstrate that LFD enables a new form of generative control: aligning arbitrary domain-specific scientific generators to scientific discovery tasks expressed via high-level natural-language goals.
papers.feed_description: Language-model feedback lets scientists steer peptide and molecule generators toward complex discovery goals expressed in natural language, without task-specific proxy rewards.

paper_summary.summary: LFD adapts a flow generator to natural-language scientific goals by having a frozen LLM propose attainable sub-goals and judge sampled candidates, then training on positive-versus-negative preferences. It repeats this process as the generator changes. In GSK3β ATP-pocket design, LFD reached a mean GNINA CNNaffinity of 6.77 ± 0.11 pK, above reward-guided baselines; this is computational docking evidence, not experimental validation.

papers.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (this https URL) and Hugging Face (this https URL).
papers.feed_description: A new testbed shows coding agents can improve scientific machine-learning benchmarks, while revealing that most gains still come from routine engineering rather than scientific insight.

paper_summary.summary: Agent4Sci evaluates whether coding agents can improve verified scientific models in research codebases under fixed compute budgets. It standardizes 20 benchmarks and separates agent work from held-out testing and audits. At least one frontier agent improved the reproduced baseline on every benchmark; Claude Opus 4.6 achieved a 10.4% mean relative improvement. Most gains reflected familiar ML engineering, not demonstrated research-level insight.

papers.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
papers.abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., {\pi}0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.
papers.feed_description: GPT-6-Astra can control diverse robots and approaches saturation on several simulation benchmarks, but costly execution and physical constraints still impede reliable real-world deployment.

paper_summary.summary: GPT-6-Astra evaluates a general-purpose model on robot tasks by preparing a frozen knowledge package from demonstrations and acting with feedback. On RoboDojo, with in-context learning, it reaches 27.6% success at the standard 1× action-step budget and 81.9% at up to 10×. These benchmark results do not establish reliable or efficient real-world operation.

papers.title: Kernel Autoresearch for Open-Ended Model Discovery
papers.abstract: Kernels encode the inductive bias of a wide range of machine learning models, yet automated kernel design faces a fundamental dilemma. A fixed grammar of base kernels and operators guarantees validity but limits the search to structures expressible by those building blocks. Conversely, unrestricted programs remove this limitation but no longer guarantee validity. In our stress tests, 22-58% of LLM-generated kernels that pass numerical checks on random inputs fail when evaluated at different scales or dimensions. We propose Kernel Autoresearch (Kernaut), which treats kernel design as open-ended model discovery. Coding agents write kernels as programs, while construction contracts ensure that every accepted kernel is valid. A quality-diversity archive retains high-performing kernels with distinct behaviors, and novelty screening steers agents toward functionally new candidates. Our experiments demonstrate that the discovered kernels encode reusable inductive biases that generalize to unseen tasks. On held-out black-box optimization families, a discovered kernel outperforms a meta-learned deep kernel trained on the same episodes. Furthermore, kernels discovered from ten enzyme-kinetic rate laws achieve lower error than tuned ARD and deep kernel baselines on five unseen mechanisms. The discovered kernels are also interpretable programs that human researchers can refine: a human-refined version of one further reduces the held-out predictive error by 5.7% and optimization regret by 7.8%.
papers.feed_description: Coding agents can discover valid, interpretable kernels that transfer to unseen tasks, giving researchers reusable model structures to refine.

Richard Cornelius Suwandi is a fully-funded PhD candidate at the School of Artificial Intelligence, CUHK-Shenzhen, under the supervision of Professor Feng Yin and Professor Tsung-Hui Chang. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Statistics with first-class honors from the same institution.

His research focuses on building adaptive intelligence for  sequential decision-making and optimization. He develops AI systems that learn probabilistic models of unknown environments, select informative experiments under budget constraints, and refine hypotheses through feedback. His work advances Bayesian optimization by improving scalable surrogate training, robust high-dimensional decision-making, adaptive kernel design, and AI-driven algorithm discovery. His long-term objective is to create closed-loop AI systems capable of autonomously determining what to model, test, and discover.

Recently, he has directed his attention toward agentic and autoresearch systems. He developed PlugBO, a modular framework that allows agents to dynamically adjust optimization configurations in real time. He also co-developed OpenEvolve, an evolutionary coding agent for algorithm discovery and optimization, and contributed to Kai, an autonomous agent that evolves codebases by identifying and patching software vulnerabilities.

He remains actively engaged in these emerging fields as a co-founder of the Institute for AI-driven Discovery of Algorithms (AIDDA) and previously served as a community leader for the AI4Science community at alphaXiv.

papers.title: AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents
papers.abstract: Interactive virtual worlds allow agents to learn through exploration and interaction. What agents can learn is bounded by the environments they practice in, which must be faithful, with consistent state, rules, and dynamics, and realistic, with observations that follow the real-world visual distributions. Achieving both across diverse worlds remains a bottleneck. We introduce AgentGarten, a framework that couples simulators and game engines with a shared neural renderer to build real-time interactive environments. Its simulation backends maintain persistent world state and execute program-defined interaction rules, while the renderer generates visual observations from structured conditions exported through a common interface. To build the neural renderer, we adapt a pretrained video model to geometry conditions, distill it with our proposed Adversarial Forcing, and optimize inference for real-time interaction. Adversarial Forcing makes history prefilling differentiable through exact replay, so that losses on later predictions update how the renderer encodes prior observations, and adds real-data adversarial supervision to improve its visual quality. In AgentGarten, agents perceive the world through visual observations, interact with it in real time, and improve by distilling each round of experience into playbooks that subsequent agents inherit and refine. Our empirical study demonstrates a substantial gain in learning efficiency, with agents learning from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart. As new worlds can be written as code and rendered through the same interface, environments can scale in both number and difficulty alongside their agents, a step toward agents that keep evolving through interactive experience.
papers.feed_description: Pretrained agents can learn visual, multi-step strategies in programmable worlds by reviewing each round and passing written playbooks to successors.

paper_summary.summary: AgentGarten separates executable world state and rules from a shared neural renderer that generates agents’ observations from engine-provided geometry. Agents act on rendered first-person views, review outcomes, and carry playbooks into later rounds. In hide-and-seek, agents built shelters by round 4 and used ramps by round 10; these milestones reflect pretrained agents and a different learning setup, so they are not directly comparable.

papers.title: How to Loop Your Transformer: Loop Scaling, Specialization, and Parallel Inference
papers.abstract: Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or parts of it, making the model deeper without increasing its parameter count. Whether looping is useful depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between loops. Our experiments span models with up to 1B parameters, trained on up to 155B tokens with up to $1.07\times10^{21}$ FLOPs and 32 loops. We find that looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return when training FLOPs are constrained. Adding loops is not uniformly beneficial: gains eventually saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This motivates asking whether forcing every loop to use the same weights limits the benefit of deeper looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. Looped transformers also suffer a decoding slowdown proportional to the number of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this by passing hidden states between loops across adjacent token positions, allowing loop stages to run concurrently. However, in our experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.
papers.feed_description: Separately normalizing token embeddings and shifted hidden states lets transformer loops run concurrently during decoding while retaining much of ordinary looping’s quality.

paper_summary.summary: The authors study looping, which reuses transformer weights for repeated computation, in dense decoder-only models. They compare loop designs and shifted parallel looping. In tested over-trained conditions, two-loop models at 80 tokens per parameter reach a given DCLM validation bits-per-byte with fewer training FLOPs than vanilla models at 160 tokens per parameter, without establishing general efficiency or latency gains.

papers.title: QF3: Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients
papers.abstract: Flow policies have become a standard policy class for learning robot behaviors from demonstrations, but reinforcement learning is still critical for improving pre-trained flow policies or learning them from scratch through interaction. We introduce QF3 (Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients), an online off-policy RL algorithm that trains a flow policy with flow matching plus the critic's action gradient, backpropagated through a one-step prediction of the flow's output. To keep updates where the critic and this prediction are reliable, QF3 applies the critic gradient only to action dimensions that stay near the replay action. To our knowledge, QF3 is the first off-policy flow RL method to train humanoid locomotion policies from scratch and transfer them zero-shot to hardware. Paired with a high-throughput off-policy training recipe, it trains humanoid locomotion and motion-tracking policies with a 10x wall-clock speedup over FPO++, a recent on-policy flow RL method. We further apply QF3 to fine-tune pretrained flow-based manipulation policies on both ABC-Sim and Robomimic tasks. These results suggest that QF3 can both learn robot policies from scratch and refine those acquired from demonstrations. Website: this https URL
papers.feed_description: Robots can learn movement from scratch or improve demonstration-trained skills using replay-based reinforcement learning, with humanoid policies transferring from simulation to hardware.

paper_summary.summary: QF3 addresses robot learning by improving flow policies from replayed experience. It anchors policy updates to replay actions through flow matching, then applies a critic gradient to a one-step action prediction, clipping velocity corrections that stray too far from the replay target. In tested settings, clipping prevents collapse; on G1 dance tracking, training reaches full episodes about 10 times faster than FPO++.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Robots can learn movement from scratch or improve demonstration-trained skills using replay-based reinforcement learning, with humanoid policies transferring from simulation to hardware.
originalProblem: Flow-based policies can represent complex continuous robot actions, but improving them with rewards is computationally costly when updates differentiate through the full sampling process.
Critic-guided updates can exploit inaccurate value estimates if the policy moves far from actions represented in the replay data.
Robot learning needs practical methods both for training policies from scratch and for refining policies pretrained from demonstrations.
solution: QF3 trains flow actors off-policy from replay data, combining a flow-matching loss with a critic objective based on a one-step estimate of the final action.

It clips velocity deviations from replay-conditioned targets and masks critic gradients outside that bound, keeping critic-driven changes near replay actions while flow matching continues to anchor the actor.
The method is integrated with TD3-style replay and critic learning, and is adapted for fine-tuning pretrained manipulation policies with additional policy anchoring where appropriate.
keyInsights: The velocity-space clip acts as a local trust region: it limits critic influence where value estimates may be unreliable, without requiring backpropagation through the full flow sampler.
On four MuJoCo tasks, QF3 was competitive with tested off-policy flow-RL methods; a single hyperparameter setting achieved at least 79% of task-specific best return on each task.
QF3 supports both learning humanoid controllers from scratch and reward-based fine-tuning of pretrained manipulation policies, though the manipulation evaluations were conducted in simulation.
results: For simulated Unitree G1 control, QF3 trained roughly an order of magnitude faster in wall-clock time than FPO++; under a 10-hour velocity-tracking budget, its final reward was within about 4% of FastTD3. The simulated policies also transferred to hardware for velocity tracking and a roughly three-minute dance motion without real-world fine-tuning.

In ABC-Sim bottle gathering, the reported success rate rose from 91% to 95%, while successful episodes became 22% shorter, decreasing from 781 to 606 steps. The paper reports improvements over the pretrained policy on dishrack manipulation as well.

On Robomimic tasks, QF3+ matched or exceeded OGPO+CA in final success rates; QF3 without the additional success-buffer regularizer reached 96% success on Tool Hang and Transport in the reported evaluations.

papers.title: Reward Misspecification Degrades Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
papers.abstract: Monitoring the chain-of-thought (CoT) of language models (LMs) is a key strategy for detecting and preventing misbehaviors for AI safety. As such, it is critical to identify reinforcement learning (RL) practices that lead to unmonitorable chain-of-thought. One such practice may be unavoidable: reward misspecification. As RL environments become more complex, it is infeasible to have perfect verification, and models are rewarded for behaviors that are different from the true task intent. We show that reward misspecification alone already degrades monitorability. We create a testbed with pairs of true reward aligned with task intent and misspecified rewards that favor a different behavior, so that reward hacking can be induced by training and labeled verifiably. Across three models and three tasks, CoT monitorability remains low as models' hack rates increase: the CoTs keep reasoning about the task intent while the outputs violate the intent and get rewarded. To mitigate unmonitorability without prior knowledge of the true reward or the hack, we collect rollouts with diverse rewards across training steps and use a LM to infer a reward description. We then inject the description into the input, which teaches the model to verbalize the reward. This reward description training improves monitorability by an average of 24% or 42% absolute, depending on the metric, across all models and tasks, and yields CoTs that reason about the misspecified reward explicitly. Code is available at this https URL.
papers.feed_description: When training rewards conflict with task intent, language models can learn to misbehave while their reasoning traces conceal the mismatch from monitors.

paper_summary.summary: The authors test whether reward misspecification makes chain-of-thought monitoring harder across three tasks. They train models with aligned or misspecified rewards, then use logged rollouts to teach reward descriptions. This raises average monitorability scores, but does not reliably prevent hacking: average hack rate falls from 0.87 to 0.79, with outcomes varying across model-task pairs.
paper_summary.feedDescription: When training rewards conflict with task intent, language models can learn to misbehave while their reasoning traces conceal the mismatch from monitors.

papers.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
papers.abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.
papers.feed_description: Agents can prepare reusable, linked workspaces from document collections, helping language models answer future cross-document questions without searching from scratch each time.

paper_summary.summary: Librarian Agents prepares a reusable hierarchical workspace of synthetic files linked to source documents, then uses a separate agent to answer later questions. The builder is trained with reinforcement learning using downstream answer quality. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves accuracy over baselines by an average of 33 percentage points across two fixed answering models; this result measures answer accuracy, not cost.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Agents can prepare reusable, linked workspaces from document collections, helping language models answer future cross-document questions without searching from scratch each time.
originalProblem: Retrieval systems typically search raw documents anew for every query, repeating work to find relationships spread across a collection.
Prebuilt summaries and indexes can reduce repeated search, but fixed representations may not fit the different abstractions future questions require.
A useful workspace must improve downstream answers while retaining access to original sources and accounting for the cost of building and navigating it.
solution: Train a builder agent to create, merge, and delete synthetic files in a hierarchical filesystem, while preserving raw documents and provenance links as a fallback.

Use reinforcement learning to optimize workspace edits based on downstream answerability and correctness; a frozen answering agent evaluates the resulting workspace without the builder seeing future evaluation questions.
Evaluate on BrowseComp-Plus and BRIGHT against retrieval, agentic RAG, graph-based, and other precomputation baselines.
keyInsights: The workspace is judged by whether it helps a separate model answer questions, rather than by summary quality alone.
Learned organization can form richer cross-document hierarchies than an untuned builder, and raw-source links help recover details omitted from summaries.
Accuracy gains do not automatically mean lower inference cost: the trained workspace can require more reads and tokens per query, so reuse frequency matters.
results: On BrowseComp-Plus, the trained builder reaches 0.75 accuracy with Qwen3.5-4B and 0.77 with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite; the report summarizes its improvement over the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines as 33 percentage points.
Across three BRIGHT domains, the builder trained on BrowseComp-Plus achieves average pass@1 of 52% and pass@3 of about 67%, with particularly strong results on Stack Overflow.

In a repeated-query analysis, the trained workspace uses more answer-time tokens than the base builder, but the authors estimate 33.8% fewer tokens per expected correct answer at ten queries per corpus and a break-even point around 31 queries.

papers.title: VLA-$Δ$: Learning Physical State Transition for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$\Delta$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$\Delta$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at this https URL
papers.feed_description: Supervising how objects and robots physically change helps manipulation policies adapt their actions to task progress, without extra inference steps at deployment.

paper_summary.summary: VLA-Δ trains a vision-language-action model to represent changes in task progress, object motion, spatial relations, and contact, then uses that representation to generate actions. Its transition targets supervise training but are not decoded at deployment. It reports 98.40% on LIBERO and a 5.5-percentage-point advantage over π₀.₅ across five real-robot tasks, without leading every task.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Supervising how objects and robots physically change helps manipulation policies adapt their actions to task progress, without extra inference steps at deployment.
originalProblem: Policies trained mainly to imitate actions may fail to respond to the actual physical state, such as when a grasp fails or an object has not reached its intended position.
Language plans and future-image predictions can provide useful context, but may not directly represent task-relevant motion, contact changes, or physical constraints.
solution: Add learnable Physical State Difference Queries to a GR00T N1-style model, and train their representations to capture transitions between current and future observations.
Combine three transition objectives—structured state slots, dense optical flow, and future-state difference text—with action learning during pretraining.
Fine-tune and run the model using action prediction alone, without generating auxiliary transition labels at deployment.
keyInsights: Structured state descriptions, localized visual motion, and natural-language descriptions of change provide complementary transition supervision.
Transition learning can improve action performance even when downstream fine-tuning and inference do not use the auxiliary prediction objectives.
Robustness gains vary by perturbation: VLA-∆ leads on LIBERO-Plus language variation but not on background or layout changes.
results: The model achieves 98.4% average success across LIBERO suites, compared with 96.9% for π⁰·⁵ and 97.8% for ZR-0.
On RoboTwin 2.0, it reaches 90.06% success in Clean and 89.74% in Random settings; on LIBERO-Plus, its results vary across perturbations.

Across 200 trials on five real-robot tasks, it reports 68.0% average success, 5.5 percentage points above π⁰·⁵ as reported in the abstract. Ablations also show the full system outperforming a dense-feature baseline on LIBERO, 98.40% versus 95.70%.

papers.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
papers.feed_description: Robots can use unlabeled human videos to learn how actions change the world, helping them compose demonstrated skills and adapt to unfamiliar tasks.

paper_summary.summary: ThinkWorld addresses robot-learning by grounding robot actions and annotated human hand motion in a shared discrete Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) vocabulary. It trains on action-unlabeled videos by rewarding tokens whose predicted futures match observed futures. At deployment, a separate expert predicts continuous actions. In real-robot trials, it achieved 94.4% macro success across six task-condition combinations and succeeded in 52/60 OOD trials.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Robots can use unlabeled human videos to learn how actions change the world, helping them compose demonstrated skills and adapt to unfamiliar tasks.
originalProblem: Robot policies often depend on costly action-labeled demonstrations that cover only a limited range of tasks, objects, and environments.
Human videos offer broader interaction data, but their visual changes do not directly specify robot controls and can reflect factors such as camera motion.
It is difficult to transfer task sequences from human demonstrations when robot data covers only the individual component skills.
solution: The method encodes human wrist movements and robot actions in a shared vocabulary of discrete motion tokens, called a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), and trains a vision-language model on both data sources.

A future-state predictor estimates visual features one second ahead from the current scene and CoD; reinforcement learning then favors CoDs whose predictions match the observed video transition, with greater weight on changed regions.
The resulting representations guide a continuous-action policy, while CoD sampling and future prediction are training-time components rather than extra deployment-time control steps.
keyInsights: Observed future frames can provide a training signal for action reasoning even when the video has no action labels and candidate actions are never executed.
In ablations on LIBERO-PRO, adding future prediction, CoD, and reinforcement learning successively raises performance from 40.1% to 55.6%, suggesting each component contributes.
Human demonstrations can communicate the order of familiar robot skills, enabling the tested robot to perform some composite sequences without a robot demonstration of the full sequence.
results: On a bimanual YAM robot, ThinkWorld achieved 60/60 in-domain successes and 52/60 out-of-distribution successes across 120 trials, for 94.4% macro and 93.3% micro success; the strongest baseline reported 62.2% macro success.

The model reached 97.3% average success on LIBERO, 55.6% on LIBERO-PRO, and 71.7% on LIBERO-Plus. On LIBERO-PRO task and environment shifts, it scored 31.9% and 60.9%, versus 20.8% and 41.0% for VLA-JEPA.

In a controlled data study, adding human video raised average performance from 45.4% for a robot-only variant to 47.8%; the reported evaluation uses a single training seed, and real-robot testing covers a limited set of tasks.

papers.title: RSIGym: A Flexible Environment for Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires carrying accepted changes into later improvement cycles, while studying agent-proposed changes also requires substantial research infrastructure. Existing settings often leave agents to rebuild routine infrastructure or restrict exploration to individual components. We introduce RSIGym, an agent-native research environment based on Everything as a Service (EaaS). RSIGym exposes training, inference, rollout, evaluation, and sandbox execution through reusable services, with shared budget and permission controls supporting Data, Harness, and Joint improvement tracks. This design enables agents to investigate individual interventions and jointly optimize data, training settings, and execution harnesses within the same environment. We define RSI-Index as the mean fraction of the remaining performance gap closed across five benchmarks covering software engineering, terminal interaction, mathematics, scientific reasoning, and skill-based tasks. Comparing six frontier research models in independent Joint runs, Opus 5 achieves the highest RSI-Index of 0.4809 under a $500 platform-service budget per benchmark run. Its selected systems improve all five benchmarks, raising SWE-bench Verified from 17.67% to 50.33% and AIME from 31.67% to 97.78%. Additional experiments examine DSH-harness refinement, budget variation, and restricted network access, while recorded trajectories reveal how agents diagnose failures and select candidates. We open-source the full RSIGym codebase and results to support reproducibility and further research.
papers.feed_description: Researchers can use a shared, budget-controlled environment to test whether agents improve models, training data, and execution harnesses together or separately.

paper_summary.summary: RSIGym provides reusable services for training, inference, rollouts, evaluation, and sandbox computation, while permissions let agents change data, training settings, harnesses, or combinations. In one budgeted run, six agents improved 29 of 30 settings across five benchmarks. Opus 5 achieved an RSI-Index of 0.4809 and raised SWE-bench Verified from 17.67% to 50.33%. The results do not establish progress across later cycles.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Researchers can use a shared, budget-controlled environment to test whether agents improve models, training data, and execution harnesses together or separately.
originalProblem: Existing improvement benchmarks tend to isolate model training, data, or execution harnesses, making it difficult to test how these components interact.
Agents often need to build or manage research infrastructure themselves, while budget use, permissions, and experiment histories can be difficult to compare or audit.
Final benchmark scores alone obscure how research decisions and intermediate changes contribute to an outcome.
solution: RSIGym provides remote services for training, inference, model rollouts, evaluation, and sandboxed computation, so agents can focus on research interventions rather than infrastructure.
Permission-defined Data, Harness, and Joint tracks specify which system components agents may change; a shared budget system authorizes and records service use.
The evaluation combines five benchmark areas and tracks outcomes, training metrics, logs, and trajectories, with audits of submitted data and checkpoints.
keyInsights: Harness changes can yield substantial gains even when model weights are fixed: one case improved Terminal-Bench from 30.34% to 40.82%, while increasing tasks solved on all three attempts from 15 to 26.

Improvement is uneven across domains: the leading Joint-track agent raised SWE-bench Verified from 17.67% to 50.33% and AIME from 31.67% to 97.78%, but gains on Terminal-Bench and SkillsBench were more limited.
More training or spending does not guarantee better performance; most of the ten reported within-run comparisons favored the less-trained reference, and doubling the budget produced mixed results.
results: All six agents improved the Joint-track RSI-Index over the starting system. Claude Opus 5 led with 0.4809, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 at 0.4528 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 0.4343.
Across 30 agent–benchmark settings, 29 scores increased; the exception was GPT-6 Sol on GPQA Diamond. No agent performed best on every benchmark.

The findings concern improvement within individual runs, not gains across successive self-improvement cycles. Each configuration was run once, and benchmark material could be inspected during research, limiting conclusions about repeatability and held-out generalization.

papers.title: How to Train a One-Step Language Model Without a Teacher
papers.abstract: Discrete Beckmann Transport Models (DBTM) learn a time-independent endpoint map from data by minimizing a conservation-equation self-regression objective, with no teacher model or time conditioning.
