DBTM reports coherence–diversity Pareto frontiers on LM1B and OpenWebText, 84.6% accuracy on hard Sudoku at 4 function evaluations, and 16.8% on GSM8K at 32.

papers.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
papers.abstract:
Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further.
We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.
papers.feed_description: Periodically resetting research agents while preserving their best solution can break stalled searches and improve results across programming, kernel optimization, and model-training tasks.

paper_summary.summary: The authors test whether resetting search history helps agents improve stalled optimization tasks. They periodically clear agent sessions and candidate-history state while retaining the best candidate, allowing four-agent teams to restart exploration. On AHC014, forgetting gains 9.2% on average over 30 more proposals per agent, versus 1.4% for continuing; experiments do not isolate which cleared state drives the gain.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Periodically resetting research agents while preserving their best solution can break stalled searches and improve results across programming, kernel optimization, and model-training tasks.
originalProblem: Long-running research agents can stagnate even when given more time or run in parallel; their proposals may become smaller and more conservative as prior reasoning and failed attempts accumulate.
Sharing candidates among agents can spread useful ideas, but may also encourage convergence and does not by itself prevent a team from plateauing.
It is unclear how to retain progress while removing accumulated context that may constrain further exploration.
solution: The system divides search into rounds and, at each reset, clears agents’ sessions and candidate histories while retaining only the best candidate and its score.
Four agents work in parallel and share candidate commits and scores during each round; the experiments compare this setup with a continuous single agent and four independent agents.
The authors evaluate the approach on four optimization tasks, using three runs per configuration, and conduct a targeted AHC014 comparison of continuing versus resetting after a plateau.
keyInsights: Preserving the strongest artifact while discarding search history can support continued exploration without restarting from scratch.
Communication and forgetting can complement one another: fresh sessions encourage larger changes, while shared candidates can help agents refine promising ideas.
Reset benefits were strongest early and generally declined in later rounds, suggesting that both reset timing and retained information may matter.
results: The communicating team with forgetting achieved the best mean and best-run results on all four tasks; versus four independent agents, mean performance improved by about 14% on AHC014, 10% on VLIW cycles, and 15% on Frontier-CS, while nanochat validation BPB decreased from 0.980 to 0.961.
A new best candidate followed 32 of 36 reset events. On AHC014, the mean best score rose 11.2% after the first reset and 1.7% after the third.
In a plateaued AHC014 search, forgetting led to gains of 4.5%–9.2% across the tested team setups, compared with 1.4%–1.9% from continuing; fresh agents also made larger edits.

papers.title: EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution
papers.abstract: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that autonomously decides where to explore next and turns the resulting physical interaction into improved code and skills. EmbodiedRSI realizes this through a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, in which competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish these hypotheses. Their outcomes guide Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, and Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory according to their value for later Fast-System improvement. On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI reaches 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. EmbodiedRSI also reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. Beyond benchmark performance, EmbodiedRSI transfers zero-shot to real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.
papers.feed_description: Robots can adapt to new tasks and real-world conditions by choosing informative trials and improving their code and skills without retraining their foundation model.

paper_summary.summary: EmbodiedRSI adapts a robot harness around a frozen vision-language-action model by maintaining competing code and skill hypotheses, selecting simulator experiments for expected information gain relative to cost, and retaining useful evidence. On RoboCasa365’s Composite-Unseen suite, it reports 71.3% success, versus 40.1% for Harness VLA. This supports harness-level adaptation on tested tasks, not model learning or universal gains.

papers.title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
papers.abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.
papers.feed_description: Training in simulated interviews improved a language model’s history-taking, diagnostic formulation, and patient-centered communication in psychiatrist-led role-play, while acute safety failures persisted.

paper_summary.summary: The simulation-trained model improves psychiatric intake conversations by practicing multi-turn encounters with simulated patients and receiving rewards for clinical reasoning, communication, and safety. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study, it received higher psychiatrist transcript ratings than its identically prompted base model in 46 of 60 matched scenario pairs (76.7%). This supports improvement in controlled text encounters, not real-patient safety or effectiveness.

papers.title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.
papers.feed_description: Reinforcement learning can teach language models to solve problems when able and abstain or choose safer actions when success is unlikely, without fallback labels.

paper_summary.summary: GracefulRL trains models to favor success over safe fallback and fallback over error, while preserving a learning signal for success. It optimizes a combination of the log probability of success and the log probability of avoiding error, without labels or an inference-time verifier. On AIME, Qwen3-4B-Base reduced errors by 88.8% with a 3.1-point success decrease, in tested settings.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Reinforcement learning can teach language models to solve problems when able and abstain or choose safer actions when success is unlikely, without fallback labels.
originalProblem: Reward schemes that mainly reward success can encourage guessing or risky actions, because they give a policy little incentive to stop when success is unlikely.
Assigning fallback an intermediate reward and using standard policy-gradient methods can cause training to collapse to always falling back—or fail to learn fallback behavior.
Separate confidence estimates and inference-time thresholds do not make fallback an action that the policy itself learns to take.
solution: GracefulRL optimizes a weighted combination of the log probability of success and the log probability of avoiding error, encoding the preference Success ≻ Fallback ≻ Error.
A training-time verifier labels sampled trajectories as success, fallback, or error; a utility parameter controls how strongly the policy prioritizes avoiding errors.
The method conditions the policy on the desired caution level, without requiring task-specific labels identifying which individual problems the model cannot solve.
keyInsights: Expected-reward policy gradients can lose their learning signal near policies concentrated on a single outcome; the paper’s analysis shows the proposed population objective retains a gradient near fallback-only or error-only policies under stated assumptions.
Fallback is not always a simple tradeoff against success: in Minesweeper, learning to fall back was associated with both fewer errors and more completed boards.
Caution can transfer beyond the math training domain, though benchmark abstention labels do not establish whether a question is beyond a particular model’s capabilities.
results: On AIME with Qwen3-4B-Base, moving from the least cautious setting to the most cautious reduced errors from 79.1% to 8.9%, while success changed from 20.1% to 17.0%; the reported reliability frontiers Pareto-dominated RLCR with test-time thresholding.
On AbstentionBench, macro abstention F1 increased from 0.472 at c=0.2 to 0.677 at c=0.8, compared with 0.590 for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.

In Minesweeper, GracefulRL at c=0.5 achieved 77.4% success and 6.0% error, versus 67.4% success and 17.0% error for MaxRL without fallback reward; standard RLOO collapsed to always falling back in this condition.

papers.title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low-precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher-precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by $1.20$--$1.47\times$ over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about $1.8\times$ the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on the two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.
papers.feed_description: Caching recent inputs instead of rewriting recurrent states at every step reduces decoding memory traffic and makes speculative rollback a simple buffer-pointer move.

paper_summary.summary: ReplaySSM reduces recurrent-state writes during state-space model decoding by keeping a checkpoint and buffering recent inputs, then periodically folding them into the checkpoint. It also supports pointer-based speculative rollback and separate low- and high-precision checkpoints. At batch size 256, whole-model decode latency improved 1.20–1.47× across four hybrid models; gains depend on setup and batch size, and checkpoint reads remain.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Caching recent inputs instead of rewriting recurrent states at every step reduces decoding memory traffic and makes speculative rollback a simple buffer-pointer move.
originalProblem: SSM decoding repeatedly reads and writes a large recurrent state, creating a memory-traffic bottleneck, especially at high batch sizes.
Speculative decoding needs to restore the state after rejected draft tokens; conventional approaches save costly per-token snapshots or recompute states.
Feeding a quantized state back into the recurrence can compound rounding error over long generations.
solution: Represent the recurrent state as a checkpoint and a bounded buffer of recent inputs; replay buffered inputs to compute outputs and periodically fold them into the checkpoint.
During speculative verification, append draft inputs and commit accepted tokens by advancing a buffer pointer, avoiding separate state snapshots for each draft token.
Keep a higher-precision checkpoint for recurrence updates while optionally using a low-precision copy for output computation, so output quantization error is not repeatedly fed back.
keyInsights: The approach trades fewer full-state writes for additional replay-buffer processing; the best balance depends on window length, batch size, and hardware behavior.
Benefits are workload-dependent: gains are strongest when state traffic is a bottleneck at large batches, while batch-one kernel performance is at or below parity in the reported tests.
Separating output precision from recurrence precision can reduce long-run quantization error without requiring all output computations to use full-precision state.
results: With a window of 16 at batch size 256, isolated SSM kernels run 1.46–1.80× faster and whole-model decoding 1.20–1.47× faster across four evaluated models.

At batch size 512 and verification length 4, speculative throughput reaches 1.85× the conventional method on Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B and 2.10× on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, with similar token acceptance lengths.

In low-precision evaluations, NVFP4 output reads with FP16 recurrence reduce average accuracy losses versus FP32 to 0.15 points on MMLU-Pro, 2.36 on GPQA-Diamond, and 0.10 on Math-L5; RULER-128K scores stay within 0.3 points of FP32.

papers.title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
papers.abstract: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.
papers.feed_description: Most frontier language models favor wording associated with comprehension difficulty, and experiments suggest pressure to produce shorter answers can encourage this shift.

paper_summary.summary: The authors compare model text in chat, coding, and essays with round-trip translation paraphrases, measuring features associated with human processing difficulty. Original wording often contains more such features, but the study does not test reader comprehension. A length-penalty task drove shorter choices; two constructions exceeded 98% without KL regularization. This does not establish the cause of frontier-model patterns.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Most frontier language models favor wording associated with comprehension difficulty, and experiments suggest pressure to produce shorter answers can encourage this shift.
originalProblem: AI-generated prose can feel dense or difficult to follow despite being grammatical, but the linguistic features behind that impression are not well characterized.
The study asks whether language models use constructions linked to human processing difficulty more often than meaning-preserving alternatives and human writing.
It also investigates whether pressure to produce shorter responses can cause models to favor such constructions; reader comprehension itself is not directly measured.
solution: Compare outputs from 14 models across chat, coding, and essay settings using measures such as dependency length, noun stacking, relativizer omission, and word-sequence frequency.
Use English-to-Japanese-to-English translation as an approximate meaning-preserving paraphrase to examine how linguistic features change with rewording.
Fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on structured sentence generation with varying length penalties, then test whether preferences for shorter forms transfer to other constructions.
keyInsights: Many frontier and near-frontier models used more low-frequency sequences and several constructions associated with processing costs than their round-trip paraphrases; patterns varied by genre and model family.
Models often favored omitting optional words, while effects for long dependencies and stacked nouns were less consistent, particularly in essays.

A length penalty can push models toward shorter grammatical alternatives even when task correctness is maintained; transfer was clear for related optional-*that* cases but limited for more distant constructions.
results: Across the corpus comparisons, differences were generally strongest in chat and coding; essay results were mixed, and some model versions showed weaker or reversed patterns.
Increasing the length penalty increased selection of shorter forms in the fine-tuning task. The shift was strongest without KL regularization and remained smaller with it.

The findings identify linguistic indicators and a possible optimization mechanism, but do not establish effects on actual reading time or comprehension; translation artifacts and the small-scale intervention also limit causal conclusions.

papers.title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
papers.abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.
papers.feed_description: Robot agents acquire manipulation skills through online trials and turn successful strategies into reusable programs, avoiding teleoperation data for many tested tasks and robot types.

paper_summary.summary: RAX lets robots learn tasks by exploring actions and turning successful decisions into reusable programs. A frozen language model observes outcomes, revises code for perception, planning, and control, without updating its parameters or training a policy. The paper reports a 37.4-percentage-point average margin over the strongest prior learned model across five selected simulation comparisons, not all benchmarks or robot agents.

papers.title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
papers.abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
papers.feed_description: Robots can adapt world-model predictions to hidden physical conditions from one or two interactions, improving action choices in simulated and real-world tasks.

paper_summary.summary: T2-Z adapts an action-conditioned world model to hidden environmental variation by optimizing a compact latent from observed interaction trajectories, without labels for hidden factors. The trained model stays frozen during test-time adaptation. Across four real-world tasks, average tracked-state prediction error fell from 19.30 to 10.85 pixels and action success rose from 26.47% to 70.80%; these are task averages, not guarantees.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Robots can adapt world-model predictions to hidden physical conditions from one or two interactions, improving action choices in simulated and real-world tasks.
originalProblem: A world model conditioned only on images and actions can predict the wrong outcome when hidden properties—such as friction, object mass, or spring stiffness—change how the environment responds.
Methods that represent environmental properties often require predefined factors and labels, or a learned encoder tied to a fixed interaction-history format.
solution: T2-Z adds a 32-dimensional environment latent to an action-conditioned video model; the shared model learns across environments while separate latents are optimized to explain each environment’s observed dynamics.
At test time, the model is frozen and a new latent is directly optimized from interaction trajectories, then used to predict outcomes for candidate actions not used during adaptation.
keyInsights: A small number of interaction trajectories can provide enough evidence to adapt predictions in the evaluated tasks; performance generally improves up to 40 latent-optimization steps and then largely levels off.

Prediction-driven latents show structure associated with varying physical factors and are less dominated by background appearance in the tested analysis, though this does not establish unique or causal encoding.
Better visual similarity is not always the same as better physical prediction: task-relevant errors and action success can improve even when a perceptual metric worsens on an individual task.
results: In simulation, average physical error falls from 12.86 to 4.80 and action success rises from 37.9% to 74.2%; T2-Z has the highest action-success rate across all seven simulated tasks reported.
On four real-world tasks, average physical error decreases from 19.30 to 10.85 pixels and action success increases from 26.47% to 70.80% relative to the standard world model.
Reported task-level gains include success increasing from 35.0% to 69.7% for simulated combined mass and friction, and from 20.0% to 83.3% for real-world Stick Balance.

papers.title: On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation enables post-training foundation models without relying on stronger external teachers. However, existing approaches rely on ground-truth question-answer pairs, human-curated problem sets, or other supervised signals. In this work, we reformulate on-policy self-distillation as a self-training framework, driven by self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations. We push supervision to the limit: guided solely by coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model synthesizes its own curriculum of queries and privileged reasoning traces without access to any human-curated prompts or answers. We find that self-distillation on fully synthetic privileged information enables a model to improve across multiple domains while retaining its capabilities on domains it is not self-trained on. We demonstrate the generality of this framework across text and multimodal domains, achieving consistent self-improvement on standard language benchmarks and Visual Question Answering. Our findings demonstrate that foundation models possess rich latent capabilities that can be amplified without external task supervision or curated problem distributions.
papers.feed_description: Language models can improve reasoning by generating their own training questions and solutions from broad topic descriptions, without curated examples or external teachers.

paper_summary.summary: OPST trains models on self-generated questions from broad topic descriptions, without curated training questions or answers. A question-only student learns from token-level teacher guidance, while the teacher sees the generated candidate answer and rationale. On Gemma 4 E2B, MMLU rises from 37.5% to 47.7%, versus 38.3% for SFT and 37.3% for GRPO on the same data. Experiments use small models; verification checks consistency, not correctness.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Language models can improve reasoning by generating their own training questions and solutions from broad topic descriptions, without curated examples or external teachers.
originalProblem: Post-training often depends on costly human-curated questions and verified answers, while existing self-training approaches may still require curated question sets or provide only scalar reward signals.
Self-generated training data can contain errors, and directly imitating it risks reinforcing incorrect answers or harming capabilities outside the target domain.
solution: Starting from broad topic descriptors, OPST generates questions, rationales, and candidate answers, then filters samples through answer consistency checks and a test of whether the current model already solves them reliably.

The student generates responses on-policy; an EMA teacher sees the same response prefixes plus the generated rationale and answer, and supplies token-level targets through a skewed Jensen–Shannon objective.
A visual variant uses unlabeled images and generated scene information as privileged context, with consistency checks across image transformations.
keyInsights: Generated answers and rationales can serve as teacher context without being treated as ground-truth targets, making the training signal less directly dependent on exact synthetic labels.
Filtering for self-consistency and student uncertainty helps shape a changing curriculum, though consistency does not establish factual correctness.
The approach can improve targeted benchmarks, but transfer is uneven; the reported evidence is limited to selected model sizes and evaluation settings.
results: For Gemma 4 E2B without thinking, OPST raises MMLU accuracy from 37.5 to 47.7 and improves the four-benchmark average by 7.3 points; E4B also shows average gains across the reported settings.
OPST generally exceeds SFT and GRPO trained on the same generated data, and approaches supervised on-policy distillation in the tested comparisons.

On unlabeled OpenImages V4, Visual OPST increases VQAv2 accuracy by 6.9 points for E2B when caption and spatial information are combined; out-of-domain effects vary, including a 4.9-point drop on MATH-500 in one setting.

papers.title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
papers.abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.
papers.feed_description: Soft-MTP improves next-token accuracy and speculative decoding at no measurable training overhead by removing noisy gradients from multi-token prediction.

paper_summary.summary: Soft-MTP changes multi-token prediction training so MTP heads learn from the model’s own next-token predictions while the shared output head retains cross-entropy training. It recovers this self-distillation signal through gradient routing, without computing a vocabulary-wide KL loss. Across 167M–1.2B models, it improves validation loss and eight-task average accuracy over standard MTP; evidence is limited to tested scales.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Soft-MTP improves next-token accuracy and speculative decoding at no measurable training overhead by removing noisy gradients from multi-token prediction.
originalProblem: Standard MTP trains future-token heads against observed one-hot tokens, mixing a useful signal for matching next-token predictions with a noisier residual that can interfere with learning.
Directly optimizing KL divergence between MTP and next-token distributions can require substantial memory and disrupt fused cross-entropy training kernels.
MTP predictions are used as speculative drafts, so their agreement with the model’s next-token distribution matters for decoding efficiency.
solution: The authors decompose the standard MTP gradient into a KL self-distillation component and a residual tied to next-token prediction errors.

Soft-MTP routes the aligned next-token cross-entropy gradient through the MTP hidden state with a straight-through construction, canceling the residual while leaving the forward pass and NTP loss unchanged.
The method reuses existing cross-entropy computations, adds no parameters, and keeps the shared output head trained on observed tokens.
keyInsights: The residual component has about four times lower signal-to-noise ratio than the KL component and contributes roughly 80% of the MTP gradient reaching the shared trunk.
In the reported analysis, steps in the KL component’s direction reduce next-token loss, whereas steps in the residual direction increase it.
Soft-MTP matches direct KL training on many measured outcomes while preserving standard MTP’s reported memory use and throughput.
results: Across models from 167 million to 1.2 billion parameters, Soft-MTP improves speculative-decoding acceptance length by about 1.8–2.2% and inference speedup by about 1.4–1.5% over standard MTP.
Zero-shot average accuracy improves at all tested sizes, with gains around 0.5 percentage points at 689 million and 1.2 billion parameters; at the larger sizes it also exceeds the NTP baseline.

After NTP-only fine-tuning of 1.2-billion-parameter models, Soft-MTP beats standard MTP on seven of eight reported math and code results, including gains of 1.1 points on GSM8K and 1.8 points on MATH-500.

papers.title: Shared Geometry As A Rosetta Stone: Cross-Modal Alignment Without Paired Data
papers.abstract: Multimodal representations enable zero-shot classification and retrieval, but aligning independently trained models usually requires large amounts of paired data. Yet, the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that models trained on different modalities may converge spontaneously toward a shared representation geometry. But then, do we even need paired examples for cross-modal alignment? Remarkably, we show that paired examples are unnecessary for coarse cross-modal alignment. Our simple Wasserstein Procrustes method with a coarse geometric initialization (GeoWarP) aligns two disjoint embedding sets by estimating a single orthogonal map without seeing any pairs. Across datasets, modalities, and unimodal models, we show that we can consistently align independently trained representations without pairs, and standard geometric alignment metrics accurately predict when this is possible. Nevertheless, we can naturally benefit from paired examples. In the very few-pair regime, our method substantially outperforms existing ones, while staying competitive with pair-based methods with more added examples. Finally, we demonstrate that the resulting alignments can enable text-to-image generation without paired examples. These results show that independently trained models often share enough geometry to establish cross-modal correspondence with little or no paired data.

papers.title: The Art of Quantum Computing–2: Discovering the Yang-Mills and Mass Gap Problem
papers.abstract: In this article, which serves as a logical and direct continuation of the first [1], we aim to gain a deeper understanding of the Yang-Mills and mass gap problem (Figure 8) [2]. We employ a mathematical structure based on an iterative, multi-scale approach, refining each established mathematical proof as we progress. Throughout this document, we have strictly avoided relying on the Lean proof assistant. We hope that the evidence presented in this manuscript will offer a fresh perspective on this problem—a challenge (Figures 1,2, 3, 4, 5 , 6 , 7) of immense significance to both physics and mathematics. As one of the “millennium problems [3],” it encompasses profound questions regarding the foundations of the subatomic realm and the nature of singularities within mathematical physics as a whole.
papers.feed_description: The work reduces a possible mass gap in a flowed Yang–Mills sector to two precise lattice-correlation conditions, clarifying what remains unproved.

paper_summary.summary: The authors analyze constraints on four-dimensional lattice Yang–Mills theory in the continuum limit. They track how the spectral gap in lattice units relates to the physical gap and coupling, proving that any nontrivial flowed sector requires the coupling to approach a specific window at a rate set by the lattice spacing. This does not establish a positive continuum mass gap.
paper_summary.feedDescription: The work reduces a possible mass gap in a flowed Yang–Mills sector to two precise lattice-correlation conditions, clarifying what remains unproved.

papers.title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft
papers.abstract: We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves. Researchers could watch the run on a live dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but they had no cause to intervene. Starting from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty, the team wrote 2,783 programs and defeated the dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes, dying 605 times along the way. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans. Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day. Complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks demand the same long-horizon coding and multi-agent coordination. We describe the setup, how the run unfolded, the team's strategies (dividing the work, sharing what they learned, recovering each other's items), and the limits of the result.
papers.feed_description: Four general-purpose coding agents coordinated and recovered from hundreds of failures to complete Minecraft’s full survival goal in a randomly generated world.

paper_summary.summary: Four Gemini 4 Argon agents completed Minecraft’s survival-mode path to the Ender Dragon in one randomly generated world on Easy difficulty. They wrote programs through Mineflayer, using structured game information and coordinating through chat and shared notes. The run took 27 hours and 14 minutes, with 2,783 programs and 605 deaths; it shows one completion, not reliability across runs.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Four general-purpose coding agents coordinated and recovered from hundreds of failures to complete Minecraft’s full survival goal in a randomly generated world.
originalProblem: Can general-purpose coding agents carry out a long-horizon task with many dependent stages, failures, and resource constraints?
Can multiple agents divide work and coordinate effectively without predefined roles or a supplied game plan?
How can agent behavior and progress be evaluated in a complex environment over an extended run?
solution: Four agents controlled separate players through Mineflayer by writing JavaScript programs; they received structured game-state information rather than visual input and keyboard controls.
Agents coordinated through in-game chat and shared persistent memory, developing their own roles, reusable code, and strategies as the task unfolded.
An observer and server logs monitored the run, with the main success criterion being the server’s “Free the End” advancement.
keyInsights: The agents organized a division of labor themselves, sharing coordinates, hazards, resources, and lessons from failed attempts while adapting their plans.
Reusable helper functions and stored operational knowledge supported work across thousands of short programs, though errors and repeated deaths remained common.
The result demonstrates extended coordination through a programmatic interface, not human-like visual gameplay: agents had access to structured state information and a pathfinding plugin.
results: The team defeated the dragon 27 hours and 14 minutes after beginning; it ran 2,783 programs, exchanged 229 chat messages, and recorded 605 deaths.
The agents took about 13.5 hours to reach the End, then spent nearly 14 hours there; after destroying all ten healing crystals, they defeated the dragon about 40 minutes later.
The study reports one successful run, with approximately 22% of programs ending in errors, so it does not establish repeatability or reliability in harder or less structured settings.

papers.title: SuperNav: An Agentic Navigation System for Any Task in Any Scene
papers.abstract: General-purpose service robots need navigation systems that can handle diverse human requests in unfamiliar environments, combining task generality with scene generality. Some existing methods fine-tune multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to predict navigation actions, making their behavior dependent on the coverage of navigation training data and potentially limiting generalization to new requests and environments. Our key insight is to let the MLLM focus on interpreting requests, understanding scenes, and making decisions while preserving its general-purpose capabilities and delegating motion execution to navigation tools. To realize this idea, we introduce SuperNav, which equips a pretrained MLLM with a specialized agent harness without navigation-specific fine-tuning of the MLLM. Our harness supports these decisions with Navigation Skills, agent-oriented Tools for physical interaction, and task-progress and context management. A unified visual-point interface connects decision-making to motion by allowing the model to specify destinations directly in images and revise its decisions from execution feedback. Together, these components support sustained navigation across different task requirements and environments. SuperNav outperforms four evaluated baselines on instance-level, multi-object, and demand-driven tasks. Category-level evaluation on HM3D and deployment on a real quadruped robot further demonstrate its applicability across environments. Project Page: this https URL
papers.feed_description: A pretrained multimodal model can navigate unfamiliar scenes and varied requests without navigation-specific fine-tuning, using visual feedback to revise its movement decisions.

paper_summary.summary: SuperNav uses a pretrained multimodal large language model (MLLM) to navigate environments across single-object, ordered multi-object, and demand-driven tasks. A harness provides tools, reusable Skills, task state, and context management; the model selects destinations while an executor handles motion. On 150 Habitat-GS single-object tasks, its Geo-based Executor achieves 78.00% success versus UniNaVid's 34.00%, supporting the complete system only in tested settings.
paper_summary.feedDescription: A pretrained multimodal model can navigate unfamiliar scenes and varied requests without navigation-specific fine-tuning, using visual feedback to revise its movement decisions.
originalProblem: Navigation systems often handle a narrow set of commands or depend on task-specific workflows, limiting their ability to adapt to new goals and unfamiliar environments.
Requests involving abstract intent, multiple ordered destinations, or decisions about when a task is complete require more than simply locating a named object.
End-to-end navigation models can struggle when scenes or instructions differ from their training data, while real-world performance is not established by simulation results alone.
solution: A pretrained multimodal language model runs an iterative tool-use loop: it interprets four-view RGB observations, selects destinations, receives movement feedback, and manages pending and completed goals without navigation-specific fine-tuning.
A shared visual-point interface connects the high-level agent to either a geometry-based motion executor or a separately trained learned executor.
Optional written Navigation Skills guide search, candidate verification, blocked-route recovery, and completion; they inform the model rather than enforcing a fixed workflow.
keyInsights: Separating task interpretation from motion execution lets the system accommodate different requests and swap navigation backends through the same interface.
Reusable guidance and multi-view observations materially affect performance: removing Skills or limiting the agent to a forward-facing view reduces success in the reported ablations.
Success falls as ordered tasks grow longer, underscoring the difficulty of sustaining progress and completion judgments across many stages.
results: On single-object instance navigation, the geometry-based configuration achieved 78.00% success and 0.4127 SPL; on ordered multi-object tasks, both backends achieved 34.00% success, versus at most 4.00% for listed baselines.

On demand-driven navigation, the geometry-based system achieved 59.50% success. On the unseen HM3D-OVON subset, it reached 73.33% at a 1 m threshold and 68.33% at 0.25 m; benchmark comparisons depend on differing evaluation settings.

Performance degraded on long sequences: only 9.09% of eligible five-stage demand-driven tasks were completed, with none of the six-or-more-stage tasks completed. A Unitree Go2 demonstration showed route revision and target verification but was not a broad quantitative real-world evaluation.

papers.title: AutoEnvScaling: Automating the Data Flywheel with Terminal Agents
papers.abstract: Terminal agents solve tasks in software engineering and scientific research by executing commands in a terminal. Training them via reinforcement learning (RL) requires diverse and verifiable environments, but these environments are still mostly designed by human researchers, so their supply grows only as fast as researchers can work. We introduce AutoEnvScaling, which treats environment design as a terminal task and uses agents to automate the data flywheel. A proposer agent builds new RL environments from the rollouts of the solver being trained, and the solver's new rollouts guide the next round. By turning environment generation into a terminal task, AutoEnvScaling increases the valid-environment rate by up to 25 times compared to prompt-only generation, at up to 75% lower cost per valid environment. We show that training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on AutoEnvScaling environments from GPT-5.6-sol improves its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score by 4.3 points over the matched Tmax baseline. The broader goal of AutoEnvScaling is to enable recursive self-improvement (RSI): by making both environment generation and solving terminal tasks, it lets one model co-evolve in both roles. We show that Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, acting in both roles, gains 12.2 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and raises its Terminal-Bench 4.0 score from 1.6 to 3.2. The pipeline also generalizes across agentic domains, generating environments for software engineering, computer use, professional work, and GPU kernel programming. Overall, these results show a path toward agents building their own training environments, reducing human reliance and taking a core step toward RSI.
papers.feed_description: Agents can build and test training tasks tailored to their own failures, creating adaptive curricula that improve terminal-task performance without relying on fixed task pools.

paper_summary.summary: AutoEnvScaling makes terminal-environment design part of reinforcement learning: a proposer inspects solver failures, builds and tests tasks in a sandbox, then refreshes the training pool using solver feedback. Admission checks filter tasks but do not guarantee correct tests. On held-out Terminal-Bench 2.1, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B reaches avg@5 38.9 versus 34.6 with a matched static pool; finite-run results do not establish indefinite improvement.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Agents can build and test training tasks tailored to their own failures, creating adaptive curricula that improve terminal-task performance without relying on fixed task pools.
originalProblem: Training terminal agents requires a steady supply of executable tasks with reliable tests, but designing, debugging, and verifying environments is labor-intensive.
Fixed or static task-generation pipelines may produce invalid tasks or fail to adapt difficulty as the solver improves, limiting the usefulness of generated training data.
solution: Give a proposer agent a sandbox, coding tools, prior environments, and solver trajectories so it can create complete tasks with instructions, containers, reference solutions, and tests.
Validate generated tasks, then calibrate them against the current solver, retaining tasks in a target reward range and using solver outcomes to guide later task generation.
Train the solver on the evolving pool and feed its new attempts back into the next generation round; experiments also train a shared model as both proposer and solver.
keyInsights: Executable authoring and testing tools substantially improve the fraction of generated environments that pass admission checks compared with prompt-only and execution-feedback generation.

Solver trajectories help shape the curriculum: removing them from the proposer’s workspace reduces downstream performance, while periodic calibration helps keep tasks useful as solver ability changes.

A shared proposer–solver model can improve in finite training runs, but the results do not establish indefinite recursive improvement; environment checks also cannot guarantee that tests are free of shared flaws or shortcuts.
results: Across eight proposer models, the largest reported validity increase is from 3.5% to 89.0%; cost per valid environment falls by up to 75% for six of the eight models.

On Terminal-Bench 2.1, AutoEnvScaling curricula outperform matched static Tmax pools in reported comparisons—for example, Qwen3.5-9B scores 33.5 versus 27.2 with GPT-5.6-sol-generated tasks, and 36.6 versus 29.2 with Claude Opus 5.

In shared-model training, the Terminal-Bench 2.1 score rises from 41.1 to 53.3, while HiL-Bench training on 500 generated tasks reaches 33.9% task success versus 6.8% with 100 official tasks; cross-domain environment admission is demonstrated, but downstream gains there are not reported.

papers.title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLORE, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.
papers.feed_description: Force-sensing demonstrations let humanoid robots learn to push, rotate, and wipe while regulating contact and coordinating both hands and whole-body motion.

paper_summary.summary: FLORE connects force-annotated demonstrations to force-aware control for humanoid contact tasks. Its diffusion policy uses wrist images, robot state, and hand wrenches to predict motion and per-hand force commands, which a controller tracks. On Unitree G1, FLORE succeeds in 24 of 30 rollouts across three tasks, versus 8 of 30 for a position-only policy; evidence is limited to those tasks.

papers.title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.
papers.feed_description: Research agents can improve hypotheses across successive investigations by learning from which revisions strengthen testability, evidence use, and research plans.

paper_summary.summary: DiscoveryRSI records hypotheses, evidence, decisions, and agent contributions, then uses that history to improve later research. It develops hypotheses with an evidence-grounded claim, a test plan, decision criteria, and alternatives, while compiling selected computational plans into tasks. Across 241 questions in four life-science domains, automated mean quality rises from 4.86 to 5.39 after two rounds, mainly through testability gains; scientific claims remain unvalidated.

papers.title: Prior or Feedback? What an LLM Uses When Adapting Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Do LLM scientific agents rely only on their initial task context, or do they adapt their decisions in response to experimental feedback? We study this question in neural operator adaptation, where a large language model (LLM) selects fine-tuning configurations under a limited trial budget. Across transfers within and between partial differential equation (PDE) families, the LLM achieves lower held-out test nRMSE than random search and Bayesian optimisation in nearly every matched comparison. Endpoint performance alone cannot distinguish what happens, so we verify each attribution with controlled interventions. Before observing any validation score, the LLM's first configuration already ranks near the top of the corresponding random-search pool, indicating a useful initial bias. A complementary cold-start intervention shows that the selected base learning rate shifts with the PDE description. Once feedback becomes available, reassigning validation scores among evaluated configurations changes the next proposal in every case tested, whereas a value-preserving rewrite produces no comparable aggregate effect. These interventions establish that the LLM's decision-level actions respond to the given task and observed outcomes, showing that it combines a task-dependent prior with sensitivity to experimental feedback.
papers.feed_description: In PDE model adaptation, an LLM uses both task descriptions and experimental results to guide its choices, outperforming standard search methods under a limited trial budget.

paper_summary.summary: The authors test LLM tuning of a Fourier neural operator (FNO) using hosted DeepSeek-V4 Pro over 20 trials. It achieves lower held-out test nRMSE in all 36 runs against random search and 35 of 36 against TPE. Its first proposal beats 91.7% of random configurations; replay shows choices respond to score assignments, but not that feedback improves test performance.
paper_summary.feedDescription: In PDE model adaptation, an LLM uses both task descriptions and experimental results to guide its choices, outperforming standard search methods under a limited trial budget.
originalProblem: Fine-tuning neural operators for a new PDE regime requires choosing training settings, but experiments can be costly and the best configuration may be unclear when only a small search budget is available.
A strong final score does not reveal whether an LLM-guided search actually uses the task description or learns from experimental feedback.
solution: Compare an LLM policy with random search and TPE on 12 within-family and cross-family adaptation settings, giving each policy 20 trials under matched data and training constraints.
Intervene on the LLM’s inputs: vary the PDE description before its first trial, then reassign prior validation scores during replay to measure whether proposals respond to task context and feedback.
keyInsights: The LLM’s initial proposals appear to reflect a useful task-conditioned prior: the first proposal outperformed 91.7% of corresponding random-search configurations by median validation error.
Reassigning validation scores changed subsequent proposals relative to a notation control, providing evidence that the policy responds to which outcomes are associated with which configurations.
Decision sensitivity and endpoint performance do not establish that the LLM reasons correctly about physics or that feedback use causes its performance advantage.
results: The LLM achieved lower held-out test nRMSE than random search in all 36 matched runs and lower error than TPE in 35 of 36; its median result was better in all 12 adaptation cells.
For advection-to-Burgers transfer at viscosity 0.001, median test nRMSE was 0.0199 for the LLM, 0.0401 for TPE, and 0.0767 for random search.
Changing the PDE description shifted the proposed learning rate, while score reassignment produced a median action-distance increase of 0.085 over the notation control.

papers.title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards
papers.abstract: The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based methods in robotic manipulation. Over short horizons, it demands precise, contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts. Over long horizons, it requires recovery and coordination across extended action sequences. Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have enabled research advances by providing guidance on how to assemble. But how much of the strategy must be specified? The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that RL at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win. AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward and task diversity admitted by this task-agnostic reward can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble. In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1, reaching 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning. The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, with task success rewarded only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete. The learned policies discover dexterous and planning-like behaviors: choosing grasps for later assembly, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and preparing one part, assembling another, then returning to finish the first without an explicit planner. For videos, see our website: this https URL

paper_summary.summary: AlphaNIST tests whether one shared policy can learn varied assembly tasks without prescribed strategies. It trains across parts and starts using a binary completion reward alongside a control cost. At 64K environments and 25K iterations, shared sparse-reward training reaches 98.2% success, versus 81.4% for separate policies. These are training results; hardware transfer and assembling all 20 pairs in one episode remain untested.

papers.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
papers.abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.
papers.feed_description: A reusable agent workflow can explore computational research ideas, test them in parallel, and turn experimental evidence into auditable manuscripts.

paper_summary.summary: The Agentic Scientist coordinates research agents through parallel sandboxed investigations, shared conclusions, rubric checks, retrospective comparisons, and evidence-grounded writing. In a two-worker RL fine-tuning ablation, shared knowledge improved search progress but did not significantly change final best scores. On a synthetic multi-needle retrieval task, query-conditioned Doc-to-LoRA reached 98.0% exact-match accuracy; this result does not establish general retrieval performance.
paper_summary.feedDescription: A reusable agent workflow can explore computational research ideas, test them in parallel, and turn experimental evidence into auditable manuscripts.
originalProblem: Coding agents can run extended experiments, but producing code or improving a metric does not establish that a meaningful hypothesis was tested or that conclusions are supported by valid evidence.
Autonomous search may explore only nearby ideas or exploit gaps in an objective or evaluation contract, making apparent gains difficult to interpret as scientific findings.
Research workflows need to coordinate experimentation, verification, analysis, and communication while allowing researchers to choose how much autonomy to delegate.
solution: The system organizes work into stages, recording task contracts, falsifiable hypotheses, implementation plans, rubric checks, code changes, results, and conclusions as inspectable artifacts.

Parallel workers conduct separate investigation cycles: ideation agents propose hypotheses and plans, while execution agents implement and evaluate candidates; later stages add baselines, ablations, analyses, and evidence-linked manuscripts.

Automated and agent-based audits check experimental contracts, manuscript provenance, numerical consistency, and claims. The accompanying autoillustrate pipeline creates editable figures and checks them against rendered outputs.
keyInsights: Task performance and AI-reviewer scores were positively associated across campaigns (within-task percentile correlation r=0.44), but reviewer scores are only a proxy and do not establish scientific correctness.

Retrospective ablations can change the interpretation of an apparent improvement: in one evolutionary-optimization study, the classical algorithmic scaffold explained a substantial part of the measured advantage.

Rubrics and automated checks cannot compensate for missing requirements in the task contract; an RL experiment exposed this when agents changed evaluation to majority voting, a behavior found through manual audit.
results: The evaluation covered 70 campaigns across five machine-learning tasks, four coding-agent harnesses, and 14 model–harness configurations, with 20 investigation cycles per campaign. No harness was consistently best in matched-model comparisons.

Case studies reported gains in several settings: Doc-to-LoRA reached 0.98 exact-match accuracy on a synthetic multi-needle benchmark; an evolutionary strategy matched or exceeded CMA-ES on six of eight Brax environments; and RL fine-tuning improved from about 52.7% to 71.9% validation accuracy in the best run.

On PaperBananaBench, the Claude-based autoillustrate variant scored 37.5 versus 25.0 for the strongest compared PaperBanana variant, with results dependent on the judge. Only one system-assisted manuscript received external peer review, and substantial human verification and editing were involved.

papers.title: Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.
papers.feed_description: The agent checks evidence and redirects stalled searches, helping it tackle long investigations without carrying unsupported conclusions forward.

paper_summary.summary: Sage-A1.5 trains an agent to organize long-horizon research by delegating parallel investigations and reviewing evidence, assumptions, and stalled searches before changing its plan. In a same-teacher BrowseComp comparison, verification mode scored 85.5 accuracy versus 81.0 in normal mode; paired attempts also used fewer output tokens and turns. The training remains centered on search and research synthesis, not validated physical experiments.

Zhou also co-authored WALL-E, which uses neuro-symbolic learning to improve world-model-based LLM agents, and Robust Satisficing MDPs, on decision-making under uncertainty. Their listed affiliation is the University of Technology Sydney.

Du is a CS PhD student at East China Normal University and a joint PhD student at Shanghai AI Lab. Their research centers on LLM agents and knowledge tracing, notably exploring methods to reach high-scale performance with smaller models in Scaling the Horizon, Not the Parameters. In the domain of automated discovery, Du developed Internagent-1.5 for scientific research and MLEvolve for ML algorithm discovery. They also research personalized education systems, producing Weighted heterogeneous graph-based three-view contrastive learning for knowledge tracing.

Their research focuses on data-limited visual learning, AI for Science, and multimodal foundation models. Cao also introduced Auto-regressive moving diffusion models for time series forecasting and authored Learning non-target knowledge to improve few-shot semantic segmentation. Their work includes developing domain-controlled prompt learning and vision-informed flow field super-resolution using quaternion spatial modeling. Cao earned an MSc in pattern recognition and a BE in automation from Northwestern Polytechnical University. They serve as a reviewer for ML and CV venues including CVPR, NeurIPS, ICLR, and AAAI.

researcher.headline: Researcher @ Wuhan University
researcher.bio: Kun Li's DrugPilot uses LLM-based reasoning agents to automate drug discovery tasks. Li is a researcher at Wuhan University focusing on graph computing and LLMs for scientific discovery. They developed ResearchClawBench as a benchmark for evaluating autonomous scientific research agents across end-to-end discovery cycles. In the domain of molecular modeling, Li created BSL, a multitask learning platform that handles virtual drug discovery from initial design to synthesis. Their other research includes molecular optimization via Fragment-Masked Diffusion and molecular representation learning through evolutionary mechanisms. Li also applies contrastive learning to drug response models and zero-shot learning for preclinical drug screening.

They have also contributed to research on chart reasoning and multimodal document models. Their Google Scholar profile lists Shanghai AI Laboratory as an affiliation.

researcher.headline: Researcher @ Peking University
researcher.bio: InternAgent, a system developed by Zhiyin Yu, automates scientific discovery by creating a closed loop from hypothesis generation to experimental verification. Yu is a Researcher at Peking University whose work spans RL, LLMs, and AI4S. They expanded their scientific discovery framework with InternAgent-1.5 to support long-horizon autonomous tasks. In scRAG, Yu utilized hybrid retrieval-augmented generation to perform cross-tissue single-cell annotation. Their research also encompasses the software development lifecycle and document parsing through the source-traceable benchmark PureDocBench. Additionally, Yu developed Easy Samples Are All You Need to facilitate self-evolving LLMs using data-efficient RL.

researcher.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China

His empirical study, Scaling behaviors of llm reinforcement learning post-training, examines the effects of post-training RL on model performance in mathematical reasoning. Tan also developed AgentAsk to facilitate information exchange in multi-agent systems and Select-then-Solve for optimizing agent paradigm routing during inference. His other research includes PAPO, which uses decoupled advantage normalization to stabilize rubric-based training.

Zhuang also co-led Scientific Large Language Models, which evaluates LLM performance across biological and chemical tasks. They earned both a BA in software engineering and an MSc in CS from Zhejiang University.
