papers.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
papers.abstract: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.
papers.feed_description: Researchers can use this benchmark to test whether coding agents can improve published systems across computer science, against the authors’ code on held-out workloads.

paper_summary.summary: FrontierCS 2 tests whether agents can improve research artifacts by rebuilding missing contributions in repositories. Agents receive development feedback, then judges test their selected patches against the original code on held-out workloads. Claude Opus 5.5 passed 58% of its runs, but no agent passed on 16 tasks. Results cover one run per agent-task pair, not human comparisons.

Their research includes benchmarking graph structure learning methods and developing error-aware routing for sparse video generation. They have also studied critic stabilization in PPO.

researcher.name: Siddhant Ray
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ University of Chicago, Previously Cloud Networks Researcher @ Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya
researcher.bio: Siddhant Ray co-authored CacheBlend, which speeds LLM serving for RAG by fusing cached knowledge. They are a PhD student in CS at the University of Chicago, advised by Junchen Jiang and Nick Feamster. Their research focuses on efficient inference systems for LLMs and Physical AI, including VLA architectures and serving for long-horizon workloads. In METIS, they developed quality-aware RAG configuration adaptation to balance response quality and delay. Ray earned an MSc in EEIT from ETH Zurich and a BTech from VIT Vellore.

researcher.name: Bo Peng
researcher.headline: Previously CS BA Student @ Peking University
researcher.bio: Bo Peng coauthored HunyuanVideo 1.5, a technical report on a video-generation model. They are a senior in Peking University’s Turing Program and founder of Public Judge, an online platform for competitive programming contests. Their research focuses on theoretical CS, especially cryptography and private information retrieval (PIR). Their work includes PRFs with Weak Programming Privacy, which applies pseudorandom functions to PIR, and SNARKs from LWE, which uses non-black-box reductions. At Northeastern University, Carnegie Mellon University, and Peking University, they researched succinct arguments, PIR, and garbled circuits.

topAffiliation.description: Part of the Peking University Turing Program.

researcher.name: Ruyi Ji
researcher.headline: Postdoctoral Fellow @ University of Michigan, Previously CS PhD Student @ Peking University
researcher.bio: Ruyi Ji co-created Frontiercs, a benchmark for evaluating evolving intelligence through dynamic and adaptive challenges. Ji is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Michigan working with Xinyu Wang on program synthesis. They previously earned a CS PhD and undergraduate degree from Peking University, where they were a member of the programming language research laboratory and the inaugural Turing Class. Ji’s research includes CCLemma, which uses e-graphs to guide lemma discovery for inductive proofs, and Beyond tests, which repairs program vulnerabilities via crash constraint extraction. They also developed methods for Question selection to optimize user queries during interactive program synthesis. Their recent work explores constrained sampling for LLMs using MCMC techniques and scaling synthesis through abstract semantics.

topAffiliation.description: Working with Prof. Xinyu Wang.

researcher.name: Shuo Yang
researcher.headline: EECS PhD Student @ UC Berkeley
researcher.bio: Shuo Yang co-authored Sparse VideoGen to accelerate video diffusion transformers by utilizing spatial and temporal sparsity. Yang is an EECS PhD student at UC Berkeley, where they are advised by Ion Stoica and work within the Sky Computing Lab and LMSYS. Their research focuses on ML systems, specifically improving the inference efficiency and serving capacity of generative models. Yang also developed S-LoRA, a system for serving thousands of concurrent LoRA adapters through unified memory management. Additionally, they contributed to WorldModelBench for evaluating video generation models and Kimi Linear, an efficient linear attention architecture. Their work involves optimizing throughput and memory for LLMs and video diffusion models within scalable software infrastructure.

topAffiliation.description: Advised by Ion Stoica; member of Sky Computing Lab and LMSYS.

researcher.name: Haocheng Xi
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ University of California, Berkeley, Previously CS BE Student @ Tsinghua University
researcher.bio: Haocheng Xi co-developed Humanity's Last Exam, a benchmark evaluating expert-level reasoning in LLMs across diverse academic disciplines. He is a PhD student at UC Berkeley in the Berkeley AI Research group specializing in efficient ML. His research focuses on low-precision quantization and sparse attention for generative models, including the development of NVILA for efficient visual language models. Xi created SpargeAttn to accelerate inference through sparse attention and received the Best Paper Award at MLSys 2026 for StreamDiffusionV2, a system for real-time interactive video generation. He previously held research internships at NVIDIA and earned his BE from the Yao Class at Tsinghua University.

topAffiliation.description: Advised by Prof. Kurt Keutzer; works closely with Prof. Song Han in MIT.

researcher.name: Xinyang Han
researcher.headline: CPH PhD Student @ University of California, Berkeley
researcher.bio: Xinyang Han's Agents' Last Exam evaluates the long-horizon reasoning and specialized capabilities of frontier AI agents. Han is a CPH PhD student at UC Berkeley in the Yala Lab, where they study AI agent evaluation, digital labor, and multimodal CV. Their research includes MLS-Bench, a framework for assessing AI systems on their ability to build other models, and MatrAIx, which simulates environments with billions of persona agents. They also developed Unsupervised universal image segmentation to partition images without manual labels. Han previously completed an undergraduate degree in EECS at UC Berkeley.

topAffiliation.description: Worked in the Yala Lab.

researcher.name: Melissa Pan
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ UC Berkeley, Previously ECE MSc Student @ Carnegie Mellon University (CMU)
researcher.bio: The MAST taxonomy by Melissa Pan identifies and categorizes common failure patterns in multi-agent LLM systems. Pan is a PhD student at UC Berkeley in the Sky Computing Lab, where she researches ML systems and datacenter computing with a focus on sustainability. In Lotus, she developed semantic operators to enable LLM-based data processing with accuracy guarantees. She also co-authored Measuring agents in production and Barbarians at the gate to examine the impact of AI on systems research. Before joining Berkeley, Pan completed a Master’s at CMU focused on sustainable resource management for microservices and spent three years as a software engineer at IBM working on the Db2 core engine. She holds a Bachelor's degree in Computer Engineering from the University of Toronto.

topAffiliation.description: Advised by Prof. Matei Zaharia and affiliated with the Sky Computing Lab.

researcher.name: Mayank Mishra
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ UC Berkeley, Previously Research Engineer @ MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab
researcher.bio: Mayank Mishra co-developed Bloom, a 176-billion-parameter multilingual LLM designed for open-access research. He is a PhD student at UC Berkeley researching model architecture, scaling, and optimization. Previously, Mishra led pretraining and architecture research at the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab for IBM’s Granite Models. His work includes Cross-Layer Attention, which reduces Transformer KV cache size by sharing keys and values across multiple layers. He also co-authored StarCoder and developed PaTH Attention, which applies Householder transformations for position encoding. Mishra earned a B.Tech in Electrical Engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi.

topAffiliation.description: Exploring pretraining and model architectures.

researcher.name: Boxi Yu
researcher.headline: Senior Research Fellow @ Lero, Previously CS PhD Student @ The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
researcher.bio: Boxi Yu developed UTBoost to rigorously evaluate the performance of coding agents on the SWE-bench benchmark. They are a Senior Research Fellow at the Lero Research Centre, where they research software engineering, Trustworthy AI, and LLM agents. Yu’s work includes Retromorphic Testing, which constructs dual program architectures to automatically generate test oracles. They also conducted an empirical study comparing classical ML and deep learning for log-based anomaly detection. More recently, Yu introduced SWE-ABS to identify inflated success rates in LLM benchmarks through adversarial strengthening. They completed a PhD in CS at The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and previously attended South China University of Technology.

researcher.name: Sijia Liu
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ Princeton University, MSc Student @ Carnegie Mellon University, BA Student @ Peking University
researcher.bio: Sijia Liu’s Humanline incorporates human perceptual biases into alignment objectives to match the performance of online reinforcement learning using offline data. They are a CS PhD student at Princeton University advised by Karthik Narasimhan, researching LLM post-training and long-horizon agents. During a three-year tenure as a Research Scientist at Amazon AGI, Liu contributed to the Amazon Nova family of models and developed post-training methods for the Alexa Prize SocialBot. Their additional research includes DeCRIM, which uses a decompose-and-refine approach for complex instruction following, and ContextRL, an RL objective for grounding long-horizon reasoning. Liu is a research intern at the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence and holds an MSc from Carnegie Mellon University and a BA from Peking University.

topAffiliation.description: Advised by Prof. Karthik Narasimhan at Princeton Language and Intelligence; research focuses on LLM post-training and long-horizon agents.

researcher.name: Kerem Akillioglu
researcher.headline: Visiting Researcher @ UC Berkeley, CS PhD Student @ University of Waterloo
researcher.bio: Kerem Akillioglu’s Research Challenges in Relational Database Management Systems for LLM Queries identifies the performance bottlenecks that occur when traditional data systems process LLM-based queries. Akillioglu is a PhD student at the University of Waterloo and a Visiting Researcher at UC Berkeley in the EPIC Lab. Their research focuses on building and optimizing data systems for LLM workloads and exploring the architectural intersection of database management and LLMs. They also authored Optimizing Data Systems for LLM Workloads and The Duality between Large Language Models and Data Management Systems. Prior to doctoral studies, Akillioglu completed an MSc at the University of Waterloo where they researched query optimization for streaming graph data. Their background includes a software engineering role at Admost and research internships at Nanyang Technological University and the Bekaert R&D Centre. Akillioglu serves on program committees for ACM CAIS and the Ontario Database Symposium.

topAffiliation.description: Hosted by Prof. Aditya Parameswaran; member of the EPIC Lab.

researcher.name: Yi Pan
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ UC Berkeley, Previously CS BEng Student @ Shanghai Jiao Tong University
researcher.bio: Yi Pan’s TraceLab characterizes coding agent workloads to optimize LLM serving. They are a PhD student at the UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab, advised by Ion Stoica, where they build efficient and scalable systems for LLM training and inference. Pan co-developed MuxTune to enable multi-task LLM fine-tuning in multi-tenant datacenters using spatial-temporal backbone multiplexing. Their research also includes DynaFlow, which provides programmable operator scheduling for intra-device parallelism, and Magneton, a system for optimizing ML energy efficiency via differential debugging. Pan earned a BEng from the ACM Honors Class at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and previously conducted research at the University of Washington SyFI Lab.

topAffiliation.description: Sky Computing Lab; advised by Prof. Ion Stoica

researcher.name: Mert Cemri
researcher.affiliation: UC Berkeley, Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
researcher.headline: EECS PhD Student @ UC Berkeley, Previously EEE BA Student @ Bilkent University
researcher.bio: In Why do multi-agent llm systems fail?, Mert Cemri identifies the specific error patterns and performance bottlenecks occurring in collaborative LLM architectures. He is a PhD student at UC Berkeley in the Berkeley AI Research and Sky Computing Labs, advised by Ion Stoica, Kannan Ramchandran, and Alex Dimakis. His research focuses on ML efficiency and agentic systems, particularly test-time scaling and multi-agent coordination. Cemri co-developed DigiRL to train device-control agents using autonomous RL in-the-wild. He also created SPECS, which uses speculative drafts to accelerate test-time scaling and reduce inference latency. His work includes SkyDiscover for AI-driven algorithmic discovery and Adaevolve for adaptive optimization. He previously interned as an ML engineer at Apple and conducted research on social learning at EPFL and Bilkent University.

topAffiliation.description: Ph.D. student in the Berkeley AI Research (BAIR) and Sky Computing Labs, advised by Ion Stoica, Kannan Ramchandran, and Alex Dimakis.

researcher.name: Yichuan Wang
researcher.headline: EECS PhD Student @ University of California, Berkeley, Previously CS BEng Student @ Shanghai Jiao Tong University
researcher.bio: Yichuan Wang developed LEANN, a low-storage vector index that enables on-device retrieval-augmented generation with minimal memory overhead. Wang is a PhD student at UC Berkeley advised by Joseph E. Gonzalez and Matei Zaharia. Their research focuses on ML systems, specifically LLM serving, agent infrastructure, and neural retrieval. They maintain PixelRAG, a system that performs retrieval directly over web screenshots to preserve visual elements like tables and figures. Wang also contributed to the SGLang project at LMSYS and co-developed Autellix, a serving engine for LLM agents. Currently a research scientist intern at Meta, they previously earned a B.Eng. in computer science from Shanghai Jiao Tong University.

topAffiliation.description: Advised by Matei Zaharia and Joseph E. Gonzalez; closely collaborated with Sewon Min and Ion Stoica.

researcher.name: Aiwei Ivy Zhang
researcher.affiliation: PhD Student at Georgia Institute of Technology
researcher.headline: Graduate Research Assistant @ Georgia Tech, Previously CS BA Student @ Dartmouth College
researcher.bio: Aiwei Ivy Zhang co-developed the Foundation Model for Wearable Movement Data, a foundation model for actigraphy used in mental health research. Zhang is a CS PhD student at the Georgia Institute of Technology and a researcher in the Social Dynamics and Wellbeing Lab. Their research focuses on human-centric ML and NLP, specifically building models that learn from longitudinal health data and unstructured clinical records. Zhang also developed MotionTeller, a system that integrates wearable time-series with LLMs for health and behavioral understanding. Before joining Georgia Tech, she earned a BA in Computer Science from Dartmouth College and conducted research at the Jacobson Lab and the HealthX Lab.

topAffiliation.description: Student in the School of Interactive Computing and member of the Social Dynamics and Wellbeing (SocWeb) Lab; advised by Professor Munmun De Choudhury.

researcher.name: Qizheng Zhang
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ Stanford University
researcher.bio:
I am a fourth-year CS Ph.D. student at Stanford University. I am a member of Stanford Pervasive Parallelism Lab and LMCache. My advisor is Kunle Olukotun. I have also been working with James Zou, Junchen Jiang, and Muhammad Shahbaz. I obtained my Bachelor's degree from the University of Chicago, with three majors in computer science, mathematics, and statistics.

I build AI systems that continuously learn from experience and improve over time (a topic known as recursive self-improvement), e.g. Caravan [OSDI 2024], Agentic Plan Caching [NeurIPS 2025], Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) [ICLR 2026], Meta-Harness [COLM 2026]. My interests span systems and frameworks, algorithms, and evaluation. Earlier, I had also worked on LLM inference infrastructure, e.g. CacheGen [SIGCOMM 2024], CacheBlend [EuroSys 2025 Best Paper].

I have collaborated extensively with industry partners such as SambaNova Systems, Tensormesh, Eigent AI, and Microsoft Research. My research has also made it into production, with ACE deployed at Anyshift and SCX.ai.

In a previous life, I worked on computer networking and operating systems. I had a lot of fun hacking OS kernels and building low-latency network transport for video streaming.

The pronunciation of my first name (Qizheng) is very close to that of “keygen” in public key encryption. I also go by Alex.

topAffiliation.description: Member of Stanford Pervasive Parallelism Lab and LMCache; worked with Kunle Olukotun, James Zou, Junchen Jiang, and Muhammad Shahbaz.

researcher.name: Kaiyuan Liu
researcher.headline: Research Assistant @ Social RL Lab, CS BS/MS Student @ University of Washington
researcher.bio: Kaiyuan Liu co-created LiveCodeBench Pro, which uses competitive programming to benchmark LLM reasoning. Liu is a CS BS/MS student at the University of Washington and a Research Assistant at the Social RL Lab. Their research centers on RL and multi-agent systems, including the development of Agents' Last Exam for agentic evaluation. They also developed AutoCode to use LLMs as problem setters and FrontierCS to automate the synthesis of coding challenges. Previously, Liu researched brain representations of decision-making at the Allen Institute and designed hybrid memory-disk architectures as an ML Engineer at VecML. They currently serve as the University of Washington ICPC coach and review for NeurIPS, AAAI, and AAMAS.

topAffiliation.description: Works on projects involving multi-agent systems, reinforcement learning, and large language models; mentored by Natasha Jaques.

researcher.name: Wenyuan Huang
researcher.headline: CS Advanced Algorithms Researcher / Lecturer @ X-Camp Academy, Undergraduate Research Assistant @ University of Wisconsin-Madison
researcher.bio: Wenyuan Huang, who goes by Harry, is a UW–Madison undergraduate in mathematics and computer science focused on LLM agents, continual learning, and reasoning. They are also interested in operating systems and ML systems, with research spanning RL and LLMs. Huang is an undergraduate research assistant at UW–Madison and previously visited UC Berkeley’s Sky Computing Lab. They competed in ICPC and were part of the champion team at the 2024 ICPC NCNA Regional. They also co-coached UW–Madison’s ICPC team for the 2025–2026 season.

researcher.name: Sherry Ruan
researcher.headline: Founder @ ComputerX.ai, Previously CS PhD Student @ Stanford University
researcher.bio: Sherry Ruan developed QuizBot, a dialogue-based adaptive learning system that uses conversational agents to facilitate factual knowledge acquisition. As the founder of ComputerX.ai and a researcher at Google Cloud AI, Ruan builds multimodal AI agents and works on variational autoencoders. They recently completed a PhD in CS at Stanford University, focusing on human-AI interaction, sequence modeling, and RL for education. Their research also includes the study Speech Is 3x Faster than Typing, which compared voice and keyboard text entry speeds on mobile devices. Ruan previously conducted research on speech recognition systems at Baidu’s Silicon Valley AI Lab and studied representation discovery in RL at McGill University.

topAffiliation.description: Founded a StartX-backed AI agent startup automating knowledge work through multimodal agents.

researcher.name: Shu Liu
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ University of California, Berkeley, Previously CS and Applied Math BS Student @ University of Wisconsin-Madison
researcher.bio: Shu Liu's Language models can easily learn to reason from demonstrations identifies that the structural format of prompts, rather than their specific content, is the primary driver of LLM reasoning performance. Liu is a CS PhD student at UC Berkeley in the Sky Computing Lab, where they are advised by Ion Stoica. Their research focuses on ML systems and distributed infrastructure for self-improving agents. They developed SkyRL, a modular RL library for training LLM agents, and SkyDiscover, a framework for automating scientific and algorithmic discovery. Liu also co-developed SkyStore, a cost-optimized object storage system used for managing data across multiple cloud regions and providers. Previously, they earned a BS in CS and Applied Math from the University of Wisconsin-Madison and held a research internship at the Max Planck Institute for Software Systems.

topAffiliation.description: Member of the Sky Computing Lab, advised by Ion Stoica.

researcher.name: Dacheng Li
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ University of California, Berkeley, Previously ML MSc Student @ Carnegie Mellon University
researcher.bio: Dacheng Li co-developed the LLM-as-a-judge framework, which utilizes LLMs to automate the evaluation of model performance via MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. Li is a CS PhD student at UC Berkeley affiliated with the Sky Computing Lab and BAIR. His research resides at the intersection of generative models and distributed systems, focusing on efficient training and inference for LLMs and visual language models. He also developed Sky-T1, an open reasoning model, and VILA-U, a unified model for visual understanding and generation. On the systems side, he created S-LoRA for scalable adapter serving and MPCFormer for secure transformer inference. Li holds an MS in ML from Carnegie Mellon University and has conducted research at Nvidia and Google.

topAffiliation.description: Advised by Prof. Ion Stoica and Prof. Joseph Gonzalez; works closely with Prof. Song Han (MIT).

researcher.name: Zerui Cheng
researcher.headline: Quant Research Intern @ Citadel Securities, EE PhD Student @ Princeton University
researcher.bio: Zerui Cheng’s Humanity's Last Exam provides an expert-level benchmark for testing the reasoning limits of frontier LLMs. He is a Ph.D. candidate at Princeton University and a quantitative research intern at Citadel Securities. His research focuses on AI evaluation and decentralized systems, such as LiveCodeBench Pro for contamination-free benchmarking in competitive programming. Cheng’s zkBridge uses zero-knowledge proofs for trustless cross-chain communication and served as a foundation for the Polyhedra Network. He also developed SPIN-Bench to evaluate strategic planning and social reasoning in agentic models. Previously a researcher at ByteDance Seed, Cheng graduated from the Yao Class at Tsinghua University and is a member of the Competitive Programming Hall of Fame.

researcher.name: Zeyu Shen
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ Princeton University, Previously Mathematics and CS BA Student @ Duke University
researcher.bio: Zeyu Shen’s LiveCodeBench Pro evaluates LLMs in competitive programming by incorporating the judging standards of Olympiad medalists. Shen is a researcher at Princeton University focusing on RL and computational economics. He developed FrontierCS to create evolving challenges for testing AI and ReliabilityRAG to provide robust defenses for RAG-based web searches. His work also includes AutoCode, a system where LLMs serve as problem setters for coding competitions. Shen’s earlier research investigated optimal algorithms for multiwinner elections and fairness in assignment problems with uncertain priorities. He has recently explored the geometry of alignment collapse during fine-tuning and the use of cognitive models to simulate human persuasion games.

researcher.name: Shang Zhou
researcher.affiliation: PhD Student, University of California, San Diego
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ UC San Diego
researcher.bio: Shang Zhou is a CS PhD student at UC San Diego studying how LLMs can solve hard coding and optimization problems. Advised by Jingbo Shang, they work on LLM benchmarks, coding agents, and generating problems and training data. As research lead at AutoCode, they built a system that uses LLMs to generate competitive programming problems. They also co-led a 20-person team benchmarking LLMs on ICPC problems. Zhou placed 22nd at the ICPC World Finals and is a Codeforces International Grandmaster.

researcher.name: Ao Qu
researcher.headline: PhD at Institute of Data, Systems and Society @ Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Previously CS Undergraduate Student @ Vanderbilt University
researcher.bio: Ao Qu is a PhD student at MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, advised by Prof. Paul Pu Liang and Prof. Jinhua Zhao. His research centers on self-evolving AI systems that learn from interaction, consolidate experience into reusable knowledge, and progressively improve their reasoning and decision-making capabilities. He studies continual learning, reinforcement learning, and multimodal intelligence to build AI systems that can proactively adapt and evolve in complex real-world environments.

topAffiliation.role: PhD at Institute of Data, Systems and Society
topAffiliation.description: Working with Paul Liang and Jinhua Zhao. Building multisensory & self-evolving agent.

researcher.name: Han Zheng
researcher.headline: Mechanical Engineering & Computational Science and Engineering PhD Student @ Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Previously Mechanical Engineering PhD Student @ University of Michigan – Ann Arbor
researcher.bio: Han Zheng's CORAL framework enables autonomous multi-agent evolution for open-ended discovery through long-running LLM agents and shared persistent memory. Zheng is a PhD student in mechanical engineering and computational science and engineering at MIT, where they research scalable planning and RL for multi-agent systems. Their work combines search and combinatorial optimization to build self-evolving agents and autonomous path-finding systems. They also developed Itinera for LLM-based urban itinerary planning and AlphaOPT for formulating optimization programs using self-improving experience libraries. Currently a research intern at Amazon AGI working on agentic post-training, Zheng previously interned at Symbotic and was a doctoral student at the University of Michigan. They hold dual undergraduate degrees from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and Zhejiang University.

topAffiliation.role: Mechanical Engineering & Computational Science and Engineering PhD Student

researcher.name: Chonghe Jiang
researcher.headline: PhD Student, IDSS @ Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Previously Operations Research MPhil Student @ Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)
researcher.bio: Chonghe Jiang co-created CORAL to facilitate autonomous multi-agent evolution for open-ended discovery. Currently a PhD student at MIT IDSS, Jiang is supervised by Jinhua Zhao and works with Paul Liang on optimization, RL, and LLM post-training. Jiang developed AlphaOPT, which employs a self-improving LLM experience library to formulate optimization programs, and FrontierOR to benchmark LLM performance in large-scale optimization algorithm design. Their research also includes graph sparsification via mixture of graphs and GETS for calibrating graph neural networks. Prior to MIT, Jiang earned an MPhil in Operations Research from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and a bachelor's degree in Mathematics from Tongji University.

topAffiliation.description: Supervised by Prof. Jinhua Zhao; also works with Prof. Paul Liang on optimization, RL, and LLM post-training.

researcher.name: Jingzhuo Hu
researcher.headline: Software Engineer Co-op @ Amazon Fulfillment Technologies & Robotics, Previously Computer and Information Technology MSc Student @ University of Pennsylvania
researcher.bio: Jingzhuo Hu authored RegDivergence-101, a benchmark for detecting cross-jurisdiction regulatory contradictions in life sciences using LLMs. Hu is a Computer and Information Technology MSc student at the University of Pennsylvania and currently holds a Software Engineer Co-op position at Amazon Fulfillment Technologies & Robotics. Their research centers on AI and its utility in navigating complex legal and regulatory frameworks. Previously, Hu worked as a Software Engineer Intern at The Commons XR, where they built Python REST APIs and serverless unit tests with Azure Functions. This role supported the backend development of an XR learning platform. At Amazon, Hu focuses on fulfillment and robotics engineering while completing their graduate studies at UPenn.

researcher.name: Zhiqing Zhong
researcher.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
researcher.headline: CS PhD Student @ The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Previously Optoelectronics Information BEng Student @ SCUT
researcher.bio: Zhiqing Zhong’s OpenRCA evaluates the capacity of LLMs to perform root cause analysis for software failures. They are a PhD student in Computer Science at The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, advised by Pinjia He. Their research focuses on AIOps and software engineering automation, specifically regarding verifiable code generation and software maintenance. Zhong developed BackportBench for automated patch backporting and SWE-effi to measure the resource efficiency of AI software agents. They previously earned a BEng in Optoelectronics Information from South China University of Technology. Zhong serves as a reviewer for TOSEM and TSE and was a junior program committee member for MSR 2024.

topAffiliation.organization: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
topAffiliation.description: Advised by Prof. Pinjia He.

researcher.name: Tong Zhao
researcher.headline: Senior Manager, Post-Training Research @ Scale AI, Previously Staff Research Scientist @ Snap Inc.
researcher.bio: Tong Zhao’s GraphRAG integrates structured relational data into retrieval-augmented generation workflows to improve how LLMs process complex knowledge. He is the Senior Manager of Post-Training Research at Scale AI and previously served as a Staff Research Scientist at Snap Research. His work focuses on representation learning and post-training, primarily applied to GNNs and recommender systems. Zhao also developed Data Augmentation for Graph Neural Networks to improve model generalization and co-created LLAGA, an assistant for combining language and graph models. He earned his PhD in 2022 from the University of Notre Dame.

topAffiliation.description: Leads a post-training research team.

researcher.name: Yunzhong He
researcher.headline: Post-training Researcher @ Scale AI, Previously Researcher @ ByteDance Inc.
researcher.bio: Yunzhong He’s Rubrics as rewards uses structured grading criteria as reward signals to train LLMs in domains lacking objective ground truth. He is a researcher at Scale AI and has held positions at Meta and UCLA, focusing on ML, NLP, and robot learning. His work on autonomous systems includes Auto-gpt for online decision making, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on multi-step web tasks. At Meta, he developed Que2search to improve query and document understanding for large-scale social search applications. He also created PRBench, which provides expert rubrics for assessing professional reasoning in high-stakes contexts. His research in robotics includes learning grounded task structures by combining language instructions with visual demonstrations.

researcher.name: Ofir Press
researcher.headline: Researcher @ FAIR, Facebook, Previously Postdoctoral Researcher @ Princeton University
researcher.bio: Ofir Press co-created SWE-bench to test if LLMs can autonomously resolve real-world software issues on GitHub. He is a researcher at Princeton University focusing on DL and NLP. Press developed ALiBi, a positional embedding method that enables Transformers to extrapolate to input lengths longer than those seen during training. He also designed SWE-agent, an agent-computer interface for automated software engineering, and contributed to Bloom, a large-scale open-access multilingual model. His research investigates the compositionality gap in model reasoning and includes methods for scaling data for software agents in SWE-smith.

researcher.name: Jiantao Jiao
researcher.affiliation: Director of Research & Distinguished Scientist, NVIDIA; Professor of EECS and Stat, UC Berkeley
researcher.headline: Director of Research & Distinguished Scientist @ NVIDIA, Assistant Professor, EECS and Stat @ University of California, Berkeley
researcher.bio: Jiantao Jiao’s Theoretically principled trade-off defines a minimax framework for balancing classification accuracy and adversarial robustness in ML models. Jiao is a Professor of EECS and Statistics at UC Berkeley and a Director of Research and Distinguished Scientist at NVIDIA. His research focuses on generative AI and LLMs, specifically RLHF, data curation, and security guardrails against jailbreaking and prompt injection. He introduced Meta-rewarding language models to facilitate self-improving alignment via meta-judgment and established pessimism principles in Bridging offline reinforcement learning and imitation learning. Jiao received his PhD from Stanford University in 2018 and co-founded the startup Nexusflow.

topAffiliation.description: Focused on AI post-training, evaluation, agents, and infrastructure.

researcher.name: Kunle Olukotun
researcher.affiliation: Cadence Design Systems Professor of Computer Science, Stanford University
researcher.headline: Chief Technologist & Co-Founder @ SambaNova Systems, Cadence Design Systems Professor, EE & CS @ Stanford University
researcher.bio: Kunle Olukotun’s Map-reduce for machine learning on multicore adapts the MapReduce model to parallelize ML algorithms for shared-memory multiprocessors. He is the Cadence Design Systems Professor of Computer Science at Stanford University. His research focus includes computer architecture, parallel computing, and programming languages. Olukotun led the development of Niagara, a multithreaded SPARC processor, and the STAMP benchmark suite for transactional memory. He also created Spatial, a programming language and compiler for application accelerators. Olukotun founded Afara Websystems and earned his PhD in computer engineering from the University of Michigan.

topAffiliation.description: Co-founded a machine learning and artificial intelligence company.

researcher.name: Karthik Narasimhan
researcher.headline: Associate Professor, CS @ Princeton University, Previously CS PhD Student @ Massachusetts Institute of Technology
researcher.bio: Karthik Narasimhan is an Associate Professor at Princeton University focusing on NLP, RL, and AI. Narasimhan co-developed GPT, a method that uses transformer-based unsupervised pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning for language understanding. His research into autonomous agents includes Tree of Thoughts for exploring multiple reasoning paths and Reflexion for agent self-correction through verbal RL. He also introduced SWE-bench to evaluate the ability of LLMs to resolve real-world software engineering issues and developed Hierarchical deep reinforcement learning to address tasks with sparse rewards.

researcher.name: Jingbo Shang
researcher.headline: Associate Professor, CSE & HDSI @ University of California, San Diego, Previously CS PhD Student @ University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign
researcher.bio: Jingbo Shang's Text is all you need adapts language representations for sequential recommendation by treating user behaviors as text sequences. papers.title: Foundation4D: Towards a unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles
papers.abstract: We introduce Foundation4D, a unified feed-forward model for geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. A shared backbone uses factorized spatiotemporal attention to efficiently combine observations across cameras and time. Our video inference pipeline uses pose graph optimization to refine camera trajectories and assembles object tracks across input windows. We also develop a data annotation pipeline and release PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips. With benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Foundation4D achieves the lowest depth AbsRel on Waymo and nuScenes, the highest detection mAP on nuScenes, and the highest occupancy mIoU on OpenOccupancy among the compared methods. Our task-combination study shows benefits for both detection and geometry: co-training detection with geometry and occupancy improves top-class mAP by 1.2 points over detection-only training, while co-training geometry with detection reduces camera-to-rig translation error by $13.4\%$ relative to geometry-only training. We further use the predicted geometry and trajectories as priors for lidarless NuRec, supporting reconstruction of driving scenes for simulation.
papers.feed_description: Multi-camera driving video can yield both 3D scene understanding and renderable reconstructions, providing priors for simulation without requiring lidar at inference.

paper_summary.summary: Foundation4D unifies multi-camera video perception and scene reconstruction, predicting depth, camera motion, 3D boxes, semantic occupancy, and renderable Gaussian primitives. Its factorized attention shares across cameras and time, while overlapping windows are assembled with pose-graph optimization and a linear-motion prior. Across 50 clips, this reduces aligned trajectory ATE from 65.55 cm to 31.26 cm, supporting trajectory consistency without resolving long-video drift.

papers.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
papers.abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: this https URL.
papers.feed_description: Language models can learn which parts of long inputs matter, reducing prefill time and memory while preserving task accuracy across diverse benchmarks.

paper_summary.summary: TokenGate reduces long-prompt prefill work by learning which tokens to retain after an intermediate layer, then sending only those tokens through the remaining layers; importance-weighted attention lets task-loss gradients train its discrete selector. On 2WikiMultihopQA with Qwen3-1.7B, it reaches 95% of full-context accuracy with 3.0× faster TTFT and 2.7× less peak prefill memory, in batch-one prefill tests on one A100.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Language models can learn which parts of long inputs matter, reducing prefill time and memory while preserving task accuracy across diverse benchmarks.

papers.title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations
papers.abstract: Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. We study $\textit{action learning}$, the problem of recovering a stochastic action from trajectory observations, yielding a common objective for reasoning about dynamical systems. We introduce $\textbf{LEAP}$ ($\textbf{L}$earned $\textbf{E}$nergy on $\textbf{A}$ction $\textbf{P}$aths), which anchors the unknown action to a tractable reference process and learns the remaining correction by comparing observed trajectories with reference trajectories. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. Once learned, the same action can be flexibly reused for path ranking and inference, mechanism steering, constrained optimization and sampling. Across stochastic physical systems, many-body orbital dynamics and molecular simulations, LEAP recovers underlying dynamics, captures dependencies across time and enables transfer across inference objectives and physical conditions. We show that $\textit{action learning}$ is a promising framework for turning trajectory observations into reusable objectives for scientific inference and control.
papers.feed_description: Learning objectives over complete trajectories lets researchers infer and steer plausible paths from simulation data, even when the underlying dynamics are unknown.

paper_summary.summary: LEAP learns a reusable cost to score trajectories from paths. It contrasts paths with samples from a reference process and combines a path log-ratio with the reference action. On a 31-body orbital benchmark, its model reaches 0.228 NRMSE versus about 1 for local models; molecular tests reuse the action for new requests. These results apply to the tested settings.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Learning objectives over complete trajectories lets researchers infer and steer plausible paths from simulation data, even when the underlying dynamics are unknown.

papers.title: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Language model agents increasingly automate post-training, but when given the full training stack they converge on supervised fine-tuning and spend most effort revising training data. Existing systems give the agent one kind of control, selecting rows from a fixed pool or calling a generator, whereas a human data engineer adjusts proportions, prunes, repairs, replaces and synthesizes the data. We design a data action space for these changes and ask whether an automated system can make the full range rather than one of them, and what structure that requires. We first run this loop with a single agent, and it reaches only one action, adjusting category proportions, while its context fills with execution output and is discarded mid-search. We therefore introduce \textbf{AutoSFT}, a multi-agent system where a meta agent separates execution from analysis, gathers proposals from independent angles, and calls a synthesis subagent for capabilities the pool cannot cover, with the model, the trainer, and the budget fixed within each comparison. Adding each component in turn helps: the executor halves context loss, the analysis subagents lift the best IFEval by $+6.5$, and synthesis adds $+3.4$ IFEval and $+2.9$ IFBench. The same loop transfers to code, where analysis adds $+3.7$ MBPP+ over a single agent that does not improve. Every result comes from runs that retrain from the base model each round, so each component's effect is individually attributable. Our findings suggest that automating SFT data research depends more on covering diverse data actions than on a stronger single action.
papers.feed_description: Multiple analysis perspectives and targeted data synthesis help agents improve fine-tuning data, including instruction-following and coding tasks.

paper_summary.summary: AutoSFT helps an agent improve supervised fine-tuning by changing training data through a structured research loop. A meta-agent selects recipes, while separate execution and analysis agents handle training and propose data changes; synthesis adds verified examples. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, analysis reaches 67.10 on IFEval versus 60.60 within 30 rounds, in single searches per configuration.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Multiple analysis perspectives and targeted data synthesis help agents improve fine-tuning data, including instruction-following and coding tasks.
originalProblem: Automated SFT systems often focus on a narrow set of data operations, such as reweighting a fixed pool, leaving other useful interventions underexplored.
A single agent handling analysis, data changes, training, and evaluation can spend substantial context on execution details and may fail to identify diverse data improvements.
Existing data may lack examples for weak capabilities, while newly generated examples need safeguards against invalidity or evaluation-set overlap.
solution: AutoSFT coordinates an executor, four analysis subagents, a synthesis subagent, and a meta agent that selects the next data recipe.
It supports six data-action families: mixture, pruning, repair, resupervision, synthesis, and ordering; generated examples are checked with verifiers, semantic review, and overlap screening.
Each round trains from the same base checkpoint under a controlled procedure, and stores hypotheses and outcomes to inform later decisions.
keyInsights: Separating job execution from research analysis reduced context compactions and shell-command activity, though this component alone was not shown to improve benchmark scores.
Multiple analytical perspectives broadened the interventions: repair and resupervision made up 55% of actions in the analysis run, unlike the mixture-focused single-agent pilot.
Targeted synthesis can improve capability-level performance, but adding examples is not sufficient for every weakness; one targeted capability remained at zero.
results: With analysis subagents, IFEval reached 67.10% at 30 rounds, versus 60.60% for the single-agent setup at 30 rounds; the single-agent run reached 62.35% after 50 rounds.
Adding synthesis raised best scores from 78.15% to 81.58% on IFEval and from 49.02% to 51.95% on IFBench.
On MBPP+, analysis reached 64.8% by round 13 and synthesis reached 65.8% by round six; the authors report a 3.7-point analysis gain over the single-agent result.

papers.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
papers.abstract: We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.
papers.feed_description: One compact embedding model can represent text, images, audio, video, and mixed inputs, enabling multimodal search and retrieval on resource-constrained devices.

paper_summary.summary: EmbeddingGemma 2 maps text, images, audio, and video into an embedding space for retrieval. Modality encoders turn media into tokens that a transformer pools into a vector; modular configurations omit encoders not needed. On MSEB(Retrieval), native audio scores 69.54 MRR@10 versus 57.59 for ASR/text, but uses more parameters. An intermediate MMEB-v2 ablation improves image and video scores, while visual-document performance remains nearly unchanged.

papers.title: EmbodiedEvo: Self-Evolving Coding Agent For Physical Intelligence
papers.abstract: Coding agents can construct executable programs and revise them through feedback, offering a foundation for embodied control without target-task fine-tuning. Through a programmatic robot interface, the agent observes the scene, executes control programs, and adapts them to the resulting physical state, serving as the closed-loop policy. However, this within-episode adaptation does not automatically preserve experience across scenes. Our trajectory analysis shows that agents spend interaction and inference budgets establishing effective operations and identifying their preconditions, while fresh agents cannot reuse these discoveries. This motivates EmbodiedEvo, a self-evolving coding agent that distills physical feedback into reusable code Skills and diagnostic Lessons. Experience is acquired on one Playground scene per task, then frozen for independent agents in unseen scenes, without updating model weights. On RoboDojo-Sim, EmbodiedEvo achieves an average score of 44.48 and a success rate of 37.82\%, surpassing all officially verified results. Paired tests show the largest gains on memory-dependent tasks and successful reuse of coordinated procedures, while fine contact control remains difficult. Experience from stronger models also improves weaker executors: Astra's experience raises Sol and Luna's success rates by 8.86 and 5.50 percentage points over no experience. Compared with raw interaction history, Skills and Lessons achieve comparable task performance at 53.0\% lower execution cost.
papers.feed_description: Robot agents can carry useful manipulation procedures and failure guidance from one explored scene into unseen scenes, improving task completion without retraining.

paper_summary.summary: EmbodiedEvo lets a robot coding agent preserve experience from one scene as executable Skills and diagnostic Lessons, then transfer them to a fresh agent in another scene. In matched RoboDojo-Sim development tests, Astra/xhigh success rose from 8.50% to 30.17%. Yet full evaluation Precision success was 13.25%, showing that inherited procedures do not ensure successful contact control.

papers.title: RSI-Forge: From Research Papers to Environments for Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Environments are the foundation of recursive self-improvement: they provide the problems agents work on and the feedback used to evaluate progress. Yet constructing challenging research environments with reliable evaluation still depends on domain experts, limiting their scale and disciplinary coverage. We introduce RSI-Forge, a multi-agent pipeline that turns published papers into executable environments for self-improvement. Three agents coordinate construction, reproduction, and review to produce tasks with automated evaluators; each paper's method is independently reimplemented to establish a baseline score. We present 210 environments across 18 fields, including 90 reviewed by independent human domain experts. Both experts and agent judges give high ratings to the potential for improving the provided starting solutions and the evaluators' ability to distinguish solution quality, whereas experts are more critical of shortcut resistance, faithfulness to the source paper, and whether a single idea can exhaust a task. To validate their use for repeated improvement, we evaluate four models over 3 successive attempts on 120 environments, with each attempt inheriting prior code and notes while model weights remain fixed. At least one model improves after the first attempt in 84% of environments. Models also outperform the reproduced paper methods in 68 of the 120 environments, demonstrating room for gains beyond these baselines. Transcript analysis identifies work beyond parameter tuning in 95% of these successful attempts. Analysis of the resulting trajectories shows that models scoring lower on these tasks explore less, more often accept gains smaller than the reported standard error, and rely more heavily on tuning to the development set. RSI-Forge provides a scalable approach to constructing research environments for training and evaluating self-improving agents.
papers.feed_description: RSI-Forge turns published research into executable tasks with automated evaluation, letting researchers test whether agents can improve solutions across diverse fields.

paper_summary.summary: RSI-Forge turns published papers into executable tasks through separate agents that construct, review, and independently reproduce each paper’s method as a baseline. Its corpus contains 210 environments across 18 fields. In 120 environments, at least one model improved score by 0.01 in 84%, and surpassed the reproduced baseline in 68; these are task results, not advances on original research problems.
paper_summary.feedDescription: RSI-Forge turns published research into executable tasks with automated evaluation, letting researchers test whether agents can improve solutions across diverse fields.
originalProblem: Research on iterative self-improvement needs many challenging tasks with reliable evaluators, but building such environments typically demands substantial domain expertise and manual effort.
Scores can be misleading when tasks permit shortcuts, lack held-out evaluation, or do not provide a meaningful baseline for measuring progress.
solution: The authors create a pipeline in which separate agents construct an environment from a paper, independently reproduce its method, and review the task and evaluator, with automated checks and repair rounds.

Each environment provides a bounded-compute objective, starting solution, development data, held-out grading set, and reproduced-paper baseline; solvers can carry code and experiment records across sessions.
keyInsights: Published papers can support a broad corpus of executable research tasks, but producing accepted environments still required a median of 170 million model tokens per environment, and 79% of the main-run environments needed repairs.

Beating a reproduced baseline on an adapted task demonstrates task-level solution improvement, not necessarily scientific progress on the original paper’s problem or improved general research capability.
Expert reviewers were more cautious than agent judges about shortcut resistance, saturation, and fidelity, indicating that automated checks and review do not eliminate the need for expert scrutiny.
results: The corpus contains 210 environments spanning 18 fields; experts reviewed 90 main-run environments and gave an average rubric score of 4.24 out of 5.

In 120 evaluated environments, at least one model improved its normalized score by more than 0.01 after the first session in 84% of tasks, and at least one model surpassed the reproduced baseline in 68 tasks.
After three sessions, median normalized scores were 0.800 for Claude Opus 5, 0.761 for GPT-5.6-sol, 0.647 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and 0.332 for Claude Haiku 4.5.

papers.title: Dino Forcing Flow Models: Do not denoise what you can predict
papers.abstract: Co-denoising pretrained representations such as DINO can substantially improve the training speed and quality of flow matching models, but it introduces a second denoising trajectory and requires carefully designed schedules. We propose a simpler alternative: predict the pretrained representation directly, then condition the model on its own prediction. This removes the need for a second ODE and any representation-specific denoising schedules, while retaining the benefits of representation guidance. Our approach converges substantially faster and achieves better generation quality as measured by FID score. On ImageNet, it outperforms the state of the art in latent space at 2x fewer epochs than prior methods; in pixel space, it improves FID over comparable prior methods by more than 20%. These results support a simple principle: do not denoise what you can predict. Our code is openly available at this https URL.
papers.feed_description: Predicting DINO features to guide image generation removes the need for a second denoising trajectory and helps models converge faster on ImageNet.

paper_summary.summary: DINO Forcing uses a pretrained DINO vision encoder to guide image generation without separately denoising a feature stream. From a noisy image, it predicts DINO features and reuses them as conditioning, with feature alignment during training. On ImageNet, it reports unguided FID 2.47 after 100 latent-space epochs and 5.53 after 200 pixel-space epochs; these comparisons are benchmark-specific, not wall-clock evidence.

papers.title: Jeva: System One Models from First Principles
papers.abstract: System one models like Jev enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent open-source practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations against Jev and open source models, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.
papers.feed_description: Jeva lets decision models reuse candidate representations across changing requests while preserving choices under reordering and explicitly recognizing when no option applies.

paper_summary.summary: Jeva makes typed decisions over requests and reusable candidate sets, including choices, Boolean judgments, and numeric scores. It encodes options separately, then lets each request representation read the full set before scoring, while caching option computations. On MLDR, hybrid caching reduced median latency from 2,102.0 ms to 75.1 ms for novel sets, with no decision changes in tested cache conditions.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Jeva lets decision models reuse candidate representations across changing requests while preserving choices under reordering and explicitly recognizing when no option applies.

papers.title: Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models
papers.abstract: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.
papers.feed_description: Strong performance on visible scenes does not guarantee that visual models retain objects beyond view, predict spatial changes, or guide actions reliably.

paper_summary.summary: The authors evaluate ten frozen visual representations for whether small probes can read visible scene structure, retain objects after they leave view, predict spatial updates under camera motion, and select goal-directed actions. VideoMAE’s out-of-view bearing error is 36.45°, versus DINOv2’s 65.38°, despite DINOv2’s stronger visible-scene readouts. These offline tests do not establish online memory or reliable robot behavior.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Strong performance on visible scenes does not guarantee that visual models retain objects beyond view, predict spatial changes, or guide actions reliably.

papers.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
papers.abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
papers.feed_description: This survey maps video understanding, generation, and interactive simulation into one framework, helping researchers compare what models infer, create, and control.

paper_summary.summary: The authors survey video understanding, generation, unified models, and video world models through how they relate observations to an evolving world. They distinguish reading, writing, sharing, and interacting, and classify models by prediction space and control timing. Their framework separates temporal smoothness from world consistency; it organizes evaluation, but does not show that current models preserve state or support decisions.

papers.title: DuoDiscover: Scaling Autonomous Discovery Beyond the Evaluation Bottleneck
papers.abstract: Evaluation has been central to advances in AI, and it is equally critical to autonomous discovery. Yet scaling autonomous discovery to real-world engineering challenges faces a fundamental bottleneck: the cost of evaluating progress. In real settings, a single true evaluation, such as a full benchmark or serving trace, can take hours, so a search can afford only a handful of true evaluations. We present DuoDiscover, a search system that jointly discovers what to optimize and how to evaluate progress efficiently, through three mechanisms. First, each worker in a fleet of coding agents co-discovers an optimization target and a fast, tailored proxy evaluator, which we call a yardstick. The agent then hill-climbs the yardstick rather than the true evaluation. Second, since search can exploit gaps between a yardstick and the true objective, fidelity tests continually recheck each yardstick's ranking and invalidate any that drift. Third, the fleet is bottom-up, with no central decomposition of the problem. A lightweight orchestrator spawns and terminates agents, briefs running ones, and seeds new agents with others' confirmed work. DuoDiscover enables autonomous optimization from software to chip architecture. We demonstrate DuoDiscover on two repository-level benchmarks and four GPU and TPU kernel suites covering hundreds of kernels. On SWE-fficiency, it doubles the average speedup of human experts. On SOL-Exec, it ranks first on 121 of 235 kernels and in the top three on 212. On the heavily optimized vLLM and SQLite engines, DuoDiscover achieves 1.92$\times$ and 1.38$\times$ gains over the base code. On a CPU microarchitecture optimization task with evaluations of up to 28 hours, DuoDiscover surpasses both AlphaEvolve-based ArchAgent v2 and the best human design, with 1.65$\times$ ArchAgent v2's gain in 16.7 days versus more than 40 days, advancing the frontier of autonomous chip design.
papers.feed_description: Coding agents can discover fast, task-specific checks to guide optimization, helping them improve software and chip designs when full evaluations take hours.

paper_summary.summary: DuoDiscover searches for code regions to optimize while building a target-specific, inexpensive evaluator for ranking edits. Workers explore with these yardsticks, test their rankings against full evaluations, and use full evaluations to confirm gains. In a 20-hour, four-agent vLLM comparison, it achieved a 1.92× geometric-mean gain versus 1.07× for Claude Code, a result limited to this setup.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Coding agents can discover fast, task-specific checks to guide optimization, helping them improve software and chip designs when full evaluations take hours.
originalProblem: Autonomous code-optimization agents can test only a few candidates when each full benchmark or simulation takes minutes or hours.
Search must decide both which part of a system to optimize and how to measure local progress cheaply; an unreliable proxy can reward changes that do not improve the actual objective.
Fixed or unchecked proxy metrics may become misleading as optimization proceeds, while manually decomposing tasks limits automation.
solution: DuoDiscover assigns independent LLM coding agents to choose target code regions and create fast “yardsticks,” such as reduced workloads, profiling harnesses, or static cost estimates, for ranking edits.

Agents use yardsticks for rapid local search, while an orchestrator periodically runs the full evaluation and tests proxy rankings for agreement using Kendall’s rank correlation and a statistical test.
A yardstick that loses fidelity is invalidated, and every claimed improvement must be confirmed using the true objective; the orchestrator also coordinates, briefs, and combines agents’ work.
keyInsights: Proxy evaluation can substantially expand the search budget: in sampled tasks, yardsticks ran a median 53× faster than full kernel evaluations and 22× faster than repository evaluations.
Proxy quality is not stable. The system later invalidated 45% of validated kernel yardsticks and 41% of validated repository yardsticks, making repeated fidelity checks central to reliable search.

The approach applies across software repositories, GPU and TPU kernels, serving systems, and CPU architecture, but its advantage depends on finding a useful proxy and can be offset by setup overhead in short searches.
results: On 25 FormulaCode tasks, DuoDiscover achieved a 2.156× geometric-mean speedup over base code, versus 1.778× for Claude Code; on 100 SWE-fficiency tasks, it reached 15.02× versus 12.81× for Claude Code.

On SOL-Exec, it recorded a mean 79.74% speed-of-light score and ranked first on 121 of 235 kernels in the reported leaderboard snapshot. It also reported 4.62× over XLA on JAXBench and 2.68× over optimized Pallas kernels on TPU-Inference.

In real-world evaluations, reported gains included 1.92× across four vLLM serving objectives and a 6.31% performance improvement for the CPU prefetcher design task. These findings span different tasks and evaluation settings, and some comparisons rely on external baselines or leaderboard snapshots.

papers.title: Few-Step Generation via Data-Space Iteration
papers.abstract: Flow matching has emerged as a scalable paradigm for training high-quality generative models, but sampling from the learned probability flow requires many network evaluations. Distillation can reduce this cost to one or a few evaluations; however, one-step generation often sacrifices quality, making few-step generation the practical operating regime. Existing few-step methods perform their iterative computation along the probability flow and therefore require a fixed, manually chosen timestep discretization. This discretization is often chosen heuristically and is expensive to tune; it may also be restrictive when refinement difficulty differs across samples or spatial locations. We introduce data-space iteration, a few-step generation framework that removes flow discretization altogether. Starting from noise, a shared generator directly refines its prediction in data space, with every iteration trained to produce the best sample permitted by its capacity. Our formulation integrates with distribution matching distillation (DMD) with minimal changes, enabling a controlled comparison between iteration methods under matched training settings. On class-conditional ImageNet 256x256, data-space iteration outperforms standard discretization baselines and matches or improves upon variants selected through schedule search, without requiring schedule-specific training. These results show that data-space iteration provides a simple and effective alternative to discretized flow-space iteration for fast generation.
papers.feed_description: Refining image predictions directly lets few-step generators avoid fixed sampling schedules while matching or surpassing schedule-tuned alternatives on ImageNet.

paper_summary.summary: The authors introduce data-space iteration for few-step image generation, passing a draft between calls while retaining the original noise input instead of following a preset generation-time noise schedule. The method keeps DMD self-rollout training, which still uses noise time. On guided class-conditional ImageNet 256×256 at four NFE, it reports FID 2.29 versus 2.37 for the best of three flow-map schedules.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Refining image predictions directly lets few-step generators avoid fixed sampling schedules while matching or surpassing schedule-tuned alternatives on ImageNet.
originalProblem: Few-step generators reduce the cost of sampling from flow models, but quality depends on how the probability-flow trajectory is divided into discrete time intervals.
In self-rollout training, the chosen schedule affects the states seen during training, so testing alternative schedules can require training additional generators.
A shared flow-time schedule may not be well suited to the differing refinement needs of samples or image regions.
solution: Iteratively refine a data-space estimate from an initial noise input, using a shared generator conditioned on the original noise and refinement index; no intermediate flow states or re-noising steps are used.
Train the generator within a distribution matching distillation setup using frozen real and auxiliary fake flow models, while retaining self-rollout training.
Adapt a pretrained SiT velocity network with an added projection for the current estimate and an embedding for the refinement index; the flow-time input is fixed during this rollout.
keyInsights: Changing the rollout space removes flow-time discretization from the sampling path, though the number of evaluations and refinement-index conditioning remain design choices.
On the reported ImageNet experiments, data-space iteration generally improved FID over uniform-schedule flow-renoise and was competitive with schedule-searched flow-map generation.
FID gains did not imply improvement on every metric: data-space DMD had higher recall but lower precision than DMD in the reported four-evaluation comparisons.
results: Without classifier-free guidance, data-space DMD reached FID 3.85, 2.68, 2.47, and 2.46 at one to four evaluations; uniform flow-renoise scored 4.45, 3.22, 2.67, and 2.75.

With the tested guidance configuration, data-space DMD reached FID 3.31, 2.47, 2.33, and 2.29; at four evaluations, flow-map scored 2.86 with its uniform schedule and 2.37 with its best tested schedule.
A CIFAR-10 experiment also favored data-space DMD over DMD at two to four evaluations, but not at one evaluation; the main evidence is limited to the tested image-generation settings.

papers.title: Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly ship with explicit "thinking modes", yet their counterpart, "no-thinking", has received far less attention. We study LLMs' no-thinking behavior along two axes. a. How to measure no-thinking? Prior work typically defines no-thinking through proxies such as a disabled thinking mode or the absence of long traces. These proxies are unreliable: disabled thinking modes may still emit reasoning, while long traces may contain filler rather than genuine inference. We instead normalize each response into a pre-answer trace and final answer, and evaluate it at three levels: (i) Empty-Thinking Rate for strict answer-only compliance; (ii) instruction-aware Question-Pre-answer Relevance for similarity between the question and pre-answer trace; and (iii) LLM-as-judge Explicit Inference Rate for visible explicit inference. Together, these metrics distinguish answer-only output, relevant but non-inferential text, and explicit inference. b. How does no-thinking vary across tasks and models? We evaluate six prompting interventions on six LLMs across Boolean, multiple-choice, and open-ended questions. We find that explicit no-think controls cannot reliably eliminate visible inference. Models instead exhibit "Thinking Inertia": explicit inference persists even under strict controls and becomes more prevalent as the answer space opens. Accuracy remains stable on Boolean and multiple-choice tasks, whereas open-ended tasks reveal a trade-off between answer-only compliance and task accuracy. Rewriting the same questions across answer spaces shows that supplying candidate answers makes answer-only responses easier to produce. These findings establish no-thinking as a non-trivial capability: stopping explicit reasoning cannot be assumed from model settings or instructions alone and deserves systematic evaluation alongside reasoning ability.
papers.feed_description: LLMs often continue showing explicit reasoning despite no-thinking instructions, especially on open-ended questions, and strict answer-only prompts can reduce accuracy.

paper_summary.summary: The study measures whether models show visible inference before answering when instructed not to think. It separates answer-only compliance, question relevance, and explicit inference, then compares answer formats on matched questions. For Qwen3-32B, open-ended responses had 0% answer-only compliance and 90.14% visible inference, versus 62.5% and 36.90% for Boolean verification; this concerns output, not hidden computation.
