papers.title: TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) routing distributes inference work across different models, advancing the cost-quality Pareto frontier of LLM serving. While coarse-grained routing at the session or query level has been widely adopted in production systems, recent algorithmic work shows that fine-grained token-level routing can yield substantial efficiency and quality gains. However, efficiently serving token-level routed inference poses significant challenges to existing systems. Built on single-LLM assumptions, current systems suffer from severe step desynchronization and frequent batch admission delays under token-level routing, and they also impose high implementation complexity on developers. To address these challenges, we design TokenRouter, an efficient and developer-friendly serving system for token-level routed LLM inference. TokenRouter follows the principle of request-centric programming, model-centric execution: developers describe routing logic from the perspective of a single request, while the runtime launches a subserver for each LLM and dispatches requests asynchronously. Each subserver employs a delayed-batching scheduler, whose optimal hyperparameters are derived from a mathematical throughput model of the system. Across diverse routing algorithms, workloads, and model pairs, TokenRouter achieves 2.01-64.15x higher decoding throughput than existing systems, substantially advancing the serving efficiency of token-level LLM routing. Our code is available at this https URL.
papers.feed_description: TokenRouter lets developers serve token-by-token model routing through a simple interface, while its runtime coordinates models asynchronously to improve decoding throughput.

paper_summary.summary: TokenRouter serves inference with per-token routing between language models, using asynchronous subservers and delayed batch admission. Developers define routing and state handoffs; each model server buffers arrivals and uses a throughput model to select a threshold. On R2R’s AIME setup at concurrency 4, it reports 244.56 generated tokens/s versus 89.62 for official R2R, a serving-efficiency result under routing assumptions.
paper_summary.feedDescription: TokenRouter lets developers serve token-by-token model routing through a simple interface, while its runtime coordinates models asynchronously to improve decoding throughput.
originalProblem: Most LLM serving systems assume a request stays on one model, making token-level routing difficult to run efficiently.
Different model speeds and irregular handoffs cause synchronization stalls, delayed batch admission, and extra cache-management work.
Implementing and comparing routing policies often requires modifying complex scheduler and serving infrastructure.
solution: Provides a route/send/receive interface that lets developers define per-request model handoffs while the runtime handles scheduling and message transfer.
Runs each model in an independent asynchronous subserver, allowing other requests to progress during handoffs and preserving serving state when requests return.
Uses delayed batching and a throughput model to select batch-admission thresholds; adds optimizations including CUDA graphs and automatic KV-cache allocation.
keyInsights: Token-level routing efficiency depends not only on the routing policy but also on how serving handles model switches, batching, and cache state.
Asynchronous execution removes cross-model waiting, while delayed batching can rebuild larger model-local batches from irregular arrivals.
Scheduling gains are most pronounced under concurrency; the reported scheduling components did not improve throughput in the concurrency-one ablation.
results: Across 15 algorithm–workload combinations at concurrency four, TokenRouter achieved 2.01–64.15× the throughput of the stronger baseline and 2.03–63.64× lower latency than standard serving.
In an ablation at concurrency eight, throughput rose from 132.78 tokens/s with CUDA-graph optimizations to 296.86 with asynchronous execution, then to 372.48 with delayed batching.

Across tested routing algorithms and model configurations, the system improved throughput over official implementations; performance was also reported across different model pairs and cross-node settings, though the evaluation centers on one GPU platform and model family.

papers.title: Evo$^2$: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution
papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are increasingly used to improve language model systems without human intervention through either weight updates or harness improvements. Existing approaches typically pursue these directions separately: some methods update model weights using self-generated experience, while others rewrite the harness that defines how an agent uses prompts, tools, context, and execution feedback. However, these approaches overlook the relationship between model weights and the agent harness. To connect these processes and ensure effective and smooth agent self-evolving, we propose Evo$^2$, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. For harness updates, we design a unified dual-role pipeline that a single policy serves as both a Proposer, which writes harness edits, and a Reflector, which diagnoses their effects and guides revision. For weight updates, harness modifications and their execution outcomes guide the training of both the Proposer and the Reflector. We further develop EvoTIDE, a training pipeline that recovers usable trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, then combines SFT with interleaved GRPO across the two roles. Extensive experiments across three coding benchmarks demonstrate that Evo$^2$ significantly outperforms existing self-evolution methods. It achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, compared with 62.6% and 41.0% for the strongest baseline, respectively. We also show that the evolved harnesses transfer to different tasks without further evolution and rank first in cross-benchmark evaluations. Our dual-role harness improvement framework is also able to extend to self-evolution with proprietary models, improving a GPT-5-mini agent's performance from 24.4% to 48.3%. These results demonstrate the applicability of the framework Evo$^2$ across domains and its broad transferability across models and tasks.
papers.feed_description: Agents that learn from their own software changes can improve both their coding and memory performance, while carrying useful changes to new tasks.

paper_summary.summary: Evo² connects harness evolution with model training: one shared policy proposes and assesses harness edits, while evaluated outcomes train later searches. With the task executor fixed, its held-out Qwen3.8-27B Polyglot pass@1 is 82.1%, versus 62.6% for GEA. A controlled comparison reports 78.0% for the trained evolver versus 61.8% untrained, a 16.3-point gain; this supports a training contribution, not its sole responsibility for gains.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Agents that learn from their own software changes can improve both their coding and memory performance, while carrying useful changes to new tasks.
originalProblem: Agent improvement often focuses either on training model weights or editing the harness that directs a model, leaving the two sources of improvement largely disconnected.
Harness edits can be invalid or incomplete, and useful strategies discovered in one search branch may not be reused in another.
It is unclear whether harness improvements generalize across tasks, work with fixed-weight models, or extend beyond coding.
solution: Evo² co-evolves harnesses and a shared model policy that acts as both Proposer, making edits, and Reflector, assessing outcomes and directing revisions or crossovers.
Its tree-based search records candidate harnesses and evaluations, while a strategy library lets the Reflector transfer mechanisms between branches.
EvoTIDE trains the shared policy with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on search outcomes, recovering usable edits from incomplete rollouts and rewarding changes tied to task performance.
keyInsights: Harness search can supply training experience for the agent that conducts the search, allowing workflow improvements and policy improvements to reinforce each other.
A shared policy for proposing and reviewing edits can use evaluation results and execution traces to decide whether to revise, combine, or retain a candidate.
Some harness changes transfer across benchmarks and domains, but results remain dependent on the evaluated tasks and the reliability of their metrics.
results: With Qwen3.8-27B, Evo² scored 82.1% pass@1 on Polyglot, 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, and 58.0% on LiveCodeBench; it ranked first in five of six reported cross-benchmark transfer directions.

On a 60-task SWE-bench Verified subset with fixed-weight models, Evo² achieved 48.3% with GPT-5-mini and 47.8% with Claude Haiku 4.5; on memory benchmarks it scored 60.4 F1 on LoCoMo and 71.5% accuracy on LongMemEval-S.

Ablations reported improvements from training the evolver of 16.3 points on Polyglot and 9.3 points on LoCoMo, with a further 4.1-point Polyglot gain attributed to crossover. The SWE-bench ablation gain was 5.0 points but had weaker statistical evidence (p=.086).

papers.title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.
papers.feed_description: Tests of self-evolving agents reveal that adapting to new tasks often disrupts earlier skills, exposing a key limitation for long-running deployments.

paper_summary.summary: The authors test whether self-evolving agents can learn task streams while retaining earlier skills, using three harness-update methods around a frozen model. GEPA and Meta-Harness change shared harness components, while ReasoningBank retrieves stored experiences. Across four constructed streams, aggregate performance improves in most settings, but greater plasticity is associated with lower stability; topic drift yields near-zero or negative gains.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Tests of self-evolving agents reveal that adapting to new tasks often disrupts earlier skills, exposing a key limitation for long-running deployments.
originalProblem: Self-evolving agents are often tested on relatively stable, single-domain tasks, leaving open whether they can adapt across changing tasks while retaining earlier capabilities.
Shared prompt and memory updates may help the current task but harm other tasks, and final benchmark scores can conceal that interference or forgetting.
Frequent weight updates can be costly, motivating evaluation of nonparametric adaptation that changes an agent’s harness while keeping its underlying model fixed.
solution: The authors evaluate three harness-update approaches—ReasoningBank’s retrieved memories, GEPA’s rewritten strategy prompt, and Meta-Harness’s persistent workspace edits—using the same fixed model.
They test the methods on four streams with topic, workflow, domain, and compound distribution shifts, using a shared harness without task labels or announced block boundaries.
They measure aggregate performance alongside plasticity on the current task group and stability on other groups, separating learning gains from interference and forgetting.
keyInsights: Self-evolution can improve average performance while still degrading performance on previously learned or not-yet-seen task groups; stronger within-group learning was associated with larger stability losses.
Shared instructions can generalize a task-specific rule too broadly, while retrieval can surface a memory that is topically similar but prescribes the wrong workflow.
Topic similarity alone is insufficient to decide whether an experience applies: BFCL-Miss and BFCL-Base had highly similar query embeddings despite requiring conflicting clarification behavior.
results: Across four streams, ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness achieved mean terminal advantages of +2.5, +3.7, and +1.4 percentage points, respectively; GEPA also had the highest plasticity (+6.2 pp.) and largest stability loss (−4.3 pp.).
Plasticity and stability were negatively correlated across the 12 method-by-scenario comparisons (r = −0.72, p = 0.008); topic drift produced near-zero or slightly negative net changes overall.

In compound drift, BIRD-derived exploratory instructions reduced pre-training BFCL-Miss accuracy by 6.8 pp. with GEPA and 4.8 pp. with Meta-Harness. In workflow and compound streams, 52% of BFCL-Miss episodes retrieved BFCL-Base memories, illustrating retrieval collisions between incompatible workflows.

papers.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents can handle increasingly complex tasks, navigating long trajectories of observations and actions. As these trajectories grow, key-value (KV) cache I/O and storage become the dominant cost. Trajectories can also exceed the LLM's maximum context length, requiring control over active cache growth. Prior work uses context engineering to reduce cache size by trimming or summarizing history. However, modifying the trajectory prefix invalidates subsequent cached states and triggers costly re-prefilling of retained context. Task accuracy can also suffer when too little context is retained to limit re-prefill costs. We propose cache engineering as a new scheme. It allows agents to directly control their active KV cache without modifying the trajectory or re-prefilling retained context. Specifically, agents can proactively use drop to exclude selected cache from future attention and repos to adjust retained keys' position encodings. We formalize these cache operations and identify history dependence as a serving challenge: identical token sequences can yield different cache states under different cache operation sequences, making prefix matching insufficient for correct cache reuse. Thus, we co-design the AKV serving engine. It provides a stateless interface compatible with existing serving APIs, while internally managing stateful cache reuse, eviction, and restoration. Experiments show that a tool-response rolling-drop cache policy improves average benchmark scores by 1.7 points and reduces average cost by 27.7%, compared with conventional threshold-triggered summarization. With AKV, it achieves up to 1.2x the output throughput and a 1.5x speedup in P95 request latency. Recursive self-improvement of cache policies further reduces cost by 7.1% over expert design. Our code is at this https URL.
papers.feed_description: Agents can discard old tool results from attention without rewriting history or recomputing retained context, reducing inference costs while preserving task performance.

paper_summary.summary: AKV lets agents manage active key–value cache states without changing message histories. It drops selected states from future attention and reuses compatible retained states, avoiding some recomputation. Across three models and four benchmarks, it reports a 1.7-point average pass-rate gain and 27.7% lower estimated API-equivalent cost than threshold-triggered summarization, with results limited to evaluated settings.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Agents can discard old tool results from attention without rewriting history or recomputing retained context, reducing inference costs while preserving task performance.
originalProblem: Long-running agents accumulate large KV caches, increasing memory use, attention work, and inference cost while potentially reaching context or position limits.
Text summarization and trimming reduce prompt length but can discard useful information and invalidate cached states for the retained history, causing repeated prefill computation.
Existing cache optimizations often rely on system-level signals and do not directly let an agent specify which prior states should remain available for future attention.
solution: The paper defines cache operations—append, drop, and reposition—that modify the active cache while leaving the agent’s logical text trajectory intact.
AKV, built on SGLang, tracks cache-operation history in an extended radix tree so it can distinguish computationally different cache states, reuse matching states, and restore evicted states.
Its main policy retains reasoning and recent tool responses while dropping older tool-response cache; repositioning updates retained keys’ positional encodings and resets positions for later tokens.
keyInsights: A cache state is determined not only by its retained tokens and positions, but also by which earlier entries were visible when those tokens were computed; token-prefix matching alone is therefore insufficient for safe reuse.
Older tool-response cache can be dropped while retaining reasoning cache: reported ablations favored this strategy over dropping reasoning or both categories.
Dropping entries does not reset position indices. Repositioning addresses position limits, and on a reported BrowseComp-Plus subset raised the tool-drop policy score from 55% to 62%.
results: Across MiniMax-M2.7, GPT-OSS-120B, and MiroThinker-1.7-Mini on four benchmarks, AKV averaged 1.7 percentage points higher scores and 27.7% lower estimated cost than the standard summarization baseline; cost was 21.9% lower than with lower-threshold text engineering.

In GPT-OSS-120B serving tests on eight NVIDIA A800 GPUs, AKV’s P95 latency was 1.51× lower and output throughput 1.18× higher than Standard at the compared peak-throughput settings. At the same batch size, full-attention time fell by 59.8% and total decode-step time by 16.0%.

Automated policy refinement reported cost reductions of 15.6% and 17.8% versus Standard while maintaining its accuracy for policies from two search iterations; results varied across models and benchmarks.

papers.title: Measure Equivalence as a Guide for Learning SPDE Priors from Replicated Fields
papers.abstract: Learning a Gaussian prior from replicated spatial fields requires deciding not only how much flexibility to add to a reference model, but where it belongs: as a correction to the reference covariance, or as a change to the differential operator that defines it. Gaussian-measure equivalence theory separates these cases in the continuum, but on any fixed discretization all nondegenerate Gaussians are equivalent, so the distinction can only be seen under mesh refinement. We study this in a leaky-aquifer SPDE where uncertain pumping, spatially varying leakage, and heterogeneous conductivity enter through the source, a lower-order term, and the principal part of the operator. Only the last changes the measure class. From 200 replicated fields whitened against a fitted reference, a diagonal refinement statistic decays to zero for source and leakage departures but stays at the plateau (≈ 0.061) predicted for a conductivity lens. Models of the wrong class fail in characteristic ways. A stationary model absorbs source variability by driving its range to infinity (b𝜅 ≈ 3 × 10\u207b\u2075 against a true 𝜅\u2080 = 6), and correction-only models fitting a conductivity change incur a KL cost that grows linearly with resolution, so reference-based complexity measures become discretization dependent. A combined model that adapts the principal operator and learns a finite-rank source correction recovers b𝜅 = 6.08 on the source-only population and separates the conductivity field from the source subspace when both are present. Replicated data can therefore decide whether to correct a Gaussian reference or change its operator; deciding wrongly yields a well-fitting but structurally incorrect model.
papers.feed_description: Replicated spatial fields can reveal when a Gaussian prior needs a different underlying operator, rather than merely a flexible covariance correction.

paper_summary.summary: The authors develop a refinement diagnostic to distinguish whether replicated fields call for changing the generating operator or adding a covariance correction. It whitens fields against a reference and tracks residual variance as grids refine. In synthetic experiments, a conductivity lens retains a statistic near its 0.060732 plateau, while deflated source-only energy declines; the method is not tested on aquifer data.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Replicated spatial fields can reveal when a Gaussian prior needs a different underlying operator, rather than merely a flexible covariance correction.

papers.title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
papers.abstract: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.
papers.feed_description: Live competition reveals whether cybersecurity agents can adapt as opponents patch attacks between rounds, exposing gaps static, single-role tests miss.

paper_summary.summary: CyberArena tests agents in live contests: each attacks an opponent’s service while patching its own. Across three rounds, services change and objectives rotate. In solo play, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 4.8, and GLM-5.3 each solved 30 of 40 challenges; their round-three capture rates in contests were 52%, 37%, and 35%. This separates the agents, but does not isolate patching as the cause.

papers.title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
papers.abstract: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.
papers.feed_description: Training lets looped language models reuse one recurrence’s attention cache across others, keeping cache memory constant as depth grows without sacrificing quality.

paper_summary.summary: The authors introduce BeNice!, a fine-tuning method that trains looped language models to use the final recurrence’s key–value cache in earlier recurrences, reducing cache storage without removing recurrent computation. On a 770M model, shared-cache validation perplexity is 11.86 versus 21.61 after standard finetuning. Simulated serving shows 23.6% higher throughput at 2 requests per second; at low load, performance matches baseline.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Training lets looped language models reuse one recurrence’s attention cache across others, keeping cache memory constant as depth grows without sacrificing quality.

papers.title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.
papers.feed_description: Branching agent rollouts let language models learn which interaction turns help, while bounded targets keep updates stable across sequential training batches.

paper_summary.summary: TreeOPSD trains long-horizon agents by branching continuations from shared histories, backing up verifier rewards into turn-level credits, and converting credits into bounded targets for policy updates. On Deep Research, it reaches a 21.20 exact-match average, versus 17.59 for TreePO, which uses the trees and credits but fixed-credit updates. This comparison covers the reported setup, not general convergence guarantees.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Branching agent rollouts let language models learn which interaction turns help, while bounded targets keep updates stable across sequential training batches.
originalProblem: Terminal-only rewards provide weak guidance about which intermediate turns helped or hurt an agent’s eventual outcome, making credit assignment difficult over long interactions.
During sequential mini-batch training, the policy changes while rollouts remain fixed, so applying the same advantages throughout can continue pushing updates past an appropriate target.
Critics, process-level labels, and external teachers can add training complexity, annotation needs, or inference cost.
solution: Sample alternative continuations from shared interaction prefixes, then back up verifier-based trajectory advantages through the resulting tree to estimate turn-level credits.
Convert each turn’s credit into a bounded Bernoulli target relative to the frozen behavior policy, using a length-normalized log-likelihood ratio to measure policy change.
Repeatedly minimize Forward KL from these fixed targets to the current policy, so updates weaken at the target and can reverse after overshooting.
keyInsights: Tree-based branching supplies intermediate credit from terminal outcomes, while shared prefixes are scored once rather than counted repeatedly for every descendant trajectory.
The distillation update matches the tree policy-gradient direction at the behavior policy but has a finite destination as the student changes across optimizer blocks.
Pointwise credits and the affine target mapping performed better than the tested listwise-credit and logistic-mapping alternatives; the findings remain tied to the sampled trees and verifier rewards.
results: On Multi-Hop QA, Qwen3-4B scored 44.13 on average, versus 43.37 for GRPO and 43.40 for TreePO; Qwen3-30B-A3B scored 45.93, versus 44.80 and 45.05, respectively.
On Deep Research, Qwen3-4B scored 15.45 on average, versus 12.18 for GRPO and 13.07 for TreePO; at 30B-A3B, it scored 21.20, 4.97 points above GRPO’s 16.23.

Additional evaluations on smaller Qwen3 and Llama models, five-seed comparisons, and open-web benchmarks generally supported the approach, though results varied across benchmarks and the experiments cover a limited set of tasks and model families.

researcher.name: Cheems Wang
researcher.headline: Research Fellow, Department of Automation @ Tsinghua University, Previously ML PhD Student @ University of Amsterdam
researcher.bio:
Dr. Cheems Wang is a Research Fellow at Tsinghua University, where he works closely with Prof. Xiangyang Ji, and an adjunct associate professor in mathematics. He obtained his Ph.D. in machine learning from the University of Amsterdam, where he worked in the Amsterdam Machine Learning Lab (AMLab) under the supervision of Prof. Max Welling and Prof. Herke van Hoof.

His research studies the learning paradigms that let large models adapt: meta-learning, multi-task learning and reinforcement learning. The thread through his work is fast adaptation with reliable uncertainty, from neural processes and Bayesian meta-learning during his Ph.D. to task sampling and efficient RL post-training of large reasoning models today.

He has published more than 40 top-tier conference and journal papers, plus articles in Nature Communications, IEEE T-PAMI and Science China Information Sciences; 8 were selected as orals or spotlights. The result he is proudest of since leaving AMLab, the birthplace of the VAE, is Model Predictive Task Sampling, in which a small generative model steers the optimization of large ones. It is published in Nature Communications and the code is on GitHub.

Mao is an Automation PhD student at Tsinghua University and a research intern with the Qwen team at Alibaba Tongyi Lab. Their research focuses on RL and LLM reasoning, specifically developing efficient decision-making algorithms and agentic post-training methods. Within the THU-IDM team, they co-created Latent Reward, a symbolic framework that uses LLMs to improve credit assignment in episodic RL. Mao also introduced Supported value regularization for offline RL to provide theoretically grounded value estimation. They previously earned a BA in Physics from the Zhiyuan Honor College at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. Mao’s recent work includes developing Group Prioritized Off-Policy Optimization to improve the reasoning performance of LLMs using fewer training rollouts.

papers.title: DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain a hidden forward--reverse consistency force that joint positive--negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce DiffusionART (Diffusion Reinforcement with Aggregation-First Reward Tilting), which aggregates each prompt's rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 times fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards.
papers.feed_description: Diffusion models can be fine-tuned with black-box rewards for image and video quality without task-specific stability tuning, using far fewer GPU hours in video experiments.

paper_summary.summary: DiffusionART improves text-to-video generators using output-level rewards. It pools prompt rewards and outputs into a shared direction, applies it to reverse-denoising states, and restores predictions according to their drift. On HunyuanVideo-13B under equal weighting of visual- and motion-quality rewards, final-50-step mean reward is 13.018, versus 10.105 for DiffusionNFT and 8.510 for Flow-GRPO-Fast; GPU-hour gains apply to this experiment.
paper_summary.feedDescription: Diffusion models can be fine-tuned with black-box rewards for image and video quality without task-specific stability tuning, using far fewer GPU hours in video experiments.

researcher.bio: Yang You’s Open-Sora generates video content through an efficient, open-source implementation of diffusion transformer models. He is a Presidential Young Professor at the National University of Singapore, where he directs the HPC-AI Lab. His research integrates ML infrastructure with HPC to increase the speed and scalability of large-scale model training. You is also known for LAMB, an optimizer that utilizes large batch sizes to reduce the training time of models like BERT. He developed Colossal-AI to provide a unified framework for distributed parallel training and inference across diverse hardware. His other contributions include LARS for convolutional networks and sequence parallelism methods for handling long-context LLMs.
